NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Visual Field D:
What & why
Visual field defects = loss of part of the visual field, produced by lesions anywhere along the visual pathway — from the retina to the occipital cortex.
The core concept: the pathway is arranged so the site of the lesion produces a characteristic, predictable field defect — so the defect localises the lesion. The single organising principle is the optic chiasm: lesions BEFORE the chiasm affect one eye (monocular); AT the chiasm affect both temporal fields (bitemporal); AFTER the chiasm affect the same side of both eyes (homonymous). One of the highest-yield clinical applications of neuroanatomy.
The visual pathway
  • Retina → optic nerve (one eye) → OPTIC CHIASM → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) → optic radiations (temporal = Meyer's loop; parietal) → occipital (visual) cortex.
  • The crossing rule: at the optic chiasm, fibres from the NASAL retina (which see the TEMPORAL field) CROSS to the other side; the temporal retinal fibres stay uncrossed → so after the chiasm each optic tract carries the same half of the visual field from BOTH eyes → a post-chiasmal lesion gives a homonymous defect.
The before / at / after framework: before chiasm (optic nerve) → monocular loss; at chiasm → bitemporal loss (crossing nasal fibres); after chiasm → homonymous loss (contralateral field of both eyes).
The decisive fork: where along the pathway?
Lesion siteField defectCause
Optic nerve (before chiasm)monocular vision loss (that whole eye)optic neuritis (multiple sclerosis), ischaemia, glaucoma
Optic CHIASMBITEMPORAL hemianopiapituitary tumour, craniopharyngioma (§5)
Optic TRACThomonymous hemianopia (contralateral) — "left homonymous hemianopia = RIGHT optic tract lesion"stroke, tumour
Optic radiation — TEMPORAL (Meyer's loop)contralateral SUPERIOR homonymous quadrantanopiatemporal lobe lesion (stroke, tumour)
Optic radiation — PARIETALcontralateral INFERIOR homonymous quadrantanopiaparietal lobe lesion
Occipital cortexhomonymous hemianopia with MACULAR SPARINGPCA stroke
The PITS rule for quadrantanopias
Homonymous quadrantanopia = contralateral PITS: Parietal = Inferior defect; Temporal (Meyer's loop) = Superior defect.
  • The logic: the temporal fibres (Meyer's loop) loop down and forward through the temporal lobe and carry the superior field → temporal lesion → superior quadrantanopia; the parietal fibres carry the inferior field → parietal lesion → inferior quadrantanopia.
The mnemonic: PITS — Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior. Think: "Temporal lesion = can't see the Sky (Superior); Parietal lesion = can't see the ground (Inferior)."
Bitemporal hemianopia: chiasmal compression

Bitemporal hemianopia = an optic CHIASM defect — loss of both temporal (outer) fields (the crossing nasal fibres are compressed). The direction of compression tells you the cause:

Quadrants worseCompressionCausePopulation
Upper quadrant worseINFERIOR compression (from below)pituitary tumourmore common in adults
Lower quadrant worseSUPERIOR compression (from above)craniopharyngiomamore common in children
The logic: the chiasm sits above the pituitary; a pituitary tumour grows UP → compresses the lower chiasmal fibres first → the SUPERIOR field goes first (upper quadrant worse); a craniopharyngioma presses DOWN → the INFERIOR field goes first (lower quadrant worse). The rule: bitemporal hemianopia → image the pituitary/chiasm (pituitary tumour until proven otherwise).
The key localising principles
  • "How many eyes?" — one eye → lesion anterior to the chiasm (optic nerve/retina); both eyes → lesion at or behind the chiasm.
  • "Same side or opposite?" (binocular) — bitemporal (outer fields both eyes) → chiasm; homonymous (same side both eyes) → behind the chiasm (tract/radiation/cortex).
  • "Hemianopia or quadrantanopia?" (homonymous) — complete hemianopia → optic tract or occipital cortex; quadrantanopia → optic radiation (PITS).
  • Macular sparing → occipital cortex (dual blood supply / large cortical representation → spared in PCA stroke).
  • Congruency: defects become more congruent (identical in both eyes) the further back the lesion (occipital = most congruent).
Causes by pattern
  • Monocular loss → optic nerve: optic neuritis (multiple sclerosis), ischaemic optic neuropathy, GCA, glaucoma, retinal artery/vein occlusion (amaurosis fugax = transient monocular loss → carotid/embolic).
  • Bitemporal hemianopia → chiasm: pituitary tumour, craniopharyngioma.
  • Homonymous hemianopia/quadrantanopia → tract/radiation/cortex: stroke (commonest), tumour, abscess — the field defect helps localise the lobe.
Assessment / investigations
  • Confrontation visual field testing (bedside) → then formal perimetry (maps the defect precisely).
  • Fundoscopy (papilloedema, optic atrophy), pupils (RAPD in optic nerve lesions).
  • Neuroimaging (MRI/CT): pituitary MRI for bitemporal defects; brain imaging for homonymous defects (stroke/tumour). Determine the cause from the localisation.
Exam pearls
Organising rule
The field defect localises the lesion; the chiasm: before → monocular; at → bitemporal; after → homonymous.
Monocular loss
Optic nerve (before chiasm) — optic neuritis, ischaemia, glaucoma.
Bitemporal hemianopia
Optic chiasm → upper quadrant worse = inferior compression = pituitary tumour (adults); lower quadrant worse = superior compression = craniopharyngioma (children).
Homonymous hemianopia
Contralateral optic tract ("left homonymous hemianopia = right optic tract lesion").
Quadrantanopia = PITS
Parietal = Inferior, Temporal (Meyer's loop) = Superior.
Occipital cortex
Homonymous hemianopia with MACULAR SPARING (PCA stroke).
Localise the cause
Bitemporal → image the pituitary; homonymous → think stroke/tumour (localise the lobe).
Amaurosis fugax
Transient monocular loss → carotid/embolic (TIA).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Thoracic Outle:
What & why
Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) = compression of the neurovascular bundle (brachial plexus, subclavian artery, and/or subclavian vein) as it passes through the thoracic outlet at the root of the neck.
The core concept: three structures share a tight corridor — a nerve (brachial plexus), an artery (subclavian), and a vein (subclavian) — so TOS splits into three syndromes depending on which is compressed: neurogenic, venous, or arterial. Identifying which is the whole diagnostic task (presentations and urgency differ). The commonest is neurogenic; the vascular forms are rarer but potentially limb-threatening.
  • Often occurs with an anatomical predisposition (e.g. a cervical rib), precipitated by neck trauma or repetitive overhead activity.
The decisive fork: which structure is compressed?
TypeStructureFeaturesFrequency
Neurogenic TOSbrachial plexus (nerve)arm/hand pain, paraesthesia, weakness, wasting (esp. C8/T1 — ulnar distribution)commonest
Venous TOSsubclavian veinpainful, diffuse arm swelling + distended (dilated) veins; cyanotic armrarer
Arterial TOSsubclavian arterypainful arm claudication, pallor, cold, weak pulserarest, most serious
The rule (high-yield): neurogenic = pain/paraesthesia/weakness (commonest); venous = swollen, cyanotic arm + distended veins; arterial = pale, cold, claudicating arm.
Anatomy & causes
  • The thoracic outlet — three potential compression points: the scalene triangle (between anterior + middle scalene), the costoclavicular space (between clavicle + first rib), and the subcoracoid / pectoralis minor space.
  • Predisposing/causative factors: cervical rib (an extra rib from C7 — the classic bony anomaly), neck trauma (often the precipitant), anatomical variations (fibrous bands, abnormal first rib, scalene hypertrophy), repetitive overhead activity (athletes, manual workers), poor posture.
The cervical rib point (high-yield): a cervical rib is the classic anatomical predisposition → it narrows the outlet and compresses the bundle.
Clinical features (by subtype)

Neurogenic TOS (commonest):

  • arm/hand pain, paraesthesia, numbness — often in the ulnar (C8/T1) distribution (medial arm, ring + little fingers)
  • hand weakness + wasting (thenar/intrinsic muscles) in chronic cases; symptoms worse with overhead arm positions/activity

Venous TOS (subclavian vein):

  • painful, diffuse arm swelling + distended (prominent) veins — the arm looks swollen and cyanotic
  • risk of subclavian vein thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome / "effort thrombosis") — often after vigorous arm use in young, active people

Arterial TOS (subclavian artery):

  • painful arm claudication (pain/fatigue on use), pallor, coldness, weak/absent pulse, risk of distal emboli/ischaemia
  • the rarest but most serious (limb-threatening)
Examination / provocation
  • Provocation tests (reproduce symptoms / diminish the pulse by positioning): Adson's test (neck extension + head turn + deep breath → radial pulse diminishes); Roos test (EAST) (arms abducted 90°, externally rotated, repeated hand clenching → reproduces symptoms).
  • Examine: radial pulses (both arms), arm colour/temperature/swelling, neurological exam (C8/T1 — sensory, wasting), palpate for a cervical rib.
Investigations
  • Chest + cervical spine plain radiographs — identify a cervical rib or bony abnormality.
  • Venography / angiography (vascular TOS) — demonstrate subclavian vein/artery compression or thrombosis (± provocative positioning); duplex ultrasound for vascular TOS (thrombosis).
  • Nerve conduction studies / EMG (neurogenic TOS; also excludes ulnar neuropathy, C8/T1 radiculopathy).
  • MRI/CT — assess soft-tissue causes (fibrous bands, scalene anatomy).
The differential
ConditionDiscriminator
TOSpositional, neurovascular, cervical rib, provocation tests positive
Cervical radiculopathy (C8/T1)dermatomal, neck pain, root tension signs
Ulnar / cubital tunnel syndromelocalised to the elbow, ulnar territory
Carpal tunnelmedian distribution
Raynaud's / vascular diseasefor the vascular presentations
Management
The principle: conservative first; surgical decompression if conservative fails or for significant vascular compromise.
  • Conservative (first-line): physiotherapy (posture correction, scalene/pectoral stretching, strengthening), activity modification (avoid provoking positions), analgesia — most neurogenic TOS responds.
  • Surgical decompression (if conservative fails): first rib resection ± cervical rib removal, scalenectomy, release of fibrous bands — for failed conservative treatment, significant neurological deficit, or vascular TOS.
  • Vascular TOS: venous TOS with thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) → anticoagulation ± thrombolysis, then decompression; arterial TOS → surgical repair/decompression (limb-threatening).
Exam pearls
What it is
Compression of the neurovascular bundle (brachial plexus + subclavian artery/vein) at the thoracic outlet.
Three subtypes
Neurogenic (commonest — pain/paraesthesia/weakness, C8/T1), venous (swollen cyanotic arm + distended veins), arterial (claudication, pale/cold arm — rarest, most serious).
Predisposition
Cervical rib (classic), neck trauma, repetitive overhead activity, anatomical bands.
Paget-Schroetter
Venous TOS + subclavian vein thrombosis = "effort thrombosis".
Examination
Provocation tests (Adson's, Roos/EAST), pulses, C8/T1 signs, palpate for cervical rib.
Investigations
CXR + cervical spine X-ray (cervical rib), venography/angiography (vascular TOS), NCS/EMG (neurogenic).
Differential
C8/T1 radiculopathy, ulnar neuropathy, carpal tunnel.
Management
Conservative first (physiotherapy, posture); surgical decompression (first rib / cervical rib resection) if conservative fails or vascular compromise; anticoagulation/thrombolysis for venous thrombosis.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Stroke / TIA:
What & why
Stroke = a sudden neurological deficit due to a vascular cause, lasting >24 hours (or leading to death) — either ischaemic (~85%, blocked artery) or haemorrhagic (~15%, ruptured vessel). TIA = the same process but transient — focal ischaemia WITHOUT infarction (tissue-based: symptoms resolve, usually <1 hour, no infarct on imaging).
The core concept: management pivots on one question answered by an urgent CT — is it ischaemic or haemorrhagic? — because the treatments are opposite (ischaemic → thrombolyse/antiplatelets; haemorrhagic → reverse anticoagulation, never thrombolyse). And "time is brain" — stroke is a time-critical emergency: rapid recognition (FAST), immediate CT, reperfusion within tight windows.
  • A leading cause of death + disability; the deficit localises to the vascular territory.
The decisive fork: ischaemic vs haemorrhagic

The first and most important branch — you cannot treat until you know which (an urgent CT decides):

Ischaemic (~85%)Haemorrhagic (~15%)
Mechanismblocked artery (thrombosis/embolism)ruptured vessel → bleed into brain
Causesatherosclerosis, AF (cardioembolic), small-vessel disease, carotid stenosishypertension (commonest), aneurysm, AVM, anticoagulation, amyloid angiopathy
CTmay be normal early; later low densityhyperdense (bright) blood immediately
Treatmentthrombolysis/thrombectomy + antiplateletsreverse anticoagulation, BP control, neurosurgery; NO thrombolysis/antiplatelets
The rule (high-yield): URGENT non-contrast CT head first — it reliably shows blood and rules it out before any thrombolytic/antiplatelet. Never thrombolyse or give aspirin until haemorrhage is excluded.
Recognition: FAST + the deficit
  • FAST (public/first-responder screen): Face (droop), Arm (weakness/drift), Speech (slurred/aphasic), Time (call 999).
  • ROSIER score — the in-hospital stroke recognition tool (excludes hypoglycaemia; scores face/arm/leg/speech/visual).
Always check glucose (high-yield): hypoglycaemia is a classic stroke mimic → check + correct immediately. Other mimics: seizure (Todd's paresis), migraine with aura, tumour, functional, Bell's palsy.
The Oxford (Bamford) classification

Classifies ischaemic stroke by which territory + how much, using 3 features: (1) unilateral weakness/sensory deficit, (2) homonymous hemianopia, (3) higher cortical dysfunction (dysphasia, neglect):

TypeCriteriaTerritory
TACS (total anterior)all 3large MCA + ACA
PACS (partial anterior)2 of 3 (or higher cortical dysfunction alone)branch of MCA/ACA
LACS (lacunar)pure motor / pure sensory / sensorimotor / ataxic hemiparesis — NO higher cortical/visual signssmall perforators (internal capsule, pons, basal ganglia)
POCS (posterior)cerebellar/brainstem signs, isolated hemianopia, CN palsiesvertebrobasilar
Key discriminators: TACS = all 3 (worst prognosis); LACS = no cortical signs (pure motor/sensory — small-vessel); POCS = brainstem/cerebellar/visual.
Territory syndromes
📷 Image placeholder — the cerebral arterial territories (ACA, MCA, PCA) mapped onto the motor/sensory homunculus — explaining leg>arm (ACA), face+arm>leg (MCA) and isolated homonymous hemianopia (PCA)
ArteryDeficit
Middle cerebral (MCA) — commonestcontralateral hemiparesis + hemisensory loss (face + arm > leg), homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect (non-dominant)
Anterior cerebral (ACA)contralateral leg > arm weakness, behavioural change
Posterior cerebral (PCA)homonymous hemianopia (macular sparing), visual agnosia
Vertebrobasilar / brainstemcerebellar signs, CN palsies, crossed signs, "locked-in" (basilar); lateral medullary (Wallenberg — PICA) syndrome
Lacunar (perforators)pure motor (internal capsule), pure sensory (thalamus), ataxic hemiparesis
The MCA point (high-yield): the commonest territory — face + arm > leg (vs ACA's leg > arm) + aphasia if dominant (the language areas are MCA-supplied).
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — non-contrast CT head — a hyperdense acute haemorrhage vs a hypodense/loss-of-grey-white-differentiation ischaemic infarct (and the hyperdense-MCA sign)
  • Immediate non-contrast CT head — excludes haemorrhage (and mimics); may be normal early in ischaemia → still allows thrombolysis if within window and no bleed.
  • CT/MR angiography — identify a large-vessel occlusion (for thrombectomy); CT/MR perfusion — identify salvageable penumbra (extends the window).
  • Bloods: glucose (mimic), FBC, coagulation, U&E, lipids; ECG (AF); echocardiogram + carotid Doppler (source — cardioembolic vs carotid stenosis).
  • MRI (DWI) — most sensitive for early ischaemia/infarct (also defines TIA as tissue-based).
Acute management of ISCHAEMIC stroke
The principle: exclude haemorrhage → reperfuse (thrombolysis ± thrombectomy) fast → then antiplatelet + supportive care. "Time is brain."
  • Thrombolysis: within 4.5 hours of known onset with alteplase or tenecteplase (tenecteplase now endorsed alongside alteplase) — after excluding haemorrhage + no contraindications (largely bleeding-risk). Extended window: 4.5–9 hours (or wake-up stroke) may be thrombolysed if perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue (mismatch).
  • Mechanical thrombectomy: for proximal large-vessel occlusion (anterior circulation) — up to 6 hours (with thrombolysis if eligible), and up to 24 hours in selected patients with salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging.
  • Aspirin: 300 mg started within 24 hours — after excluding haemorrhage, and delayed until 24h after thrombolysis (repeat CT first) → continue 300 mg for 2 weeks, then long-term antiplatelet (§10).
  • Supportive ("stroke unit care"): admit to a stroke unit; maintain glucose/oxygenation/hydration; swallow assessment (aspiration risk — NBM until assessed); permissive hypertension (don't lower BP acutely unless very high/thrombolysing — the brain needs perfusion); VTE prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression, not early heparin).
Acute management of HAEMORRHAGIC stroke
  • Stop + reverse anticoagulation (warfarin → vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC); DOAC reversal agents).
  • Blood pressure control (lower BP more aggressively than in ischaemic stroke).
  • Neurosurgical referral — evacuation of selected haematomas, or management of hydrocephalus/raised ICP.
  • NO thrombolysis, NO antiplatelets/anticoagulants. (Subarachnoid haemorrhage has its own pathway.)
TIA management
TIA = transient (resolves), no infarct — but a warning sign of impending stroke → urgent action.
  • Give aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated).
  • Specialist assessment within 24 hours (the old ABCD² risk-stratification is no longer used to delay — all suspected TIAs seen urgently).
  • Carotid Doppler (stenosis → endarterectomy if significant), ECG (AF), brain imaging.
  • Do NOT drive + start secondary prevention (§10).
The rule: a TIA is a medical urgency (high early stroke risk) → aspirin + urgent specialist review within 24h.
Secondary prevention (after ischaemic stroke/TIA)
  • Antiplatelet: clopidogrel 75 mg daily (first-line long-term); aspirin + dipyridamole if clopidogrel unsuitable.
  • If AF (cardioembolic): anticoagulation (a DOAC) instead of antiplatelet — usually started ~2 weeks after the stroke (balancing haemorrhagic transformation risk).
  • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) — start after ~48h.
  • BP control (the biggest modifiable risk factor), diabetes control, smoking cessation, lifestyle.
  • Carotid endarterectomy — if symptomatic carotid stenosis (significant, e.g. >50–70%) on the relevant side.
  • Address the cause: AF, carotid disease, patent foramen ovale (in the young), etc.
Exam pearls
Definitions
Stroke = sudden vascular neurological deficit >24h; TIA = transient, no infarct (tissue-based); ischaemic ~85% vs haemorrhagic ~15%.
The decisive step
Urgent non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage — treatments are opposite; never thrombolyse/give aspirin until bleed excluded; always check glucose (mimic).
Recognition
FAST (Face/Arm/Speech/Time); ROSIER in hospital.
Bamford
TACS (all 3), PACS (2/3), LACS (pure motor/sensory, no cortical signs), POCS (brainstem/cerebellar/visual).
Territories
MCA (commonest): contralateral face + arm > leg, hemianopia, aphasia (dominant); ACA = leg > arm; PCA = hemianopia.
Ischaemic acute
Thrombolysis (alteplase OR tenecteplase) within 4.5h (extended to 9h/wake-up with perfusion mismatch); thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion up to 24h (perfusion-selected); aspirin 300mg after 24h (post-thrombolysis) for 2 weeks; stroke unit + swallow assessment + permissive hypertension.
Haemorrhagic
Reverse anticoagulation (vit K + PCC), lower BP, neurosurgery; NO thrombolysis/antiplatelet.
TIA
Aspirin 300mg + specialist review within 24h (urgent — high stroke risk).
Secondary prevention
Clopidogrel (or anticoagulation if AF), high-dose statin, BP control, carotid endarterectomy if symptomatic stenosis.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Restless Legs:
What & why
Restless legs syndrome (RLS), also called Willis-Ekbom disease, = a sensorimotor disorder characterised by an uncontrollable urge to move the legs, usually with unpleasant sensations, worse at rest and in the evening/night, and relieved by movement.
The core concept: RLS is defined by a specific, reproducible clinical pattern — urge to move the legs + worse at rest + worse in the evening + relieved by movement — a four-part pattern that is essentially diagnostic. The two clinical priorities: check ferritin (iron deficiency is a common, treatable cause that drives the dopamine dysfunction), and treat with dopaminergic/gabapentinoid agents. It links to iron + dopamine in the CNS.
  • A common cause of insomnia; can be primary (idiopathic/familial) or secondary (esp. iron deficiency, pregnancy, renal failure).
The decisive fork: primary vs secondary RLS

The first clinical question is whether there's an underlying/treatable cause (because treating it can cure the RLS):

Primary RLSSecondary RLS
Causeidiopathic, often familial (positive family history)an underlying condition
Onsetoften youngeroften later / with the cause
Key secondary causes—iron deficiency (± anaemia), pregnancy, chronic kidney disease/uraemia, diabetes/peripheral neuropathy, drugs
The rule (high-yield): always check ferritin (iron deficiency is the key reversible cause) and consider pregnancy, renal failure, and neuropathy. Drugs that worsen RLS include antidepressants (SSRIs/TCAs/mirtazapine), antipsychotics, antihistamines, and dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide).
Pathophysiology (the iron/dopamine link)
Central dopaminergic dysfunction, and crucially iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis (tyrosine hydroxylase) → low brain iron → impaired dopamine function. This explains both why iron deficiency causes RLS and why dopamine agonists treat it. Genetic predisposition in primary/familial cases.
Clinical features

A sensorimotor syndrome of spontaneous, continuous lower-limb movements that may be associated with paraesthesia:

FeatureDetail
Urge to move the legsuncontrollable urge (akathisia-like); usually at night and worse at rest
Paraesthesiacrawling or throbbing sensations in the legs
Periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS)repetitive leg jerks in sleep, often noted by the partner
The diagnostic criteria — the "URGE" pattern (high-yield): (1) Urge to move the legs, usually with uncomfortable sensations; (2) worse at Rest; (3) relieved by movement (Getting up/walking); (4) worse in the Evening/night. The relief-by-movement feature is defining — distinguishing it from other leg complaints.
  • Consequences: sleep disturbance/insomnia (difficulty falling asleep), daytime fatigue.
The differential
ConditionDiscriminator
RLSurge to move + worse at rest/evening + relieved by movement
Akathisia (drug-induced)generalised restlessness (not just legs), antipsychotic-related, not rest/circadian-patterned
Peripheral neuropathysensory loss/burning, not relieved by movement
Nocturnal leg crampspainful muscle contraction, not an urge
Peripheral vascular diseaseclaudication on exertion (relieved by rest — the opposite)
The key discriminator: RLS is relieved by movement and worse at rest — the opposite of vascular claudication (worse on movement).
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — based on the characteristic pattern (the four URGE criteria).
  • Ferritin — to exclude iron deficiency; the key investigation. A low-normal ferritin may still warrant iron replacement in RLS (the threshold is higher than for anaemia).
  • Consider: U&E (renal failure), glucose/HbA1c (diabetes), pregnancy test, TFTs, review the drug chart.
  • Polysomnography only if diagnostic doubt or to assess PLMS.
Management
The overarching principle: treat any underlying iron deficiency + address triggers; then dopaminergic or gabapentinoid agents for symptoms.
  • Treat the underlying cause: treat iron deficiency (oral/IV iron if ferritin low — can resolve the RLS); manage renal failure, review/stop aggravating drugs (antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines).
  • Lifestyle: sleep hygiene, avoid caffeine/alcohol/nicotine in the evening, moderate exercise, leg massage/stretching.
  • Pharmacological (troublesome symptoms): dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) ± rotigotine patch; or gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) — effective, especially if pain/neuropathy.
The augmentation caveat (high-yield): long-term dopamine agonists can cause "augmentation" (symptoms become earlier, more intense, and spread — a paradoxical worsening) → modern practice increasingly favours gabapentinoids first-line to avoid this. Also watch dopamine agonists for impulse-control disorders (gambling, etc.). Iron replacement where indicated remains a cornerstone.
Exam pearls
What it is
RLS (Willis-Ekbom disease) = urge to move the legs + worse at Rest + Relieved by movement + worse in the Evening/night ("URGE") ± paraesthesia (crawling/throbbing); often with periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS).
Primary vs secondary
Primary (familial) vs secondary — key secondary causes: iron deficiency, pregnancy, renal failure, neuropathy; worsened by antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines, metoclopramide.
Mechanism
CNS dopamine dysfunction; iron is a cofactor for dopamine → low iron → RLS (and why dopamine agonists work).
Investigations
Clinical diagnosis + ferritin (exclude iron deficiency — a higher ferritin threshold than for anaemia).
Management
Treat iron deficiency + lifestyle; dopamine agonists (pramipexole/ropinirole) or gabapentinoids (gabapentin/pregabalin) — beware augmentation with long-term dopamine agonists (shift toward gabapentinoids first-line).
Discriminator
Relieved by movement / worse at rest — the opposite of vascular claudication.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Raised Intracr:
What & why
Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) = an increase in the pressure inside the skull above normal (normal ICP = 5–15 mmHg) — a neurological emergency because the brain is enclosed in a rigid box.
The core concept: the whole topic flows from the Monro-Kellie doctrine — the skull is a fixed rigid container holding three things (brain ~1400 mL + CSF ~150 mL + blood ~150 mL), so any increase in one must be offset by a decrease in another, or ICP rises. Once the compensatory reserve is exhausted, ICP rises steeply → reduced cerebral perfusion → ischaemia → herniation → death. Priorities: recognise the syndrome early (headache, vomiting, papilloedema), spot the late/emergency signs (Cushing's triad, herniation), and lower ICP fast.
  • Causes span mass lesions, oedema, CSF obstruction, and venous problems (§3).
The Monro-Kellie doctrine
  • The rigid skull holds three components in dynamic equilibrium: brain tissue (~1400 mL) + CSF (~150 mL) + blood (~150 mL) = ~1700 mL total.
  • The principle: because the skull is rigid, CSF and venous blood are displaced first as the primary compensation — if something new appears (tumour, bleed, oedema), CSF is pushed into the spinal theca and venous blood is squeezed out to keep ICP normal at first.
The compliance curve (high-yield): compensation works up to a point — once CSF/venous reserve is exhausted, small further volume increases cause large ICP rises (flat, then steep) → decompensation.
Cerebral perfusion (high-yield): CPP (cerebral perfusion pressure) = MAP − ICP. As ICP rises, CPP falls → cerebral ischaemia → this drives the Cushing's response (§5). CSF is produced at ~500 mL/day in a normal production–absorption equilibrium; disrupting it → hydrocephalus + raised ICP.
The decisive fork: what's raising the ICP?
MechanismCauses
Mass lesion (extra volume)tumour (primary/mets), haematoma (extradural/subdural/intracerebral), abscess
Cerebral oedematraumatic brain injury, ischaemic stroke, hypoxic injury, hepatic encephalopathy
↑CSF (hydrocephalus)obstruction to CSF flow or impaired absorption
↑venous volumecerebral venous sinus thrombosis, venous obstruction
Idiopathicidiopathic intracranial hypertension (§7)
Clinical features

Early features:

FeatureDetail
Headacheworse in the morning, and worse on coughing, exertion, or moving the head — the classic raised-ICP headache
Vomitingwithout associated nausea — a characteristic feature
Lethargy + altered mental statusdrowsiness, ↓consciousness
On examinationocular (CN) palsies, papilloedema, pupillary irregularities (unilateral dilation, light defects)
The morning/positional headache (high-yield): worse on waking, lying down, bending over, coughing/straining/Valsalva — because lying flat + raised intrathoracic pressure further raise ICP.
Papilloedema (the key sign): swelling of the optic disc from raised ICP — the optic nerve sheath is continuous with the subarachnoid space, so raised CSF pressure is transmitted along the sheath → the disc bulges forward. Fundoscopy: blurred disc margins, elevated disc, loss of venous pulsation. CN VI (abducens) palsy is a false localising sign — its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to stretch (failure of abduction/diplopia).
  • Late features: persistent vomiting, Cushing's reflex/triad, reduced GCS, herniation (§5, §6).
Cushing's reflex (the emergency response)
  • Cushing's reflex = the physiological response to dangerously raised ICP → hypertension + bradycardia.
  • The logic: if ICP is high, MAP must also rise to maintain CPP (CPP = MAP − ICP) → the body drives up blood pressure (hypertension) to perfuse the brain → the hypertension triggers a reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor response).
Cushing's TRIAD (high-yield): (1) hypertension (widened pulse pressure), (2) bradycardia, (3) irregular breathing — the breathing abnormality because the respiratory centre is in the brainstem, and rising ICP compresses it. The rule: Cushing's triad = a pre-terminal sign of critically raised ICP → herniation imminent → emergency.
Brain herniation ("coning")

If ICP keeps rising, the brain is forced out of its compartment through the dural openings → herniation:

HerniationFeature
Uncal (transtentorial)the uncus compresses CN III → a fixed, dilated pupil + "down-and-out" eye on the affected side; ± contralateral hemiparesis
Tonsillar ("coning")cerebellar tonsils herniate through the foramen magnum → brainstem (respiratory centre) compression → respiratory arrest + death
Subfalcinecingulate gyrus under the falx
The critical rule (high-yield): a unilateral fixed dilated pupil in a deteriorating patient = uncal herniation compressing CN III → emergency. This is why lumbar puncture is CONTRAINDICATED in raised ICP with a mass lesion — removing CSF from below can precipitate tonsillar herniation (coning) → image (CT) first.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — a specific cause
IIH = raised ICP without a mass lesion or hydrocephalus (a diagnosis of exclusion). Classic patient: a young, obese female; risk factors include pregnancy, COCP, steroids, tetracyclines, retinoids (vitamin A), lithium.
  • Features: headache, blurred vision, papilloedema, enlarged blind spot, CN VI palsy; the key risk is progressive visual loss.
  • Investigations: neuroimaging (normal / exclude other cause) → then LP shows raised opening pressure with normal CSF constituents (LP is safe here — no mass lesion).
  • Management: weight loss + acetazolamide (↓CSF production), topiramate; vision-threatening → optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting.
See the dedicated Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension note for the full workup.
Investigations
  • Urgent CT head — identify the cause (mass, bleed, hydrocephalus, oedema) and guide emergency management; MRI for further characterisation.
  • Fundoscopy — papilloedema.
  • AVOID lumbar puncture if a space-occupying lesion / raised ICP with mass effect (herniation risk) — image first.
  • ICP monitoring (invasive, in ITU/neurosurgical settings — e.g. after severe TBI).
Management (lower the ICP)
The overarching principle: treat the cause + emergency measures to lower ICP + protect cerebral perfusion — a neurosurgical emergency.
  • Treat the underlying cause — evacuate a haematoma, resect/debulk a tumour, shunt hydrocephalus, anticoagulate CVST.
  • Positioning: head up ~30°, neutral neck (aids venous drainage).
  • Osmotic therapy: IV mannitol or hypertonic saline (draw fluid out of the brain).
  • Controlled ventilation: intubate + maintain normal/low-normal CO₂ (hyperventilation → cerebral vasoconstriction → transiently ↓ICP, used cautiously).
  • Sedation + analgesia, treat fever/seizures (reduce metabolic demand); CSF drainage (external ventricular drain) if hydrocephalus.
  • Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) — for vasogenic oedema around tumours/abscess (NOT for trauma/stroke oedema).
  • Decompressive craniectomy — surgical last resort for refractory raised ICP.
  • Maintain CPP: support MAP; avoid hypotension/hypoxia (worsen ischaemia).
Exam pearls
Foundations
Normal ICP 5–15 mmHg; Monro-Kellie: rigid skull = brain + CSF + blood; new volume → CSF/blood displaced first, then ICP rises steeply; CPP = MAP − ICP.
Early features
Morning headache (worse on coughing/bending/lying/Valsalva), vomiting without nausea, papilloedema, ↓consciousness, CN VI palsy (false localising).
Papilloedema
Raised CSF pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath → disc swelling (blurred margins, elevated disc).
Cushing's triad (LATE)
Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing (brainstem compression) → impending herniation.
Herniation
Uncal → CN III palsy (fixed dilated pupil, down-and-out eye); tonsillar ("coning") → foramen magnum → respiratory arrest.
Do NOT LP
If raised ICP with a mass lesion (→ coning) — CT first.
IIH
Young obese woman; RFs (pregnancy, COCP, tetracyclines, retinoids); papilloedema + CN VI palsy + visual loss; LP = raised opening pressure; weight loss + acetazolamide.
Management
Treat cause + head up 30°, mannitol/hypertonic saline, ventilation, dexamethasone (tumour oedema), decompressive craniectomy.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Radiculopathie:
What & why
Radiculopathy = dysfunction of a spinal nerve ROOT (as it exits the spine) → pain, sensory disturbance, weakness, and reflex loss in that root's dermatome/myotome.
The core concept: a radiculopathy is a root-level (dermatomal) problem — the deficit follows a single nerve root's dermatome and myotome, distinguishing it from a peripheral nerve palsy (nerve territory) and a cord/central lesion (UMN signs). The commonest cause is a prolapsed intervertebral disc compressing the root. The clinical skill is mapping the deficit to the root level using dermatomes, myotomes and reflexes — and recognising the red flags (cauda equina, myelopathy) that need emergency action.
  • Very common (especially lumbar → sciatica); usually a compressive LMN-type root problem.
The decisive fork: radiculopathy vs peripheral nerve palsy vs myelopathy

Three levels produce weakness — distinguishing them is the core localisation skill:

Radiculopathy (root)Peripheral nerve palsyMyelopathy (cord)
Patterndermatome + myotome (single root)peripheral nerve territorybelow the level (long tracts)
SignsLMN (↓reflex, ↓power, dermatomal sensory)LMN (nerve territory)UMN (↑tone, ↑reflexes, upgoing plantars) + sensory level
Painradicular (shooting down the dermatome)local ± nerve territoryoften painless
ExampleS1 radiculopathy → sciatica, ↓ankle jerkcommon peroneal → foot dropcervical myelopathy, cord compression
The rule (high-yield): radiculopathy follows a dermatome/myotome (root), a peripheral nerve palsy follows a nerve, and myelopathy gives UMN signs below the lesion.
Causes
  • Prolapsed (herniated) intervertebral disc — the commonest (nucleus pulposus herniates → compresses the exiting root).
  • Degenerative — spondylosis, osteophytes, foraminal stenosis (commoner in older patients).
  • Other: trauma, tumour (spinal mets), infection (abscess, herpes zoster → dermatomal), spondylolisthesis.
Clinical features

Prolapsed disc usually causes dermatomal leg pain with neurological deficits:

  • leg pain usually worse than the back pain; pain often worse on sitting; the pain is radicular — shooting/electric, radiating down the dermatome.

The deficit follows the root:

  • dermatomal sensory disturbance (numbness/paraesthesia in the root's dermatome)
  • myotomal weakness (weakness of the muscles that root supplies)
  • reduced/absent reflex (if the root subserves a reflex)
Nerve root tension signs: straight leg raise (SLR) reproduces radicular pain in lower lumbar (L5/S1) radiculopathy; the femoral stretch test is used for upper lumbar (L3/L4).
The dermatome / myotome / reflex map

Localising the root depends on knowing the reflex levels and dermatome landmarks:

Reflexes (root levels):

The common lumbar radiculopathies (sciatica)

Combining the dermatome + reflex mnemonics gives the classic root syndromes:

RootSensory (dermatome)Motor (myotome)Reflex
L3/L4anterior thigh / medial knee + shinknee extension (quadriceps)↓knee jerk (L3–4)
L5big toe / dorsum of foot, lateral shindorsiflexion of foot + big toe (EHL) → foot drop; weak hip abduction(no easily-tested reflex)

The high-yield trio: L5 = big toe, weak dorsiflexion (mimics foot drop); S1 = little toe/sole, weak plantarflexion, ↓ankle jerk; L3/L4 = medial knee, weak knee extension, ↓knee jerk. "Sciatica" = radicular pain down the back of the leg (usually L5 or S1).
RED FLAGS: cauda equina syndrome (the emergency)
Cauda equina syndrome (CES) = compression of the cauda equina nerve roots (below L1/L2) — a surgical emergency that can cause permanent paralysis + incontinence.

RED FLAG features:

  • urinary retention / incontinence, faecal incontinence
  • bilateral sciatica; bilateral or severe leg weakness
  • saddle anaesthesia (perineal sensory loss)
  • reduced anal tone on PR examination
Action: immediate hospital admission → emergency MRI lumbosacral spine → surgical decompression ASAP. The rule (high-yield): any radiculopathy with bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, or bilateral leg symptoms = cauda equina until proven otherwise → emergency MRI.
  • Other back-pain red flags (sinister cause): age <20 or >50 new onset, trauma, cancer history, fever/weight loss, night pain, thoracic pain, progressive neurology.
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — history + the dermatome/myotome/reflex exam localises the root; SLR / femoral stretch for tension signs.
  • MRI spine — the investigation of choice if red flags, severe/progressive deficit, or persistent symptoms (identifies disc prolapse/stenosis/compression); emergency MRI if cauda equina suspected.
  • Most simple radiculopathies don't need immediate imaging — treat conservatively first.
Management
The overarching principle: most improve with conservative management; escalate for red flags or persistent/severe deficit; emergency surgery for cauda equina.
  • Conservative (first-line for most): stay active / avoid bed rest, analgesia (per NICE low back pain/sciatica — NSAIDs; neuropathic agents e.g. amitriptyline/duloxetine/gabapentin/pregabalin for radicular pain), physiotherapy — most disc-related radiculopathies resolve over weeks.
  • Escalation: epidural / nerve root corticosteroid injection for persistent radicular pain.
  • Surgery (discectomy / decompression): for severe/progressive neurological deficit, or symptoms refractory to conservative treatment.
  • EMERGENCY surgical decompression: cauda equina syndrome — time-critical.
  • Treat the cause: e.g. spinal mets, infection.
Exam pearls
What it is
Spinal nerve ROOT dysfunction → dermatomal sensory loss + myotomal weakness + ↓reflex + radicular pain; commonest cause = prolapsed disc.
Localisation
Radiculopathy (root/dermatome, LMN) vs peripheral nerve palsy (nerve territory) vs myelopathy (UMN below lesion).
Reflexes
Ankle = S1–2, knee = L3–4, biceps = C5–6, triceps = C7–8.
Dermatomes
C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal, L4 knee, L5 big toe, S1 little toe/sole.
Common lumbar roots
L4 (medial knee, ↓knee jerk), L5 (big toe, weak dorsiflexion), S1 (little toe/sole, weak plantarflexion, ↓ankle jerk); sciatica = L5/S1.
Tension sign
SLR reproduces L5/S1 radicular pain; femoral stretch for L3/L4.
RED FLAG — cauda equina
Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, reduced anal tone → emergency MRI + surgical decompression.
Management
Mostly conservative (stay active, analgesia, physio, neuropathic agents); surgery for progressive deficit or refractory pain; emergency decompression for cauda equina.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Peripheral Ner:
What & why
Peripheral nerve injuries = damage to individual peripheral nerves (or the brachial plexus) → a lower motor neurone (LMN) pattern of weakness + sensory loss in that nerve's territory.
The core concept: each peripheral nerve has a predictable motor + sensory territory and a characteristic mechanism of injury (usually a specific fracture or compression point). The whole clinical skill is pattern recognition — the deficit localises the lesion: "wrist drop → radial nerve → humeral shaft fracture", "claw hand → ulnar nerve", "foot drop → common peroneal nerve". These are LMN lesions (wasting, hyporeflexia).
  • High-yield because the nerve–muscle–fracture associations are constantly tested; most are compression- or fracture-related.
The decisive fork: which nerve, from the deficit + mechanism?

Two clues together pinpoint the nerve — the motor/sensory deficit and the mechanism (fracture/compression site):

The high-yield fracture–nerve pairs: surgical neck of humerus / shoulder dislocation → axillary; midshaft humerus → radial (wrist drop); medial epicondyle → ulnar (claw hand).
LOAF muscles (median nerve): Lumbricals (lateral 2), Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis — the thenar/lumbrical muscles supplied by the median nerve; the ulnar nerve supplies all the other intrinsic hand muscles.
Median nerve & carpal tunnel syndrome
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) = compression of the median nerve as it passes under the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) at the wrist.
  • Features: pain + tingling/numbness in the median distribution (lateral 3½ fingers), worse at night, shaking the hand relieves it; thenar wasting + weakness of thumb abduction/opposition (LOAF) in chronic cases.
  • Signs: Tinel's sign (tapping over the nerve → tingling), Phalen's test (wrist flexion → symptoms).
  • Causes/associations: idiopathic (commonest), pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, obesity.
Management: wrist splint (night), corticosteroid injection, and carpal tunnel decompression surgery (flexor retinaculum release) if severe/persistent.
Ulnar nerve & cubital tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome = compression of the ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (elbow, behind the medial epicondyle).
  • Features: tingling + numbness of the 4th + 5th fingers (medial 1½), worse on elbow flexion; wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles → claw hand (hyperextended MCPs, flexed IPs of the 4th/5th fingers).
The ulnar paradox (high-yield): a more proximal (elbow) ulnar lesion produces a LESS obvious claw than a distal (wrist) lesion — because the proximal lesion also knocks out the ulnar-supplied flexor digitorum profundus to the ring/little finger (so they don't flex as much).
  • Management: elbow splinting / avoiding pressure; decompression surgery if severe.
The brachial plexus palsies
PalsyLesionMechanismPicture
Erb's palsyupper trunk (C5, C6)shoulder dystocia at birth, or traction"waiter's tip" — arm adducted + internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated; C5–6 sensory loss
Klumpke's palsylower trunk (C8, T1)shoulder dystocia, or traction on an abducted armclaw hand (intrinsic muscle paralysis); ± Horner's syndrome (T1 → sympathetic)
Erb's vs Klumpke's (high-yield): Erb's = upper (C5–6) = waiter's tip; Klumpke's = lower (C8–T1) = claw hand ± Horner's. Both may follow shoulder dystocia during birth.
The lower limb: common peroneal nerve
  • Common peroneal (fibular) nerve — winds around the neck of the fibula (superficial, vulnerable) → injured by fibular neck fracture, tight plaster casts, prolonged leg crossing/squatting, or compression.
  • Features: foot drop (weak dorsiflexion + eversion) → high-stepping gait to compensate; sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot + lateral shin.
  • Also: sciatic nerve (hip dislocation, misplaced IM injection), tibial nerve (tarsal tunnel), femoral nerve (weak knee extension, absent knee jerk).
The foot-drop differential (high-yield): common peroneal palsy vs L5 radiculopathy vs sciatic nerve lesion vs CMT.

GradeInjuryRecovery

The point: neurapraxia (e.g. "Saturday night palsy" — radial nerve compression while asleep) recovers fully; neurotmesis (a cut nerve) needs surgery.
Assessment & management
  • Assessment: characterise the motor + sensory deficit → localise the nerve; identify the mechanism (fracture, compression, laceration); examine for the classic sign (wrist drop, claw hand, winged scapula, foot drop).
  • Investigations: nerve conduction studies / EMG (confirm + localise + grade), imaging for the underlying fracture.
  • Conservative (compression/neurapraxia): remove the cause, splinting, physiotherapy, treat the underlying cause — many recover; corticosteroid injection (e.g. carpal tunnel).
  • Surgery: decompression (carpal/cubital tunnel), or nerve repair/grafting for transection (neurotmesis).
  • Foot drop / wrist drop: splints/orthoses (AFO for foot drop) + physiotherapy while awaiting recovery.

Peripheral nerve palsies = LMN pattern; the deficit + mechanism localise the nerve.

Median

Brachial plexus
Erb's (C5–6, upper) = waiter's tip; Klumpke's (C8–T1, lower) = claw hand ± Horner's; both from shoulder dystocia.
