NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Essential Trem:
Definition & The Core Concept

Essential tremor (benign essential tremor) = the commonest movement disorder — a chronic, slowly progressive, bilateral POSTURAL + ACTION (kinetic) tremor, usually of the hands/arms, worse with sustained posture + intentional movement, often improved by ALCOHOL, with a strong family history.

The core concept — distinguishing it from PARKINSON'S disease (the two most-confused tremors, with opposite characteristics): essential tremor is an ACTION tremor — it appears when the hands are DOING something (holding a posture, reaching, writing, holding a cup) and disappears at rest. Parkinson's is a REST tremor — worst when still, improving with movement. The single most useful question: “when is the tremor worst — using the hands, or resting them?”
Three more hallmarks clinch it: typically SYMMETRICAL, family-history-positive (autosomal dominant), and RELIEVED BY ALCOHOL, with NO other Parkinsonian features (no bradykinesia, rigidity or gait disturbance). Benign but can be functionally disabling. First-line = propranolol or primidone. Bimodal presentation (young adults + elderly); prevalence rises with age.
The Decisive Fork — Essential Tremor vs Parkinson's Disease
FeatureEssential tremorParkinson's disease
Tremor typePOSTURAL + ACTION — worse with movement/postureREST tremor — worse at rest, improves with movement
At resttremor improves/absenttremor present/worst
Symmetrysymmetrical (bilateral)ASYMMETRICAL (starts one side)
Frequencyfaster (~6–12 Hz), fineslower (~4–6 Hz), “pill-rolling”
AlcoholIMPROVES the tremorno effect
Family historyoften POSITIVE (autosomal dominant)usually not
Other signsNONE (isolated tremor)bradykinesia, RIGIDITY, gait/postural change
Head/voice tremorcommon (titubation, vocal tremor)uncommon
The rule: essential tremor = ACTION/postural, SYMMETRICAL, better with ALCOHOL, positive family history, NO other neurology; Parkinson's = REST tremor, ASYMMETRICAL, + bradykinesia/rigidity/gait. The single best discriminator: essential tremor is worse on ACTION; Parkinson's is worse at REST.
Clinical Features
✋ The tremor
  • Bilateral, symmetrical, POSTURAL + ACTION tremor of the hands/arms — brought out by holding the arms outstretched, holding a cup, writing, pouring, spoon-to-mouth
  • Absent/reduced at rest; worse with anxiety, caffeine, fatigue + precise tasks
  • IMPROVED by ALCOHOL (a classic, near-diagnostic feature)
🗣️ Other sites + signs
  • HEAD tremor (titubation — “yes-yes”/“no-no”), VOICE tremor (quavering); less often jaw/tongue/legs
  • NO bradykinesia, rigidity or gait disturbance (their presence points away from essential tremor)
  • Family history often autosomal dominant — ask about affected relatives
The rule: symmetrical postural/action hand tremor (± head/voice tremor), worse on action + with anxiety, better with alcohol, family history, no other neurology = essential tremor.
Investigations
A CLINICAL diagnosis (characteristic action tremor + no other signs + family history). Investigations are to EXCLUDE mimics, not to confirm it.
🩸 Exclude reversible causes
  • Thyroid function (hyperthyroidism) — a key reversible cause
  • Review drugs/substances: caffeine, salbutamol/β-agonists, levothyroxine, lithium, valproate, SSRIs, stimulants
🧠 Consider
  • Wilson's disease in the young (copper studies)
  • Alcohol/withdrawal; Parkinson's (if rest tremor/other features → ± DaT scan)
The rule: clinical diagnosis; check TFTs + review drugs/caffeine; consider Wilson's in the young; DaT scan only if Parkinson's is in question.
The Wider Tremor Differential
TremorFeature
Essential (postural/action)worse on action, symmetrical, alcohol-responsive, family history
Rest (Parkinsonian)worse at rest, asymmetrical, + bradykinesia/rigidity
Intention (cerebellar)worsens as the hand approaches a target (past-pointing, + ataxia/nystagmus/dysdiadochokinesis)
Physiological / enhancedfine, fast; worse with anxiety, caffeine, thyrotoxicosis, β-agonists
Dystonicwith abnormal posturing
The rule: action/postural = essential; rest = Parkinson's; intention (target-worsening) = cerebellar; fine/fast + trigger = enhanced physiological (thyroid/caffeine/drugs).
Management
The principle: only treat if it's bothering the patient (functional/social impact); first-line = PROPRANOLOL or PRIMIDONE; escalate to second-line drugs, then DBS / focused ultrasound for refractory disease.
General: treat only if the tremor causes functional/psychosocial impairment (many need only reassurance); reduce caffeine + review aggravating drugs; avoid relying on alcohol (transiently helps, not a treatment).
Drug (first-line)Notes
PROPRANOLOL (beta-blocker)first-line; effective in ~50–70%; regular or situational (before social events); avoid in asthma, bradycardia, heart block, uncontrolled heart failure
PRIMIDONE (barbiturate anticonvulsant)first-line alternative (esp. if propranolol contraindicated — e.g. asthma); start LOW + titrate SLOWLY (sedation, acute first-dose reaction); teratogenic
⬆️ Second-line
  • Topiramate, gabapentin, benzodiazepines (clonazepam/alprazolam)
  • Botulinum toxin for head/voice tremor
🔧 Refractory / severe
  • Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS — thalamic/VIM)
  • MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy
The rule: treat if impairing → PROPRANOLOL (1st-line; avoid in asthma) or PRIMIDONE (1st-line alternative, esp. asthma; titrate slowly; can combine) → topiramate/gabapentin/benzodiazepines → DBS / focused ultrasound for refractory.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest movement disorder; bilateral, SYMMETRICAL POSTURAL + ACTION tremor of the hands (± HEAD/VOICE tremor); worse on ACTION, better with ALCOHOL, positive FAMILY HISTORY (autosomal dominant), NO other neurology.
vs Parkinson's
Essential tremor = ACTION tremor, symmetrical, alcohol-responsive, no other signs; Parkinson's = REST tremor, asymmetrical, + bradykinesia/rigidity/gait.
Best discriminator
Essential tremor worse on ACTION; Parkinson's worse at REST.
Investigations
CLINICAL diagnosis; check TFTs + review drugs/caffeine (exclude thyroid/drug tremor); consider Wilson's if young.
Management
Treat only if impairing → PROPRANOLOL (1st-line; avoid asthma) or PRIMIDONE (1st-line alternative, esp. asthma; slow titration) → topiramate/gabapentin/benzodiazepines → DBS / focused ultrasound (refractory).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Parkinson's Di:
What & why
Parkinson's disease = a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra (pars compacta) → dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia → a movement disorder.
The core concept: Parkinson's is fundamentally a dopamine-deficiency state in the nigrostriatal pathway. Losing that dopamine tips the basal ganglia toward excess inhibition of movement → the classic motor triad of bradykinesia + rigidity + resting tremor. Because it's a dopamine-deficiency disease, almost all treatment aims to restore dopaminergic signalling — and, symmetrically, blocking dopamine (antipsychotics) or withdrawing dopaminergic drugs worsens it or causes NMS. Priorities: the clinical diagnosis (asymmetric, resting tremor, bradykinesia), excluding mimics, and staged dopaminergic therapy.
  • Common in the elderly (~60s+); the second commonest neurodegenerative disease; a clinical diagnosis.
The decisive fork: Parkinson's disease vs the mimics (parkinsonism)

"Parkinsonism" = the syndrome (bradykinesia + rigidity + tremor); Parkinson's disease is the commonest cause, but you must exclude the mimics:

Parkinson's diseaseMimics (atypical/secondary)
SymmetryASYMMETRIC onsetoften symmetric
Tremorresting tremor prominentmay be absent/atypical
Levodopa responsegoodoften poor
Key mimics—drug-induced (antipsychotics, metoclopramide), vascular, Lewy body dementia, PSP, MSA, corticobasal degeneration, Wilson's (young), essential tremor

The high-yield discriminators:

  • Essential tremor = action/postural tremor, symmetric, improves with alcohol, no bradykinesia (vs Parkinson's's resting tremor + bradykinesia).
  • Drug-induced parkinsonism = symmetric, temporally related to a dopamine antagonist (antipsychotic/metoclopramide) → always review the drug chart.
  • "Parkinson's plus" red flags (atypical syndrome, poor levodopa response): early falls (PSP), early autonomic failure (MSA), early dementia/visual hallucinations (Lewy body), vertical gaze palsy (PSP), symmetry.
The rule (high-yield): asymmetric onset + resting tremor + good levodopa response = idiopathic Parkinson's; symmetry, early falls/dementia/autonomic failure, or poor levodopa response → think a mimic.
The dopamine / basal ganglia mechanism
  • Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta → ↓dopamine to the striatum:
    • dopamine normally facilitates movement (excites the direct pathway via D1, inhibits the indirect pathway via D2)
    • ↓dopamine → the movement-suppressing indirect pathway dominates → excess inhibition of the thalamus/cortex → reduced movement (bradykinesia, rigidity)
  • Pathology: Lewy bodies (intracellular α-synuclein aggregates) in surviving neurones — the pathological hallmark (shared with Lewy body dementia).
The therapeutic corollary (high-yield): restore dopamine → improve symptoms (levodopa etc.); block dopamine (antipsychotics) → worsen Parkinson's/parkinsonism; suddenly withdraw dopaminergic drugs → NMS / parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia.
Clinical features: the motor triad
📷 Image placeholder — Parkinsonian posture and gait — stooped flexed posture, reduced arm swing, shuffling/festinant gait, hypomimic (mask-like) face and a “pill-rolling” resting tremor

The classic triad (TRAP):

FeatureDetail
Tremorresting tremor, ~4–6 Hz, "pill-rolling", asymmetric, worse at rest / with distraction, improves with movement
Rigidity"cogwheel" (tremor superimposed on lead-pipe) rigidity — increased tone throughout the range
Akinesia / Bradykinesiaslowness + poverty of movement — the core diagnostic feature; micrographia, reduced arm swing, shuffling festinant gait, difficulty initiating movement, hypomimia (mask-like face)
Postural instabilityimpaired balance (later feature) → falls
High-yield: bradykinesia is essential for the diagnosis — a resting tremor alone isn't Parkinson's. Parkinson's is characteristically asymmetric (starts on one side) — a key discriminator from mimics. Gait: stooped posture, reduced arm swing, shuffling/festinating gait, freezing, difficulty turning.
Non-motor features (often precede motor symptoms)
  • Anosmia (loss of smell — early), REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams — an early marker), constipation, depression/anxiety.
  • Autonomic: postural hypotension, urinary symptoms, erectile dysfunction.
  • Cognitive: dementia (late — Parkinson's dementia; if dementia is early/prominent → Lewy body dementia), hallucinations.
The prodrome (high-yield): anosmia + REM sleep behaviour disorder + constipation + depression can predate the motor diagnosis by years and drive quality of life.
Diagnosis / investigations
📷 Image placeholder — DaTSCAN (dopamine transporter SPECT) — reduced/asymmetric putaminal uptake (“comma” becomes a “full stop”) supporting nigrostriatal degeneration
  • Diagnosis is CLINICAL — based on the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria (bradykinesia + at least one of rigidity / resting tremor / postural instability, with supportive features and no red flags for a mimic).
  • Do NOT routinely image — MRI / DaTSCAN (SPECT) only if needed to distinguish Parkinson's from essential tremor or atypical syndromes (DaTSCAN shows reduced dopaminergic uptake in Parkinson's, normal in essential tremor).
  • Trial of levodopa: a good response supports idiopathic Parkinson's (poor response → think a mimic).
  • Review the drug chart (exclude drug-induced); consider Wilson's in young patients (copper studies).
Management (NICE NG71)
The overarching principle: dopaminergic therapy titrated to symptoms + MDT; the first-line choice depends on whether motor symptoms affect quality of life; never stop Parkinson's drugs abruptly.

First-line pharmacotherapy (the key NICE split — high-yield):

  • If motor symptoms DO affect quality of life → offer LEVODOPA (most effective for motor symptoms + activities of daily living — but more motor complications long-term).
  • If motor symptoms DON'T yet affect quality of life → a choice of levodopa, a (non-ergot) dopamine agonist, or a MAO-B inhibitor (less motor improvement, but fewer motor complications).

The main drug classes:

ClassExamplesNotes
Levodopa (+ decarboxylase inhibitor)co-careldopa, co-beneldopamost effective; carbidopa/benserazide prevents peripheral conversion (↓nausea); long-term → motor complications
Dopamine agonists (non-ergot)ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotinefewer motor complications; watch impulse-control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality), hallucinations, somnolence
MAO-B inhibitorsrasagiline, selegilineblock dopamine breakdown; mild benefit; useful early/adjunct
COMT inhibitorsentacaponeadjunct to levodopa — prolong its action (reduce "wearing off")
Amantadine—for dyskinesia
Anticholinergicsprocyclidinemainly tremor in younger patients; avoid in elderly (confusion)
Levodopa long-term motor complications (high-yield): "wearing off" (benefit fades before the next dose), "on-off" fluctuations, dyskinesias (involuntary movements at peak dose) → managed by adjuncts (dopamine agonists / MAO-B / COMT inhibitors), fractionating doses, or advanced therapies.
  • Advanced / other: deep brain stimulation (DBS) — for motor fluctuations/dyskinesia refractory to medication; apomorphine (subcutaneous), intrajejunal levodopa gel for advanced disease.
Critical safety points (high-yield): NEVER stop Parkinson's medication abruptly (or allow missed doses, e.g. NBM/absorption failure) → risk of acute akinesia + neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid dopamine-blocking drugs (typical antipsychotics, metoclopramide) — use domperidone (doesn't cross the BBB) for nausea, quetiapine/clozapine if an antipsychotic is needed. MDT care: Parkinson's nurse specialist, physiotherapy, OT, SALT, dietitian; treat non-motor symptoms.
Exam pearls
What it is
Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra → dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia; Lewy bodies (α-synuclein).
Motor triad (TRAP)
Resting "pill-rolling" tremor (4–6 Hz), cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia (essential), postural instability — ASYMMETRIC onset.
Bradykinesia is essential
Micrographia, shuffling festinant gait, hypomimia, reduced arm swing.
Non-motor (often precede)
Anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation, depression.
Diagnosis is CLINICAL
UK Brain Bank criteria; DaTSCAN only to distinguish from essential tremor (action tremor, symmetric, alcohol-responsive, no bradykinesia).
Mimics
Drug-induced (antipsychotics/metoclopramide — symmetric), vascular, Lewy body dementia (early dementia/hallucinations), PSP (falls, vertical gaze palsy), MSA (autonomic failure).
Management (NICE)
Motor symptoms affect QoL → levodopa; don't → choice of levodopa / dopamine agonist / MAO-B inhibitor.
Drug caveats
Levodopa = most effective but → wearing-off, on-off, dyskinesias; dopamine agonists → impulse-control disorders.
Safety
NEVER stop Parkinson's drugs abruptly (→ acute akinesia/NMS); avoid dopamine blockers (domperidone for nausea, quetiapine/clozapine if antipsychotic needed); DBS for refractory motor complications.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Neuroleptic Ma:
What & why
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) = a rare but life-threatening reaction to dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics) — or to sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs (e.g. levodopa) — characterised by fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental state.
The core concept: NMS is fundamentally a state of acute dopamine deficiency/blockade in the CNS → and the whole tetrad follows from that. Its danger lies in hyperthermia + rhabdomyolysis (from the rigidity), which can cause AKI and death. The clinical priorities are recognising it early, stopping the offending drug, and aggressive supportive cooling/hydration — and distinguishing it from its main mimic, serotonin syndrome.
  • A drug emergency; occurs with typical > atypical antipsychotics but any dopamine antagonist (incl. antiemetics like metoclopramide) can cause it.
The decisive fork — NMS vs serotonin syndrome vs the mimics

The critical differential — because management differs and they're easily confused:

NMSSerotonin syndrome
Triggerdopamine antagonist (antipsychotic) / levodopa withdrawalserotonergic drug (SSRI, MAOI, triptan, tramadol)
Onsetslow (days)rapid (hours)
Neuromuscular"lead-pipe" rigidity, HYPOreflexiaclonus, HYPERreflexia, myoclonus
Pupilsnormaldilated (mydriasis)
GI—diarrhoea common
Key drugdantrolene / bromocriptinecyproheptadine
The rule (high-yield): NMS = rigidity + hyporeflexia, slow onset (antipsychotic); serotonin syndrome = clonus + hyperreflexia + mydriasis, rapid onset (serotonergic drug).
  • Other mimics to exclude: malignant hyperthermia (anaesthetic-triggered — succinylcholine/volatiles), sepsis/CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis), anticholinergic toxicity, thyroid storm.
The mechanism — why it happens
  • Dopamine blockade: antipsychotics block D2 dopamine receptors → central dopamine deficiency:
    • in the hypothalamus → impaired thermoregulation → hyperthermia
    • in the basal ganglia/nigrostriatal pathway → muscle rigidity (and the rigidity itself generates heat → worsens hyperthermia)
  • Dopamine block also triggers ↑↑ glutamate release → neurotoxicity.
  • Levodopa withdrawal: suddenly stopping levodopa (or a dopamine agonist) in a Parkinson's patient causes the same acute dopamine-deficient state → NMS-like syndrome ("parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia").
The rigidity → rhabdomyolysis cascade (high-yield): sustained muscle rigidity → muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) → ↑↑CK → myoglobin → AKI.
Clinical features — the tetrad
  • Onset within hours to days of starting (or increasing) an antipsychotic — classically develops over 1–3 days.
FeatureDetail
Fever (hyperthermia)often high (>38–40°C)
Muscle rigiditygeneralised "lead-pipe" rigidity
Autonomic labilityhypertension, tachycardia, tachypnoea, labile BP, sweating
Altered mental stateagitated delirium with confusion, fluctuating consciousness
The mnemonic — "FEVER": Fever, Encephalopathy (altered mental state), Vitals unstable (autonomic), Elevated CK/enzymes, Rigidity.
Investigations
  • Raised CK — often markedly elevated (from rhabdomyolysis) — the key supporting test.
  • Leucocytosis — raised white cell count.
  • AKI secondary to rhabdomyolysis — myoglobinuria → acute kidney injury; check U&E, myoglobin.
  • Also: metabolic acidosis, ↑LFTs, deranged electrolytes; exclude infection (cultures, consider LP/CT to exclude CNS infection — a key mimic).
Diagnosis is clinical — recent dopamine antagonist + the tetrad + supportive labs.
Management — a medical emergency
The overarching principle: STOP the offending drug + aggressive supportive care (cooling + hydration) + specific pharmacotherapy in severe cases.
  • 1. Stop the antipsychotic — the immediate, essential step; if due to levodopa withdrawal → restart the dopaminergic drug.
  • 2. Supportive care (the mainstay):
    • IV fluids — aggressive hydration to prevent renal failure (protect kidneys from myoglobin), maintain urine output
    • Active cooling for hyperthermia
    • manage in a high-dependency/ICU setting; monitor + support airway/breathing/circulation; correct electrolytes; VTE prophylaxis (immobile, high-risk)
  • 3. Specific pharmacotherapy (severe cases):
    • Dantrolene — a muscle relaxant (reduces rigidity + heat generation)
    • Bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist) — restores dopaminergic tone (counters the block)
    • Benzodiazepines (e.g. lorazepam) — for agitation / mild cases
  • 4. After recovery: NMS carries significant mortality; rechallenge with antipsychotics only cautiously (lower-potency/atypical agent, low dose, slow, after full recovery) given recurrence risk.
Exam pearls
What it is
Life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) or sudden levodopa withdrawal; dopamine blockade → the syndrome.
Onset & tetrad
Onset over days (slow); tetrad = FEVER + "lead-pipe" RIGIDITY + AUTONOMIC instability + ALTERED mental state.
Investigations
↑↑CK (rhabdomyolysis), leucocytosis, AKI (myoglobinuria); exclude infection.
NMS vs serotonin syndrome
NMS = rigidity + HYPOreflexia, slow onset (antipsychotic); serotonin syndrome = clonus + HYPERreflexia + mydriasis, rapid onset (serotonergic) → cyproheptadine.
Also exclude
Malignant hyperthermia (anaesthetic-triggered), sepsis, thyroid storm.
Management
STOP the antipsychotic (or restart levodopa if withdrawal) + IV fluids (prevent AKI) + active cooling + dantrolene (rigidity) + bromocriptine (dopamine agonist); ICU.
Key danger
Rhabdomyolysis → AKI; any dopamine antagonist (incl. metoclopramide) can cause it.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Muscular Dystr:
What & why
The muscular dystrophies = a group of inherited disorders causing progressive muscle weakness and wasting, due to genetic defects in muscle structural proteins (most importantly dystrophin).
The core concept: these are primary muscle (myopathic) diseases — the defect is in the muscle fibre itself, not the nerve. The prototype is Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), caused by absent dystrophin → a young boy with progressive proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower's sign, and a very high CK. The key skills: recognise the myopathic pattern (proximal weakness), know the X-linked inheritance, and anticipate the cardiac + respiratory complications that determine prognosis.
  • Duchenne is the commonest and most severe; Becker is the milder allelic form; myotonic dystrophy is the commonest adult-onset dystrophy.
The decisive fork — which dystrophy?
Duchenne (DMD)Becker (BMD)Myotonic dystrophy
Gene/proteindystrophin — ABSENT (frameshift)dystrophin — reduced/abnormal (in-frame)DMPK gene (CTG trinucleotide repeat)
InheritanceX-linked recessiveX-linked recessiveautosomal dominant
Onsetearly (~5 yrs)later (teens–adult)adulthood (variable)
Severitysevere — wheelchair by ~12, death in 20s–30smilder, slowermultisystem
HallmarkGower's, calf pseudohypertrophy, ↑↑CKas DMD but mildermyotonia (delayed relaxation) + distal weakness + systemic
Duchenne vs Becker: same gene (dystrophin), different mutation — DMD = frameshift → no dystrophin → severe, early; BMD = in-frame → some functional dystrophin → milder, later. Myotonic dystrophy is different: autosomal dominant, a trinucleotide-repeat disorder, with myotonia + a multisystem picture.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy — the prototype
  • Genetics: X-linked recessive defect in the dystrophin gene — dystrophin anchors the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the membrane; without it, fibres are damaged by contraction and degenerate → affects boys, carried by mothers.
  • Progressive proximal muscle weakness from ~5 years — difficulty running, climbing stairs, waddling gait.
  • Calf pseudohypertrophy — calves look bulky but are replaced by fat/fibrous tissue, not true muscle.
  • Gower's sign — the child "walks up" their own legs with their hands to stand from the floor (proximal/pelvic girdle weakness) — the classic sign.
  • ~30% have intellectual impairment.
The key complication: dilated cardiomyopathy — the commonest association; cardiac + respiratory (diaphragm) muscle involvement determines prognosis.
  • Investigations: raised CK (very high — leaked from damaged muscle); definitive = genetic testing (dystrophin gene); muscle biopsy shows absent dystrophin.
  • Management: supportive — no cure; corticosteroids slow progression; plus MDT — physiotherapy, respiratory support (NIV), cardiac surveillance/treatment, orthopaedic care.
The myopathic pattern — dystrophy vs neuropathy vs NMJ
Muscle (dystrophy)Nerve (neuropathy/MND)NMJ (myasthenia)
Weakness patternproximal (shoulder/pelvic girdle)often distal (or mixed in MND)fatigable, ocular/bulbar
Wastingpresent (± pseudohypertrophy)present, with fasciculations (LMN)minimal
Sensationnormaloften abnormal (neuropathy)normal
CKoften very highnormalnormal
The rule: proximal weakness + very high CK + normal sensation = a myopathy/dystrophy (contrast MND = fasciculations + mixed UMN/LMN; myasthenia = fatigable + eye involvement).
Becker muscular dystrophy — the milder allelic form
  • Same gene as Duchenne (dystrophin), same X-linked recessive inheritance — but the mutation is in-frame, so some partially-functional dystrophin is produced → a milder, later-onset, slower course.
  • Features: like DMD but presents later (teens/adulthood), slower progression, often ambulant into adulthood, longer life expectancy.
  • Cardiac involvement (dilated cardiomyopathy) still occurs and can be significant even when skeletal weakness is mild. Raised CK; genetic testing.
Myotonic dystrophy — the commonest adult dystrophy
  • Autosomal dominant, a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion (DMPK gene) → shows anticipation (worsens/earlier onset down generations).
  • The hallmark = myotonia: delayed muscle relaxation — e.g. can't release a handshake/grip, or slow eye opening after forced closure.
Distinctive multisystem picture — unlike DMD, weakness is often distal + facial: facial weakness, ptosis, wasting of temporalis/masseter ("hatchet face"), frontal balding; distal muscle weakness + myotonia; cataracts, cardiac conduction defects/arrhythmias (need ECG monitoring), endocrine (diabetes, hypogonadism/testicular atrophy), cognitive changes, daytime somnolence.
  • Management: supportive; treat/monitor the cardiac conduction defects (pacemaker risk), cataract surgery, manage the systemic features.
General management principles
The overarching principle: no cure → multidisciplinary supportive care; anticipate + treat cardiac and respiratory complications; genetic counselling.
  • No cure — management is supportive via an MDT; corticosteroids slow progression in Duchenne.
  • Cardiac surveillance + treatment: dilated cardiomyopathy (DMD/BMD) and conduction defects (myotonic) — ECG/echo monitoring, heart failure treatment, pacemaker where needed (a leading cause of death).
  • Respiratory support: as respiratory muscles weaken → monitor FVC, non-invasive ventilation (the other leading cause of death).
  • Physiotherapy/OT (maintain function, prevent contractures), orthopaedic care (scoliosis, contractures), mobility aids.
  • Genetic counselling (X-linked in DMD/BMD — carrier mothers, 50% of sons affected; autosomal dominant + anticipation in myotonic).
  • Emerging: exon-skipping / gene therapies for specific DMD mutations.
Exam pearls
What they are
Inherited progressive muscle weakness from defects in muscle structural proteins (dystrophin).
Duchenne (DMD)
X-linked recessive, dystrophin ABSENT; boys, proximal weakness from ~5 yrs, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower's sign, ↑↑CK; 30% intellectual impairment; dilated cardiomyopathy; genetic testing = definitive; supportive + steroids.
Becker (BMD)
Same gene, in-frame mutation → milder, later onset; cardiac involvement still occurs.
DMD vs BMD
Frameshift (no dystrophin, severe) vs in-frame (reduced dystrophin, mild).
Myotonic dystrophy
Autosomal dominant, CTG trinucleotide repeat (anticipation); myotonia (can't release grip) + distal/facial weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, diabetes, frontal balding.
Myopathic pattern
Proximal weakness + very high CK + normal sensation (vs MND, neuropathy, myasthenia).
Management
No cure → MDT supportive; cardiac + respiratory surveillance (leading causes of death); genetic counselling; steroids (DMD).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Multiple Scler:
What & why
Multiple sclerosis (MS) = a chronic, autoimmune, inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (brain + spinal cord + optic nerves) — T-cell-mediated destruction of CNS myelin (oligodendrocytes).
The core concept: MS is fundamentally a disease of "lesions disseminated in space AND time" — ≥2 different CNS sites affected on ≥2 different occasions. The demyelinating plaques are scattered across the CNS (space) and occur as separate episodes over time. Because myelin can be affected anywhere, MS can present with almost any neurological symptom — but sensory disturbance, optic neuritis, and limb weakness are classic.
  • CNS only (oligodendrocytes) — spares peripheral nerves (contrast Guillain-Barré/CMT); typically a young woman (20–40); commoner further from the equator (low vitamin D/latitude link).
The decisive fork — which disease course?
CoursePattern
Relapsing-remitting (RRMS)the commonest (~85%) — discrete relapses followed by remission (partial/full recovery); no progression between relapses
Secondary progressive (SPMS)begins as RRMS, then evolves into steady progression ± superimposed relapses (many RRMS patients eventually convert)
Primary progressive (PPMS)progressive from the outset (no distinct relapses/remissions) — ~10–15%; older, more equal sex ratio
The rule: RRMS is the commonest pattern; a relapse = new neurological symptoms lasting >24h, in the absence of infection/fever, developing over days and recovering over weeks.
Clinical features — demyelination anywhere in the CNS
📷 Image placeholder — Optic neuritis with a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD); and internuclear ophthalmoplegia (failure of adduction + contralateral nystagmus) from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion
SiteFeature
Optic nerveoptic neuritis — the commonest presenting feature: subacute unilateral visual loss + painful eye movements + red desaturation
Spinal cordsensory disturbance, limb weakness (UMN), bladder dysfunction, Lhermitte's sign (electric-shock down the spine on neck flexion), transverse myelitis
Brainstemdiplopia, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), vertigo, facial sensory loss
Cerebellumataxia, intention tremor, dysarthria
Cerebrum / generalcognitive impairment, fatigue (very common), paraesthesia, numbness, trigeminal neuralgia
Classic high-yield signs:
• Optic neuritis — often the first presentation (painful visual loss, ↓colour vision, RAPD).
• Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) — lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) → impaired adduction of one eye + nystagmus in the other (bilateral INO in a young person is very suggestive of MS).
• Lhermitte's sign — neck flexion → electric-shock down the spine (dorsal column).
• Uhthoff's phenomenon — symptoms worsen with heat (hot bath, exercise, fever).
The diagnostic principle — dissemination in space + time

Diagnosis (McDonald criteria) requires lesions disseminated in:

  • SPACE — ≥2 separate CNS locations (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord).
  • TIME — ≥2 separate episodes (clinically, or MRI showing lesions of different ages — simultaneous enhancing + non-enhancing — or CSF oligoclonal bands as a substitute for dissemination in time).
The rule: MS = dissemination in space AND time — one attack in one place isn't enough (that's a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), which may progress to MS).
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — MRI brain in MS — “Dawson's fingers”: ovoid periventricular white-matter plaques oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles (dissemination in space)
  • MRI brain + spinal cord (with contrast) — the key investigation: T2/FLAIR hyperintense demyelinating plaques in characteristic locations (periventricular — "Dawson's fingers", juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord); gadolinium enhancement = active/new lesions (helps establish dissemination in time).
  • Lumbar puncture / CSF: oligoclonal bands (IgG) in CSF but NOT in serum → evidence of intrathecal (CNS) inflammation (can substitute for dissemination in time).
  • Visual evoked potentials (VEPs): delayed but preserved-amplitude responses → evidence of previous optic nerve demyelination.
  • Bloods: to exclude mimics (B12, TFT, ESR/CRP, autoantibodies, aquaporin-4 for NMO, HIV).
The differential — exclude MS mimics
  • Other demyelinating: neuromyelitis optica (NMO/Devic's — aquaporin-4 antibodies), ADEM.
  • Other: B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), SLE/vasculitis, sarcoidosis, Lyme, HIV, CNS lymphoma, functional.
The rule: MS is a diagnosis requiring exclusion of mimics + the space/time criteria.
Management
The overarching principle: treat acute relapses with steroids; reduce relapses/progression with disease-modifying therapy; manage symptoms; MDT care.

Acute relapse:

  • High-dose corticosteroids — methylprednisolone (IV 1 g/day for 3–5 days, or oral 500 mg/day for 5 days) → shortens the relapse duration but does NOT change long-term disability or the disease course.
  • Plasma exchange for severe steroid-refractory relapses. Steroids treat the relapse, not the disease.

Disease-modifying therapy (DMT) — reduces relapse frequency + progression:

  • For relapsing-remitting MS (and active disease): injectables (interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate — older, modest efficacy); orals (dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, fingolimod, cladribine); monoclonal antibodies (high-efficacy) (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab, ofatumumab).
  • Choice balances efficacy vs risk; early effective treatment reduces long-term disability. Ocrelizumab is the main option shown to help primary progressive MS.

Symptomatic management:

  • Spasticity → baclofen, gabapentin (± physiotherapy); fatigue → exercise, amantadine, energy management; bladder → assess residual volume, anticholinergics or catheterisation.
  • Neuropathic pain → amitriptyline/gabapentin/pregabalin; depression (common) → treat; mobility → physio/OT; vitamin D supplementation; MDT (neurology, MS nurse, physio, OT, continence, psychology).
Exam pearls
What it is
Autoimmune demyelination of the CNS (oligodendrocytes; brain/cord/optic nerve); young women 20–40, latitude/vitamin D link.
Diagnosis
Lesions disseminated in SPACE and TIME (McDonald criteria).
Courses
Relapsing-remitting (commonest ~85%), secondary progressive, primary progressive (~10–15%).
Classic features
Optic neuritis (painful visual loss — commonest presentation), internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF), Lhermitte's sign (neck flexion → shock), Uhthoff's (heat worsens), sensory/spinal/bladder involvement, fatigue.
Investigations
MRI (periventricular plaques/"Dawson's fingers", gadolinium enhancement), CSF oligoclonal bands (in CSF not serum), delayed VEPs.
Mimics
NMO (aquaporin-4), B12 deficiency, sarcoid, SLE, Lyme.
Relapse
Methylprednisolone (shortens relapse, no effect on progression); plasma exchange if refractory.
DMT + symptomatic
Interferon/glatiramer → orals → monoclonals (ocrelizumab/natalizumab) reduce relapses; baclofen for spasticity, amantadine for fatigue; MDT + vitamin D.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Motor Neurone:
What & why
Motor neurone disease (MND) = a group of progressive neurodegenerative disorders selectively affecting motor neurones — upper (UMN) and/or lower (LMN) — with NO sensory involvement.
The core concept: the defining signature is combined UMN + LMN signs, WITHOUT sensory loss and WITHOUT eye-movement involvement. That combination — a patient with both wasting/fasciculations (LMN) and spasticity/brisk reflexes (UMN) but normal sensation and normal eye movements — is almost unique to MND, and is the whole diagnostic key. It is relentlessly progressive and incurable — management is disease-slowing + supportive + palliative.
  • Typically late-middle-aged, ± family history; can start focally (a limb, or speech) before spreading.
The decisive fork — which MND subtype?
Subtype% / featuresSigns
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)the commonestBOTH UMN + LMN signs (the classic mix)
Progressive bulbar palsy2nd commonest; worst prognosisaffects muscles of talking + swallowing (bulbar — CN IX–XII)
Progressive muscular atrophybetter prognosisLMN signs only; anterior horn cells
Primary lateral sclerosisslowestUMN signs only
The rule: ALS = commonest, mixed UMN + LMN; progressive bulbar palsy = speech/swallowing, worst prognosis; the others are pure LMN (muscular atrophy) or pure UMN (primary lateral sclerosis).
The core diagnostic signature — mixed UMN + LMN, no sensory, eyes spared
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram: the MND signature — simultaneous LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone) and UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) in the same limb, with NO sensory loss and preserved eye movements

PRESENT — mixed UMN + LMN signs:

LMN signsUMN signs
Muscle wastingincreased tone / spasticity
Reduced tonebrisk (hyper) reflexes
Reduced reflexesupgoing plantar (Babinski)
Fasciculations (muscle twitches)—
The UMN/LMN mechanism: UMNs normally regulate (inhibit) LMNs → UMN damage → LMNs become inappropriately overactive → hyper signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia); LMN damage → the muscle loses its supply → wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia. In ALS both coexist → e.g. a wasted, fasciculating limb (LMN) with brisk reflexes (UMN) — a hallmark combination.
ABSENT — the crucial negatives: NO sensory symptoms/signs (distinguishes from neuropathy, radiculopathy, MS); extraocular (eye) muscles NOT affected (distinguishes from myasthenia gravis); no sphincter (bladder/bowel) involvement (spared until late); cognition usually preserved (though a frontotemporal dementia overlap exists).
Clinical features & presentation
📷 Image placeholder — Clinical image: wasting and fasciculations of the intrinsic hand muscles (“split hand”) and a wasted, fasciculating tongue in bulbar-onset disease
  • Typical patient: late middle age, ± positive family history.
  • Insidious, progressive muscular weakness spreading through the body — limbs, trunk, face, speech.
  • Early complaints: clumsiness, dropping things, tripping, fatigue on exercise, slurring of speech.
  • Bulbar features (progressive bulbar palsy): dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal speech, tongue wasting + fasciculations, aspiration risk.
  • Respiratory: progressive respiratory muscle weakness → breathlessness, orthopnoea, type 2 respiratory failure (the usual cause of death).
The pattern: progressive, painless weakness with mixed UMN/LMN signs, no sensory loss, sparing eye movements → MND.
The decisive fork — MND vs its mimics

MND is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion — rule out treatable mimics:

MimicDiscriminator
Myasthenia gravisfatigable weakness + EYE involvement (ptosis/diplopia); MND spares eyes
Cervical myelopathy / cord compressionsensory level + sphincter signs; MND has no sensory loss → MRI to exclude
Multiple sclerosissensory symptoms, relapsing-remitting, CNS-only
Peripheral neuropathy (CMT, diabetic)sensory involvement; MND is pure motor
Lambert-Eaton / myopathyno UMN signs, no fasciculations
The rule: sensory signs, eye involvement, or sphincter involvement should make you doubt MND and look for a mimic — MND is pure motor, eye-sparing, sphincter-sparing.
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — based on the characteristic UMN + LMN pattern (supported by the El Escorial / Awaji criteria).
  • Nerve conduction studies: normal motor conduction — helps exclude neuropathy/conduction block.
  • EMG: ↓ number of action potentials with ↑ amplitude — reflecting denervation + reinnervation (fewer, larger motor units) → supports LMN involvement.
  • MRI (brain + spinal cord): to exclude cervical cord compression + myelopathy and other structural mimics.
  • Bloods: to exclude mimics (CK mildly raised; exclude metabolic causes).
Management
The overarching principle: no cure → riluzole (modest survival benefit) + multidisciplinary supportive care + NIV + nutrition + early palliative care.
  • No treatment halts or reverses progression.
  • Riluzole (the disease-modifying drug): slows progression in ALS and extends survival modestly (~few months); mechanism: inhibits glutamate (prevents excitotoxicity). Edaravone (an antioxidant) is used in some countries.
  • Respiratory support: non-invasive ventilation (NIV, usually BiPAP) as respiratory muscles weaken → improves both survival and quality of life (a key intervention).
  • Nutrition: for dysphagia → PEG (gastrostomy) feeding is preferred to maintain nutrition (malnutrition worsens prognosis).
  • Multidisciplinary care: MDT (neurology, specialist nurse, physiotherapy, OT, SALT for speech/swallowing, dietitian, respiratory, palliative) improves survival + quality of life.
  • Symptom control: spasticity (baclofen), sialorrhoea/drooling (antimuscarinics, botulinum toxin), cramps, communication aids, emotional lability (pseudobulbar affect).
  • Early palliative care + advance care planning: given the progressive fatal course — discuss ventilation wishes, end-of-life care; involve palliative care early.
Prognosis: patients typically die of respiratory failure or pneumonia — usually within 2–4 years of onset.
Exam pearls
What it is
Progressive degeneration of motor neurones, MIXED UMN + LMN signs, NO sensory loss, EYE MOVEMENTS SPARED, sphincters spared.
Subtypes
ALS (commonest — UMN + LMN), progressive bulbar palsy (speech/swallowing, worst prognosis), progressive muscular atrophy (LMN only), primary lateral sclerosis (UMN only).
Signature combination
A wasted, fasciculating limb (LMN) with brisk reflexes + upgoing plantars (UMN) — and normal sensation.
Key negatives
No sensory signs, eyes spared (vs myasthenia = eye involvement), sphincters spared.
Exclude mimics
Cervical cord compression (MRI — sensory level/sphincters), myasthenia gravis, MS, neuropathy.
Investigations
Clinical diagnosis (El Escorial); EMG = ↓ number of APs with ↑ amplitude (denervation + reinnervation); normal motor conduction; MRI to exclude cord compression.
Management
Riluzole (glutamate/excitotoxicity inhibitor — modest survival benefit); NIV/BiPAP (survival + QoL); PEG feeding; multidisciplinary care; early palliative care.
Prognosis
Death from respiratory failure/pneumonia, usually within 2–4 years.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Meningitis / E:
What & why
Meningitis = inflammation of the meninges (membranes covering the brain/spinal cord) — usually infective (bacterial or viral). Encephalitis = inflammation of the brain parenchyma itself — usually viral (classically HSV).
The core concept: the crucial distinction is where the inflammation is — meningitis affects the coverings (→ meningism: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia) while encephalitis affects the brain substance (→ altered brain function: confusion, personality/behaviour change, seizures, focal deficits). They overlap (meningoencephalitis), but the split guides the two treatment reflexes: bacterial meningitis → immediate antibiotics and encephalitis → immediate aciclovir. Both are time-critical emergencies.
  • Bacterial meningitis has high mortality; do not delay treatment for investigations.
The decisive fork — meninges vs brain
MeningitisEncephalitis
Sitemeninges (coverings)brain parenchyma
HallmarkMENINGISM — headache, neck stiffness, photophobiaALTERED BRAIN FUNCTION — confusion, ↓consciousness, personality/behaviour change, seizures, focal deficits
Commonest causebacterial or viralviral — HSV-1
Treatment refleximmediate antibiotics (if bacterial)immediate IV aciclovir
The rule: meningism (neck stiffness/photophobia) → meningitis; altered mental state / personality change / seizures / focal deficit → encephalitis. They overlap → meningoencephalitis; if in doubt, cover both (antibiotics + aciclovir).
Bacterial vs viral meningitis
📷 Image placeholder — meningococcal non-blanching purpuric rash (negative glass/tumbler test); and Kernig's / Brudzinski's meningism signs
BacterialViral
Severitysevere, life-threateningusually self-limiting
Onsetrapid (hours)more gradual

Bacterial causes by age:

GroupCommon organisms
NeonatesGroup B Strep, E. coli, Listeria
Children / young adultsNeisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), Strep pneumoniae
Elderly / immunocompromised / pregnant+ Listeria monocytogenes (→ add amoxicillin)
Clinical features
  • The classic triad: fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status (all three in a minority — don't wait for the full triad).
  • Meningism: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea/vomiting.
  • Meningeal signs: Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski's sign (neck flexion → involuntary hip/knee flexion).
  • In infants: non-specific — fever, lethargy, poor feeding, irritability, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry.
  • Raised ICP signs: reduced consciousness, papilloedema, focal signs, seizures.
Meningococcal septicaemia: a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (doesn't fade under a glass — "tumbler test") → septicaemia, a life-threatening emergency (can occur with or without meningitis).
Investigations
  • Blood cultures + bloods: FBC, CRP, whole-blood PCR for meningococcal/pneumococcal DNA, glucose (for CSF:blood ratio), U&E, clotting.
  • Lumbar puncture + CSF (the key test): send for cell count/differential, protein, glucose (with paired blood glucose), Gram stain, culture, PCR (viral/bacterial).

CSF interpretation:

BacterialViralTB/fungal
Appearanceturbid/cloudyclearfibrin web
Cells↑↑ neutrophils (polymorphs)↑ lymphocytes↑ lymphocytes
Protein↑↑ highnormal/mildly ↑↑↑ high
Glucose (CSF:blood)↓↓ low (<0.5)normal↓ low
Contraindications to LP: signs of raised ICP / focal neurology / GCS drop / haemodynamic instability / coagulopathy → do NOT do LP (coning risk) → CT first + start treatment empirically. CRITICAL: do NOT delay antibiotics for the LP/CT — treat first if there's any delay.
Management of meningitis (NICE NG240)
The overarching principle: don't delay antibiotics; community benzylpenicillin; hospital ceftriaxone + dexamethasone; add amoxicillin for Listeria cover; notify + prophylaxis for contacts.
  • Community / pre-hospital: suspected meningococcal disease (esp. non-blanching rash) → IM/IV benzylpenicillin immediately before hospital transfer (don't delay).

Hospital — empirical treatment (start within 1 hour):

  • IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) = first-line empirical antibiotic.
  • ADD IV amoxicillin if Listeria risk (neonates, >50/elderly, immunocompromised, pregnant).
  • IV dexamethasone — give with/just before antibiotics (in those >3 months) → reduces neurological complications, esp. hearing loss (pneumococcal).
  • Do NOT routinely give aciclovir unless HSV encephalitis suspected; tailor to culture/PCR (usual course ~10 days).
  • Supportive: ABCDE, fluids/shock management (septicaemia), ICU if severe, treat raised ICP/seizures.
  • Public health: meningitis + meningococcal disease are NOTIFIABLE → inform public health; prophylaxis for close contacts (ciprofloxacin single dose, or rifampicin).
Complications: sensorineural hearing loss (commonest — audiology follow-up), seizures/epilepsy, hydrocephalus, focal deficits, cognitive impairment, death; Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal septicaemia).
Encephalitis — the "aciclovir" reflex
📷 Image placeholder — HSV encephalitis — MRI showing unilateral medial temporal lobe oedema/hyperintensity
Inflammation of the brain parenchyma — usually viral; the crucial treatable cause is herpes simplex virus (HSV-1).
  • Causes: HSV-1 (the key one — treatable), other herpesviruses (VZV, CMV, EBV), enteroviruses, and autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor — the key non-infective cause).

Clinical features:

  • Altered mental state / ↓consciousness, confusion, personality + behaviour change; fever, headache, seizures, focal neurology (dysphasia, hemiparesis).
  • HSV encephalitis targets the temporal lobes → memory/behaviour/psychiatric features (can mimic psychiatric illness).

Investigations:

  • LP/CSF: lymphocytic picture (like viral meningitis), ↑protein, normal glucose; HSV PCR (the diagnostic test — but can be negative very early).
  • MRI: temporal lobe changes (oedema/hyperintensity) in HSV encephalitis.
  • EEG: may show temporal lobe abnormalities/periodic discharges.
Management — the reflex: suspected encephalitis → start IV aciclovir NOW (empirically — do NOT wait for PCR; early treatment saves brain/lives; continue if HSV confirmed). Supportive care (ICU, seizures, raised ICP); treat autoimmune encephalitis with immunotherapy (steroids/IVIG) + tumour search. Mirrors "suspected bacterial meningitis → start antibiotics now".
Exam pearls
Meningitis vs encephalitis
Meningitis = meninges (MENINGISM: neck stiffness/photophobia); encephalitis = brain parenchyma (ALTERED BRAIN FUNCTION: confusion, behaviour change, seizures); overlap = meningoencephalitis.
Bacterial causes by age
Neonates → GBS/E. coli/Listeria; children/adults → meningococcus/pneumococcus; elderly/pregnant/immunocompromised → + Listeria (add amoxicillin).
Signs
Kernig's, Brudzinski's; non-blanching rash → meningococcal septicaemia (tumbler test — emergency).
CSF
Bacterial = neutrophils, ↑↑protein, ↓↓glucose, turbid; viral = lymphocytes, normal glucose, clear; TB = lymphocytes, ↑↑protein, ↓glucose, fibrin web.
LP caution
Do NOT do LP if raised ICP/focal signs → CT + treat empirically; NEVER delay antibiotics.
Meningitis management
Community → IM benzylpenicillin; hospital → IV ceftriaxone + dexamethasone (+ amoxicillin if Listeria risk); notifiable + contact prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin); commonest complication = hearing loss.
Encephalitis
Usually HSV-1 → temporal lobes; CSF lymphocytic + HSV PCR, MRI temporal lobe changes; START IV ACICLOVIR IMMEDIATELY (empirically); consider autoimmune (anti-NMDA).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ménière's Dise:
What & why
Ménière's disease = a chronic inner-ear disorder — the triad of episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus, with aural fullness — caused by endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the inner ear).
The core concept: the diagnosis is the classic triad + ear fullness, in episodic attacks lasting minutes–hours, on a background of fluctuating then progressive sensorineural hearing loss. It sits within the wider peripheral vertigo differential — so the key skill is placing it correctly among the causes of vertigo (BPPV, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, acoustic neuroma) and distinguishing peripheral from central vertigo (the must-not-miss being a posterior circulation stroke).
  • Typically middle-aged adults; usually unilateral (initially); a relapsing condition that can significantly affect quality of life.
The decisive fork — peripheral vs central vertigo

Before diagnosing Ménière's (a peripheral cause), place the vertigo — peripheral (inner ear) vs central (brainstem/cerebellum); the central causes are the dangerous ones:

FeaturePeripheral (inner ear)Central (brainstem/cerebellum)
Onsetsuddengradual (except stroke)
Durationshort (secs–mins)persistent
Hearing loss/tinnitusoften present (except BPPV)usually absent
Coordinationintactimpaired (cerebellar signs)
Other neurologynoneataxia, diplopia, CN signs, limb signs
HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) — distinguishes peripheral from central: head impulse test shows a corrective saccade in peripheral dysfunction (eyes overshoot then refixate) but is normal in central. A reassuringly peripheral picture = abnormal head impulse + unidirectional horizontal nystagmus + no skew.
The rule: peripheral vertigo = sudden, short-lived, ± hearing loss/tinnitus, intact coordination; central = persistent + other neurology → exclude stroke (also tumour, MS, vestibular migraine).
The peripheral vertigo differential — where Ménière's sits
CauseDiscriminator
Ménière's diseasetriad (vertigo + SNHL + tinnitus) + aural fullness, attacks mins–hours, recurrent
BPPVbrief (seconds) vertigo triggered by head position; no hearing loss; Dix-Hallpike +ve, treated with Epley
Vestibular neuronitisacute prolonged vertigo (days) after viral illness; NO hearing loss
Labyrinthitislike vestibular neuronitis + hearing loss (labyrinth involved)
Acoustic neuromagradual unilateral SNHL + tinnitus + imbalance
The key discriminators: Ménière's = the triad + fullness, attacks lasting mins–hours; BPPV = seconds, positional, no hearing loss; vestibular neuronitis = no hearing loss; labyrinthitis = with hearing loss.
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — Cross-section of the membranous labyrinth showing endolymphatic hydrops — distension of the endolymphatic space causing combined cochlear (hearing loss/tinnitus) and vestibular (vertigo) dysfunction
  • Endolymphatic hydrops: excess endolymph accumulates in the membranous labyrinth (impaired reabsorption/drainage) → distension → episodic dysfunction of the cochlea (hearing loss + tinnitus) and vestibular apparatus (vertigo).
  • This explains the fluctuating early course and the combined cochlear + vestibular symptoms.
Clinical features — the triad + fullness
📷 Image placeholder — The Ménière’s triad — episodic vertigo (minutes–hours) + fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus, with a sense of aural fullness in the affected ear
FeatureDetail
Episodic vertigorecurrent attacks lasting minutes to hours (often with nausea/vomiting); the most disabling feature
Sensorineural hearing lossfluctuating initially (typically low-frequency), becoming progressive + permanent; usually unilateral
Tinnitusin the affected ear
Aural fullnessa sense of pressure/fullness in the affected ear
The attack pattern: clusters of attacks over weeks, with periods of remission; between attacks the patient may be well (early), but hearing progressively declines over years. Nystagmus during attacks; drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) — sudden falls without warning — occur in later disease.
Assessment / investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Pure-tone audiogram of early Ménière’s — a fluctuating low-frequency (rising) sensorineural hearing loss that later becomes progressive/permanent
  • Diagnosis is clinical — the characteristic triad + episodic pattern; usually a specialist (ENT) diagnosis.
  • Audiometry: confirms a sensorineural pattern of hearing loss (typically low-frequency, fluctuating early) — the key test.
  • Exclude other causes: MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma (unilateral SNHL) and central causes; the vertigo differential (BPPV → Dix-Hallpike; central → HINTS).
  • Rinne/Weber confirm sensorineural loss.
Management
The overarching principle: acute symptom relief (vestibular sedatives) + long-term prophylaxis (betahistine + lifestyle) + specialist input; inform DVLA.
  • Acute attack: vestibular sedatives / antiemetics — prochlorperazine (fast relief of vertigo/nausea), antihistamines (cyclizine, cinnarizine) — short-term only; reassurance, safe environment.
  • Prophylaxis: betahistine (a histamine analogue) — first-line to reduce attack frequency; lifestyle — low-salt diet, reduce caffeine/alcohol, avoid triggers (a mainstay); diuretics (e.g. thiazide) sometimes used to reduce endolymph.
  • Refractory (specialist): intratympanic steroids or intratympanic gentamicin (ablates vestibular function — but ototoxic, hearing-loss risk); surgery (endolymphatic sac decompression, labyrinthectomy).
  • Supportive: hearing aids (for progressive SNHL), vestibular rehabilitation, tinnitus support.
DVLA: patients must inform the DVLA and stop driving during active disease (sudden, unpredictable vertigo attacks) until symptoms are controlled.
Exam pearls
What it is
Episodic vertigo + sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness, from endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph).
Attack pattern
Attacks last minutes–hours, recurrent, usually unilateral; hearing loss fluctuates then becomes progressive/permanent.
Peripheral vs central (HINTS)
Peripheral = sudden, short, ± hearing loss, intact coordination; central = persistent + other neurology → exclude stroke.
vs other peripheral causes
BPPV (seconds, positional, no hearing loss, Dix-Hallpike/Epley), vestibular neuronitis (no hearing loss), labyrinthitis (+ hearing loss), acoustic neuroma (gradual unilateral SNHL).
Investigations
Audiometry (sensorineural, low-frequency fluctuating); MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma.
Management
Acute → prochlorperazine/antihistamines (vestibular sedatives); prophylaxis → betahistine + low-salt diet; refractory → intratympanic steroids/gentamicin, surgery; hearing aids.
Other
Inform the DVLA (sudden vertigo attacks); usually specialist (ENT) managed.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Idiopathic Int:
What & why
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) = raised intracranial pressure with NO identifiable cause (no mass, no hydrocephalus, no venous thrombosis), causing headache and papilloedema — with a normal CSF composition (formerly "benign intracranial hypertension" / "pseudotumour cerebri").
The core concept: raised ICP without a space-occupying lesion — it mimics a brain tumour clinically (headache + papilloedema) but imaging is normal. The classic patient is a young obese woman, and the overriding priority is protecting VISION — the papilloedema can cause permanent visual loss if untreated. It's a diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Increasingly common (rising with obesity); strong female + obesity association; "benign" is a misnomer given the sight-threatening risk.
The decisive fork — idiopathic or secondary raised ICP?

IIH is diagnosed only after excluding secondary causes of raised ICP:

Must excludeHow
Space-occupying lesion (tumour, abscess)normal neuroimaging (MRI)
Hydrocephalusnormal/small ventricles on imaging (not dilated)
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosisMR/CT venography (a key mimic — same young-woman/COCP demographic)
Meningitisnormal CSF (cells/protein/glucose)
The rule: IIH = raised ICP (raised CSF opening pressure) + papilloedema + NORMAL imaging + NORMAL CSF composition, with no other cause (the modified Dandy criteria). The key mimic to exclude: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — same demographic (young woman, COCP, pregnancy) → always do venography.
Risk factors
  • The classic patient: a young obese female — the single most important association.
  • Other risk factors: pregnancy, combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP), steroids, tetracyclines, retinoids (isotretinoin), lithium; excess vitamin A.
The drug mnemonic: think "the acne/hormone drugs" — tetracyclines (acne antibiotics) and retinoids (isotretinoin) are classic culprits (young women on acne treatment).
Clinical features
📷 Image placeholder — bilateral papilloedema — a swollen optic disc with blurred margins, engorged veins and loss of the optic cup (the cardinal sign of raised ICP in IIH)
FeatureDetail
Headachefeatures of raised ICP — worse in the morning, on coughing/straining/lying down
Papilloedemabilateral optic disc swelling — the key sign; risk to vision
Visual symptomsblurred vision, transient visual obscurations (brief greying with posture change), enlarged blind spot, visual field loss
CN VI (6th nerve) palsyfalse localising sign (horizontal diplopia)
Pulsatile tinnitus"whooshing" in the ears — a characteristic symptom
The vision points: papilloedema → enlarged blind spot → progressive visual field loss → permanent blindness if untreated — the reason IIH needs urgent treatment; CN VI palsy is a false localising sign (not a focal lesion). Consciousness + cognition are preserved (unlike a mass lesion) — helps distinguish from a tumour.
Investigations
  • Neuroimaging FIRST (MRI + MR venography): normal (no mass, no hydrocephalus, excludes venous sinus thrombosis) — must be done before LP.
  • Lumbar puncture (diagnostic): raised CSF opening pressure (>25 cmH₂O) — the diagnostic finding; normal CSF composition (distinguishes from meningitis). LP can also be therapeutic (removing CSF transiently lowers pressure) — safe here because imaging is normal.
  • Ophthalmology (essential): fundoscopy (papilloedema), visual fields (perimetry), visual acuity, OCT — to monitor vision (the key outcome measure).
Management
The overarching principle: weight loss + acetazolamide, with the overriding goal of protecting vision; escalate to surgery if sight-threatening.
  • Conservative: weight loss (the key disease-modifying step — even modest loss reduces ICP and can be curative); stop the causative drug (COCP, tetracyclines, retinoids, steroids).
  • Acetazolamide (1st-line drug): a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor → reduces CSF production.
  • Topiramate: an alternative; also causes weight loss (a useful dual benefit); furosemide is a further option.
  • Therapeutic LP — for temporary relief (can repeat).

Sight-threatening / refractory → surgery (vision deteriorating despite medical treatment):

  • CSF diversion — VP or lumboperitoneal shunt (lowers ICP).
  • Optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) — a window in the optic nerve sheath to protect the optic nerve/vision (preferred if vision-threatening without severe headache).
  • Venous sinus stenting — for selected cases with transverse sinus stenosis + a pressure gradient.
Emerging: GLP-1 receptor agonists and bariatric surgery for weight management (given obesity's central role). Monitor vision throughout (serial visual fields) — the treatment target. Beware medication-overuse headache.
Exam pearls
What it is
Raised ICP with NO identifiable cause (normal imaging, normal CSF composition, raised CSF opening pressure) — mimics a brain tumour; a diagnosis of exclusion.
Classic patient
Young, obese woman; drugs — COCP, tetracyclines, retinoids (isotretinoin), steroids, lithium.
Features
Headache (raised ICP) + bilateral papilloedema + visual symptoms (blurring, transient obscurations, enlarged blind spot) + CN VI palsy (false localising) + pulsatile tinnitus.
Exclude CVST
Same demographic → do venography.
Investigations
MRI + MR venography (normal) → LP (raised opening pressure, normal CSF); monitor visual fields (vision is the key outcome).
Management
Weight loss + acetazolamide (± topiramate); stop causative drug; therapeutic LP; sight-threatening → CSF shunt / optic nerve sheath fenestration / venous sinus stenting.
The priority
Protect VISION (untreated papilloedema → permanent visual loss).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hydrocephalus:
What & why
Hydrocephalus = an accumulation of CSF within the cerebral ventricles causing ventricular dilatation — from a mismatch between CSF production, flow, and absorption.
The core concept: CSF is continuously produced (choroid plexus), circulates through the ventricles, and is absorbed (arachnoid villi) — a lesion anywhere in that loop causes a backlog → ventricular dilatation → raised ICP → brain injury. The classification hinges on where the problem is: obstruction of flow (obstructive) vs impaired absorption/overproduction (non-obstructive/communicating). Normal pressure hydrocephalus is the important special case.
  • Can be acute (raised ICP emergency) or chronic; a treatable cause of neurological decline.
The CSF circulation
  • Produced by the choroid plexus (in the ventricles).
  • Flows: lateral ventricles → (foramina of Monro) → third ventricle → (cerebral aqueduct) → fourth ventricle → (foramina of Luschka/Magendie) → subarachnoid space.
  • Absorbed by the arachnoid granulations/villi into venous blood.
The rule: hydrocephalus results from obstruction of flow, impaired absorption, or (rarely) overproduction — the site of the problem defines the type.
The decisive fork — obstructive vs non-obstructive
Obstructive (non-communicating)Non-obstructive (communicating)
Mechanismblockage of the ventricular drainage system / CSF flowreduced absorption by the arachnoid villi (or rarely ↑ production)
Causesobstructing tumour or cyst, congenital aqueduct stenosisinfective meningitis, SAH, congenital (Dandy-Walker), normal pressure hydrocephalus
Site of problemwithin the ventricular system (flow blocked)outside (absorption at the arachnoid villi)
The rules: obstructive = a block in CSF flow (tumour, cyst, aqueduct stenosis) → CSF can't get out of the ventricles; non-obstructive (communicating) = impaired absorption (after meningitis or SAH the arachnoid villi get "clogged", or NPH). Critical: do NOT do an LP in obstructive hydrocephalus — removing CSF below a block risks coning/herniation.
Clinical features

Features of raised ICP — the typical acute/subacute presentation:

FeatureDetail
Headacheworse in the morning (following prolonged lying supine overnight); worse on coughing/bending
Nausea & vomitingraised ICP
Papilloedemaraised ICP (fundoscopy)
Alsoreduced consciousness, visual disturbance (CN VI palsy — false localising), drowsiness
In infants/children: because the skull sutures are open → increasing head circumference, bulging fontanelle, "sunset eyes" (upward gaze palsy), irritability, poor feeding.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) — the special case
NPH = ventricular dilatation with NORMAL CSF pressure — mostly idiopathic. The characteristic triad — "Wet, Wobbly & Wacky":
• Wet = urinary incontinence
• Wobbly = gait abnormality (magnetic, shuffling, wide-based apraxic gait — often earliest/most responsive)
• Wacky = dementia (cognitive decline)
  • The key point: a reversible cause of dementia + gait disturbance — must be distinguished from Alzheimer's/other dementias, and can improve with CSF shunting.
  • Imaging: ventriculomegaly WITHOUT sulcal enlargement (big ventricles but not the generalised atrophy of Alzheimer's — the ventricles are disproportionately large).
Investigations
  • 1st-line: CT head — shows ventricular enlargement (not always), loss of the sulcal/gyral pattern, and CSF exudation from the ventricles (periventricular lucency — transependymal CSF flow).
  • NPH on imaging: ventriculomegaly without sulcal enlargement.
  • MRI: better detail — identify the level of obstruction (e.g. aqueduct stenosis) and the cause (tumour).
  • Lumbar puncture: diagnostic + therapeutic (measures pressure; removing CSF can help) — but DO NOT do an LP in obstructive hydrocephalus (coning risk). In NPH, a large-volume LP ("tap test") that transiently improves gait predicts a good response to shunting.
Management
The overarching principle: relieve raised ICP (EVD acutely), then definitive CSF diversion (VP shunt) + treat the underlying cause.
  • Acute — 1st-line: external ventricular drain (EVD) — a temporary measure to reduce ICP (drains CSF externally in an emergency).
  • Medical: acetazolamide and furosemide — reduce CSF secretion by the choroid plexus (temporising; acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor).
  • Definitive (depends on the cause): treat the cause (e.g. debulking a resectable obstructing tumour); ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt for long-term CSF drainage (ventricles → peritoneum) — the mainstay for chronic/NPH; endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) — an alternative for obstructive hydrocephalus (creates a new drainage route, bypassing the block).
  • NPH: VP shunt — gait is the most likely symptom to improve.
Shunt complications: infection, blockage, over-drainage → be alert for shunt malfunction (recurrent raised ICP).
Exam pearls
What it is
CSF accumulation in the ventricles → ventricular dilatation → raised ICP; from obstruction, impaired absorption, or (rarely) overproduction.
Obstructive vs communicating
Obstructive (non-communicating) = block in CSF flow (tumour, cyst, aqueduct stenosis); non-obstructive (communicating) = impaired absorption (post-meningitis/SAH, Dandy-Walker, NPH).
No LP if obstructive
Removing CSF below a block risks coning.
Features
Raised ICP — morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema; infants → ↑head circumference, bulging fontanelle, sunset eyes.
NPH = "Wet, Wobbly, Wacky"
Incontinence + gait + dementia, with normal CSF pressure + ventriculomegaly without sulcal atrophy → a reversible dementia → VP shunt.
Investigations
CT 1st-line (ventricular enlargement, loss of sulcal pattern, periventricular CSF exudation); LP diagnostic + therapeutic (NOT if obstructive).
Management
Acute → external ventricular drain (EVD); acetazolamide/furosemide (↓CSF production); definitive → VP shunt + treat cause; ETV for obstructive.
Shunt complications
Infection, blockage, over-drainage.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Huntington's D:
What & why
Huntington's disease (HD) = an autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing a triad of movement disorder (chorea), cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbance.
The core concept: the archetypal CAG trinucleotide repeat disorder — an expanded repeat in the HTT gene → toxic huntingtin protein → degeneration of the basal ganglia (especially the striatum/caudate). This basal ganglia loss explains the chorea, and the disease shows anticipation (worsens down generations). The clinical hallmark is a middle-aged adult with personality/mood change + involuntary movements. It is incurable — management is supportive.
  • Poor prognosis: ~10–20 years' life expectancy from symptom onset; death often from aspiration/pneumonia.
The genetics — a CAG trinucleotide repeat disorder
  • Autosomal dominant — a single copy causes disease; 50% risk to offspring.
  • Trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, which codes for the huntingtin protein → an abnormal, toxic huntingtin protein → neurodegeneration.
Anticipation: a feature of trinucleotide repeat disorders where successive generations have MORE repeats → earlier age of onset + increased severity down the generations. More CAG repeats → earlier onset + more severe disease; expansion tends to occur especially through the paternal line.

Cross-ref genetics/inheritance physiology — autosomal dominant + anticipation.

Pathophysiology — basal ganglia degeneration
  • The toxic huntingtin protein causes degeneration of the striatum (caudate + putamen) — especially loss of GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the indirect pathway.
  • Imaging correlate: caudate atrophy → enlarged frontal horns of the lateral ventricles ("boxcar ventricles").
The chorea mechanism (cross-ref basal ganglia): loss of the indirect pathway (which normally suppresses unwanted movement) → disinhibition of the thalamus → excess, unwanted movement = chorea (the opposite of Parkinson's, where the balance shifts toward too little movement).
The decisive fork — Huntington's vs other causes of chorea
CauseDiscriminator
Huntington's diseaseautosomal dominant, family history, mid-life onset, chorea + cognitive + psychiatric, CAG repeat
Sydenham's choreapost-streptococcal (rheumatic fever), children
Drug-inducedlevodopa, antipsychotics (tardive dyskinesia), stimulants
Wilson's diseaseyoung + liver disease + Kayser-Fleischer rings
SLE / antiphospholipidautoimmune chorea
Pregnancychorea gravidarum
Other geneticneuroacanthocytosis, HD-like syndromes
The rule: middle-aged adult + family history + chorea + personality/mood change + cognitive decline = Huntington's.
Clinical features
The classic vignette: "middle-aged patient with personality changes + involuntary movements = likely Huntington's disease." Insidious, progressive worsening; typical onset 30–50 years; often begins with cognitive, psychiatric, or mood problems, followed by the movement disorder.
DomainFeatures
Psychiatric/mood (often first)personality change, depression, irritability, anxiety, apathy, psychosis; high suicide risk
Cognitiveprogressive decline → subcortical dementia (slowed thinking, executive dysfunction)
Movement disorderchorea (involuntary, random, irregular movements), dystonia, rigidity, eye movement disorders, dysarthria, dysphagia
Chorea: involuntary, random, irregular, "dance-like" movements — the hallmark hyperkinetic feature; as disease progresses, rigidity/bradykinesia and dystonia can emerge. The dysphagia point: swallowing difficulty → aspiration → pneumonia is the common cause of death.
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is by genetic testing — confirms the CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene.
  • Genetic counselling (critical): because it's a fatal, autosomal dominant, adult-onset condition, predictive testing in at-risk relatives requires careful pre- and post-test genetic counselling (major psychological and ethical implications — including for asymptomatic at-risk individuals and reproductive decisions).
  • MRI: may show caudate/striatal atrophy (supportive, not diagnostic).
  • Assess psychiatric state (including suicide risk), swallow, and function.
Management — supportive, no cure
The overarching principle: no cure → multidisciplinary supportive care; treat chorea, mood, and complications; genetic counselling for the family.
  • Chorea: tetrabenazine (a dopamine-depleting agent) for troublesome chorea; antipsychotics are an alternative.
  • Psychiatric: antidepressants for depression; antipsychotics for psychosis/agitation; monitor suicide risk.
  • Speech and language therapy (SALT) — for dysarthria + swallowing/aspiration risk.
  • End-of-life / palliative care — given the progressive, fatal course.
  • MDT: neurology, physiotherapy, OT, dietitian (nutrition/aspiration), social care, family support.
  • Genetic counselling for the patient and at-risk family members (autosomal dominant inheritance).
Exam pearls
What it is
Autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegeneration → chorea + cognitive decline + psychiatric disturbance.
Genetics
CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT (chromosome 4) → toxic huntingtin protein; anticipation (more repeats → earlier onset + more severe down generations); 50% risk to offspring.
Pathology
Striatal (caudate) degeneration → loss of the indirect pathway → chorea; caudate atrophy on MRI.
Classic
Middle-aged adult + personality/mood change + involuntary movements (chorea); onset 30–50; often psychiatric first, then movement disorder.
Progression
Dystonia, rigidity, dysarthria, dysphagia → aspiration/pneumonia (common cause of death); ~10–20 years from onset; high suicide risk.
Diagnosis
Genetic testing (CAG repeats); needs genetic counselling (predictive testing implications).
Management (no cure — supportive)
Tetrabenazine for chorea, antidepressants, SALT (speech + swallow), palliative care; MDT + family genetic counselling.
Chorea differential
Sydenham's (post-strep), drug-induced, Wilson's, SLE, pregnancy.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Head Injury &:
What & why
Head injury = any trauma to the head, from trivial to life-threatening; the clinical concern is traumatic brain injury, especially intracranial haemorrhage (extradural, subdural, subarachnoid, intracerebral).
The core concept: the whole approach is risk stratification — using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and a set of red-flag criteria to decide who needs a CT head (and how urgently), who needs admission/observation, and who can be discharged safely. The overriding physiology is the Monro-Kellie doctrine — the skull is a fixed box, so an expanding haematoma/oedema raises ICP → herniation → death. Time-critical detection of a treatable bleed is the goal.
  • Extremely common ED presentation; most are minor — the task is not to miss the dangerous minority.
The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

The GCS quantifies consciousness, scored 3 (worst) to 15 (best), across three components:

ComponentScoreResponse
Eyes (E, /4)4 / 3 / 2 / 1spontaneous / to speech / to pain / none
Verbal (V, /5)5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1orientated / confused / inappropriate words / incomprehensible sounds / none
Motor (M, /6)6 / 5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1obeys commands / localises to pain / withdraws / abnormal flexion (decorticate) / extension (decerebrate) / none
The high-yield thresholds:
• GCS ≤8 = coma → cannot protect the airway → intubate ("GCS 8, intubate").
• Motor is the most prognostically important component.
• Flexion (decorticate) vs extension (decerebrate): extension is worse (deeper/lower brainstem involvement).
  • Best-response rule: record the best response in each category; report as E_V_M_ (e.g. E3V4M5 = 12).
  • Severity: mild = GCS 13–15; moderate = 9–12; severe = ≤8.
The decisive fork — who needs a CT head, and how urgently? (NICE NG232)

The central clinical decision. NICE NG232 (2023) stratifies into CT within 1 hour vs CT within 8 hours (adults ≥16):

CT head within 1 HOUR — any of:
  • GCS < 13 on initial ED assessment
  • GCS < 15 at 2 hours after injury
  • suspected open or depressed skull fracture
  • any sign of basal skull fracture: haemotympanum, "panda"/raccoon eyes, CSF leak from ear/nose, Battle's sign (mastoid bruising)
  • post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit, or >1 episode of vomiting
CT head within 8 HOURS — some loss of consciousness or amnesia PLUS any of:
  • age ≥ 65
  • any history of bleeding/clotting disorder
  • dangerous mechanism (pedestrian/cyclist vs vehicle, ejection, fall >1 m or 5 stairs)
  • >30 minutes retrograde amnesia of events before the injury
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet pathway (NG232): a head injury with NO other CT indication but the patient is on an anticoagulant (warfarin, DOAC, heparin) or antiplatelet (excluding aspirin monotherapy) → consider CT within 8 hours (or within 1 hour if presenting >8 hours after injury).
The intracranial bleeds to detect

The CT is looking for a treatable bleed — the classic patterns:

BleedClassic feature
Extradural"lucid interval" then rapid deterioration; biconvex (lens-shaped) on CT; middle meningeal artery, temporal trauma
Subduralcrescent-shaped; elderly/alcoholics/anticoagulated; can be acute or chronic
Subarachnoidtraumatic SAH; (spontaneous → thunderclap headache)
Intracerebral / contusionwithin the parenchyma
The lucid interval: a brief recovery of consciousness after the injury, then deterioration → classic for extradural haematoma (arterial bleed expanding) → a neurosurgical emergency.
Signs of raised ICP / deterioration
  • Falling GCS — the most important sign of deterioration.
  • Cushing's reflex (late, ominous): hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing → impending herniation.
  • Pupillary changes: a fixed dilated pupil (CN III compression from uncal herniation — "blown pupil").
  • Vomiting, worsening headache, focal deficits, seizures.
The physiology: fixed skull (Monro-Kellie) → expanding haematoma → ↑ICP → herniation → brainstem compression → death.
Management
The overarching principle: ABCDE + C-spine control → GCS + risk-stratify → CT per NICE → treat bleeds/raised ICP → observe or discharge with safety-netting.
  • Immediate (ABCDE): airway with C-spine immobilisation (assume cervical injury until excluded), breathing/oxygenation (avoid hypoxia), circulation (avoid hypotension — both worsen secondary brain injury). GCS ≤8 → intubate.
  • Tranexamic acid (TXA): for head injury with GCS ≤12 and no suspected active extracranial bleeding → consider IV TXA (2 g) ASAP, within 2 hours, before imaging.
  • Reverse anticoagulation if intracranial haemorrhage: warfarin → prothrombin complex concentrate + vitamin K; DOAC → specific reversal agent.
  • Neurosurgical referral: significant bleeds (evacuation of extradural/subdural), depressed fractures, raised ICP.
  • Manage raised ICP: head-up positioning, avoid hypoxia/hypercapnia, neurosurgical measures.
  • Admission/observation: abnormal CT, persisting GCS <15, ongoing symptoms, high-risk features, or anticoagulated (even with a normal scan — delayed bleeding risk).
  • Discharge + safety-netting: if low-risk/normal CT/GCS 15 — with written head injury advice (return if worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, weakness, visual changes, seizure) and a responsible adult.
Concussion & post-concussion
  • Concussion = a transient disturbance of brain function after head injury (brief confusion, headache, dizziness, amnesia) with normal imaging — a clinical diagnosis.
  • Post-concussion syndrome: persistent headache, dizziness, poor concentration, mood/sleep disturbance for weeks–months → supportive management, graded return to activity.
Exam pearls
GCS
/15 (Eyes /4, Verbal /5, Motor /6); ≤8 = coma → intubate; report as E_V_M_; motor most prognostic; mild 13–15 / moderate 9–12 / severe ≤8.
CT within 1 HOUR (NG232)
GCS <13 initially, GCS <15 at 2h, basal skull fracture signs (haemotympanum, panda eyes, CSF leak, Battle's sign), open/depressed fracture, seizure, focal deficit, >1 vomit.
CT within 8 HOURS
