LOC/amnesia + (age ≥65, bleeding disorder, dangerous mechanism, >30 min retrograde amnesia); on anticoagulant/antiplatelet → CT within 8h even with no other indication.
Extradural
Lucid interval + biconvex CT (middle meningeal artery).
Subdural
Crescent-shaped, elderly/anticoagulated.
Deterioration
Falling GCS, Cushing's reflex (↑BP + bradycardia + irregular breathing), fixed dilated pupil (CN III / uncal herniation).
Management
ABCDE + C-spine, avoid hypoxia/hypotension (secondary injury); GCS ≤8 → intubate; TXA if GCS ≤12 (within 2h); reverse anticoagulation for bleeds; neurosurgery; safety-net on discharge.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Guillain-Barré:
What & why
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) = an acute, immune-mediated, demyelinating polyneuropathy causing rapidly progressive ascending flaccid paralysis, usually following an infection.
The core concept: a post-infectious autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin (molecular mimicry) → an acute ascending, symmetrical, LMN (flaccid) paralysis with areflexia. The two things that make it an emergency are respiratory muscle failure (the leading cause of death → monitor FVC) and autonomic instability — so the priorities are recognising it early, monitoring respiratory/autonomic function, and treating with IVIG or plasma exchange.
  • The commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis (since polio control); ~⅔ follow a preceding infection.
The decisive fork — GBS or another cause of acute weakness?

The pattern (ascending, symmetrical, areflexic, LMN, post-infectious) is the key:

Points to GBSAlternative to consider
Ascending, symmetrical flaccid weakness + areflexiaspinal cord compression (UMN signs, sensory level, sphincter involvement)
Preceding infection (1–3 weeks before)transverse myelitis (sensory level, bladder)
LMN signs (↓tone, ↓/absent reflexes)myasthenia gravis (fatiguable, ocular)
CSF albuminocytologic dissociationbotulism (descending, pupils), tick paralysis, hypokalaemia
Progression over days to ≤4 weeksorganophosphate poisoning
The rule: acute ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis + areflexia + recent infection = GBS. The key contrast is spinal cord compression (UMN signs + a sensory level + bladder involvement — a surgical emergency to exclude). GBS attacks peripheral nerves → LMN signs (flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia/areflexia) — NOT the UMN signs of a cord lesion.
Pathophysiology & triggers
  • Post-infectious autoimmune process: an infection triggers antibodies that cross-react with peripheral nerve myelin (molecular mimicry) → demyelination of peripheral nerves and roots.
  • The classic trigger: Campylobacter jejuni (gastroenteritis) — the commonest identified precedent, associated with more severe/axonal disease.
  • Other triggers: CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV, influenza/other viral URTIs, (historically) vaccines — weakness begins ~1–3 weeks after the infection.
  • Subtypes: AIDP (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy — commonest in the West), AMAN (acute motor axonal — Campylobacter-associated), and the Miller Fisher variant.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Ascending weaknesssymmetrical, starts in the legs → ascends to arms/trunk; progressive over days (nadir usually ≤4 weeks)
Areflexia / hyporeflexiaabsent/reduced reflexes — a key sign (LMN)
Sensory symptomsoften paraesthesia/pain (may precede weakness), but objective sensory loss is mild (predominantly motor)
Cranial nerve involvementbilateral facial weakness, bulbar (swallowing/speech)
Respiratory failurediaphragm/intercostal weakness → the leading cause of death → monitor FVC
Autonomic dysfunctionarrhythmias, labile BP, tachycardia/bradycardia, urinary retention, ileus
The two danger features: respiratory failure (weak diaphragm → ventilatory failure) and autonomic instability (arrhythmias, BP swings) — these drive mortality and the need for close monitoring/ICU.
Miller Fisher syndrome — the classic variant
A GBS variant with the triad: ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia (often descending, and without the typical limb weakness). Associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies (positive in ~90%). Usually follows infection; generally good prognosis.
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical (ascending flaccid paralysis + areflexia + preceding infection), supported by:
  • Lumbar puncture — CSF: ALBUMINOCYTOLOGIC DISSOCIATION = raised protein with a NORMAL white cell count (the classic finding) — reflects nerve-root inflammation; may be normal in the first week (so a normal early LP doesn't exclude it).
  • Nerve conduction studies: slowed conduction / conduction block (demyelination) — supports + subtypes; may be normal early.
  • Antibodies: anti-GQ1b (Miller Fisher), anti-ganglioside antibodies (not routine).
  • ECG + cardiac monitoring (autonomic instability); bloods to exclude mimics (U&E, potassium).
Respiratory monitoring (CRITICAL): serial spirometry / forced vital capacity (FVC) every few hours in progressing patients — a falling FVC → anaesthetic/ITU review for intubation (don't wait for hypoxia/blood gases to change — they're late).
Management — immunotherapy + supportive
The overarching principle: IVIG OR plasma exchange (not both) + intensive supportive care with respiratory/autonomic monitoring.

Immunotherapy (to hasten recovery):

  • IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) — first-line (easier to give; usually preferred).
  • OR plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) — equally effective.
  • Give ONE, not both: do NOT give plasma exchange after IVIG (it removes the immunoglobulin you just gave). Corticosteroids are NOT effective in GBS (an important negative).

Supportive care (the mainstay):

  • Respiratory: monitor FVC; ventilatory support / intubation if respiratory failure (ICU) — the key to survival.
  • Cardiac/autonomic: monitor for arrhythmias + BP instability.
  • VTE prophylaxis (immobile), catheter/bowel care (autonomic), neuropathic pain management (gabapentinoids), physiotherapy/OT, nutrition (bulbar involvement).
  • ICU admission if: severe/rapidly progressing weakness, falling FVC, bulbar involvement, or autonomic instability.
Prognosis
  • Most recover (over weeks–months), often fully or near-fully — GBS is typically monophasic (doesn't recur).
  • But: ~20% have residual weakness/disability, ~5% mortality (respiratory/autonomic complications), and recovery can be slow.
  • A small proportion → CIDP (chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy — the chronic/relapsing counterpart, >8 weeks).
  • Poor prognostic factors: older age, rapid onset, axonal subtype, ventilator requirement, preceding Campylobacter/diarrhoeal illness.
Exam pearls
What it is
Acute, post-infectious, immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy → ascending symmetrical flaccid paralysis + areflexia (LMN).
Trigger
Preceding infection 1–3 weeks before — classically Campylobacter jejuni; also CMV/EBV/Mycoplasma/HIV.
Features
Ascending weakness (legs→up), areflexia, mild sensory, bilateral facial/bulbar weakness; danger = respiratory failure + autonomic instability.
Distinguish from
Spinal cord compression (UMN + sensory level + bladder — surgical emergency) and myasthenia (fatiguable, ocular).
Miller Fisher variant
Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia; anti-GQ1b antibodies.
Investigations
CSF = albuminocytologic dissociation (↑protein, normal WCC) — may be normal in week 1; NCS = demyelination; serial FVC (falling FVC → ITU/intubation).
Management
IVIG OR plasma exchange (equally effective — give one, not both; never plasma exchange after IVIG); steroids don't work; intensive supportive care (respiratory + autonomic monitoring, VTE prophylaxis).
Prognosis
Usually monophasic, most recover; ~5% mortality (respiratory); small proportion → CIDP.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Febrile Convul:
What & why
A febrile convulsion = a seizure provoked by fever in an otherwise neurologically normal child, without CNS infection or another identifiable cause.
The core concept: a benign, self-limiting seizure triggered by a rapidly rising temperature in a young child — it is NOT epilepsy (it's a provoked seizure). Two priorities: (1) exclude a serious cause of the fever (especially meningitis/encephalitis — don't assume "just febrile") and (2) classify it as simple vs complex (complex carries higher risk). Above all — reassurance: the prognosis is excellent.
  • Common — affects ~3% of children; typically 6 months to 5 years; occurs at the peak of a fever, usually from a viral infection.
The decisive fork — simple vs complex vs febrile status

The single most important classification — it determines risk and management:

SimpleComplexFebrile status
Duration< 15 minutes15–30 minutes> 30 minutes
Typegeneralised (tonic-clonic)focal featuresprolonged
Recurrence in 24hnonemay recur within 24h—
Recoverycomplete recovery < 1 hourslower—
The rule: simple = <15 min + generalised + no recurrence in 24h + full recovery; complex = ≥1 of: prolonged (15–30 min), focal, or recurs within 24h; febrile status = >30 min. Complex febrile convulsions carry a higher risk of recurrence and a (slightly) higher risk of later epilepsy → warrant more caution.
Clinical features
  • Occur early in a viral infection as the temperature rapidly rises — it's the rate of rise, not just the peak, that matters.
  • Last < 5 minutes (typically).
  • Mostly tonic-clonic (generalised).
  • Age 6 months–5 years; the child is otherwise developmentally normal.
  • Often a family history of febrile convulsions.
The must-not-miss — exclude a serious cause of the fever

A febrile seizure is a diagnosis that requires excluding a CNS infection — the critical differential:

Must excludeRed flags
Meningitis / encephalitisneck stiffness, non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, drowsiness/altered consciousness, focal neurology, not recovering
Other serious infectionthe "red" features (pale/mottled, no response to social cues, grunting, tachypnoea)
Metabolichypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia
Epilepsyseizure without fever, or afebrile recurrences
The rule: any child with a seizure + fever must be assessed for meningitis/encephalitis — do NOT assume a febrile convulsion, especially if there are red flags, incomplete recovery, complex features, or the child is <18 months (meningitis signs are subtle in infants). Age caveat: febrile convulsions are unusual <6 months or >5 years → a seizure with fever outside this range needs closer scrutiny for another cause.
Assessment / investigations
  • Simple febrile convulsion with full recovery + clear infective source → often no investigations needed beyond finding the fever source (clinical assessment).
  • Find the fever source + exclude serious causes: examine thoroughly; urine dip/culture (UTI is a common occult source), consider bloods, blood glucose.
  • Lumbar puncture — if meningitis/encephalitis suspected (esp. <18 months, complex features, not recovering, red flags).
  • NOT routinely needed for a simple febrile convulsion: EEG, neuroimaging, routine bloods (over-investigation is a common error).
  • Complex FC / diagnostic doubt → lower threshold for admission + investigation.
Management
The overarching principle: acute seizure management + exclude serious infection + treat the fever source + reassure/safety-net the parents.
  • Admit to paediatrics if: the first febrile convulsion, OR features of a complex seizure (or diagnostic uncertainty, or the child is unwell / <18 months).

Acute seizure management:

  • Call 999 if the seizure lasts > 5 minutes.
  • Benzodiazepine rescue if recurrent/prolonged (specialist-initiated): rectal diazepam or buccal midazolam — for children with a history of prolonged febrile convulsions.
  • Supportive: protect from injury, recovery position, oxygen if needed.
  • Treat the underlying cause of the fever (the infection).
  • Antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) for comfort — but they do NOT prevent febrile convulsions → don't give them to prevent seizures.
  • No routine anticonvulsant prophylaxis — regular antiepileptics are not indicated for simple febrile convulsions.
Parental advice / safety-netting: ~1 in 3 chance of recurrence; very low risk of progression to epilepsy (reassure); how to manage a future seizure (time it, recovery position, call 999 if >5 min), and when to seek help.
Prognosis — the reassurance
  • Recurrence: ~1 in 3 — higher if young age at onset, family history, low peak temperature, or complex FC.
  • Risk of epilepsy: very low — only slightly above the general population for simple FC (~1–2%); higher with complex FC, neurodevelopmental abnormality, or a family history of epilepsy.
  • No effect on development/intelligence for simple febrile convulsions — reassure parents strongly.
Exam pearls
What it is
Fever-provoked seizure in a normal child, 6 months–5 years — a provoked seizure, NOT epilepsy.
Classification
Simple (<15 min, generalised, no recurrence in 24h, full recovery); complex (15–30 min OR focal OR recurs in 24h); febrile status (>30 min).
Features
Occur as the temperature rapidly rises (early in a viral illness); usually tonic-clonic, <5 min.
Must-not-miss
Exclude meningitis/encephalitis (neck stiffness, non-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, not recovering) — don't assume febrile convulsion, especially if <18 months, complex, or red flags.
Investigations
Simple FC → usually none (find fever source, urine dip); LP if meningitis suspected; no routine EEG/imaging.
Management
Admit if first seizure or complex; call 999 if >5 min; buccal midazolam/rectal diazepam rescue (recurrent); treat the infection; antipyretics don't prevent FCs.
Prognosis
~1 in 3 recurrence, very low epilepsy risk — reassure.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Epilepsy (clas:
What & why
📷 Image placeholder — characteristic patterns — generalised 3-Hz spike-and-wave complexes of childhood absence epilepsy, and focal/interictal epileptiform discharges localising to a lobe
Epilepsy = a tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures — defined as ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart (or 1 unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk, e.g. a structural cause). A seizure = a transient episode of abnormal, excessive, synchronous electrical activity in the brain.
The core concept: three pillars — (1) classify the seizure (focal vs generalised — because it determines the drug), (2) treat the acute prolonged seizure (status epilepticus is an emergency), and (3) advise on the practical consequences (DVLA, safety, pregnancy). Classification drives everything, because the antiseizure medication depends on the seizure type.
  • Common (~1% lifetime); most present in childhood or older age.
The decisive fork — focal vs generalised

The ILAE classification first asks: where does the seizure start?

Focal (partial)Generalised
Onsetone part of one hemisphereboth hemispheres from the start
Awarenessfocal aware (conscious) or focal impaired awarenessconsciousness usually lost
Examplestemporal lobe (aura, déjà vu, automatisms); can evolve to bilateral tonic-clonictonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, tonic, atonic
Localisingfeatures localise to the lobe (cross-ref cortical syndromes)no focal onset
The rule: focal = starts in one area (may have an aura, automatisms, or evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic); generalised = both hemispheres from the start (loss of consciousness) — this split determines the drug choice.
The generalised seizure types
TypeFeatures
Tonic-clonictonic (stiffening) → clonic (jerking); LOC, tongue-biting, incontinence, post-ictal drowsiness/confusion
Absencebrief (<10s) vacant staring/"blank", no post-ictal phase; children; 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG
Myoclonicsudden brief shock-like jerks (e.g. juvenile myoclonic epilepsy)
Tonicsudden stiffening → fall
Atonicsudden loss of tone → "drop attack"
The high-yield ones: tonic-clonic (the classic "grand mal"), absence (children, 3 Hz spike-wave, no post-ictal phase), myoclonic (JME).
Focal seizure features — localise to the lobe
LobeFocal seizure features
Temporalaura (déjà vu, rising epigastric sensation, fear), automatisms (lip-smacking, fidgeting), altered awareness
Frontalmotor features (Jacksonian march — spreading motor activity), posturing, Todd's paresis (post-ictal weakness)
Parietalsensory (tingling, numbness)
Occipitalvisual (flashes, patterns)
Todd's paresis: transient post-ictal focal weakness (can mimic a stroke). Jacksonian march: motor seizure activity "marching" along the body as it spreads across the motor cortex.
Assessment & investigations
Diagnosis is clinical — a detailed eyewitness account is the single most important thing (warning/aura, what happened, tongue-biting, incontinence, post-ictal confusion, duration).

Exclude provoked seizures / mimics first — a seizure isn't epilepsy if there's an acute provoking cause:

  • Provoking causes: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, drugs, infection (meningitis/encephalitis), eclampsia, head injury, hypoxia.
  • Mimics: syncope (vasovagal, cardiac — brief, quick recovery, situational), non-epileptic attack disorder (NEAD) (functional), TIA, migraine, panic.

Investigations:

  • EEG — supports classification (e.g. 3 Hz spike-wave = absence); a normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy (and an abnormal one doesn't confirm it).
  • MRI brain — to find a structural cause (esp. focal seizures, adults with new-onset — exclude tumour/AVM/malformation).
  • Bloods: glucose, U&E, calcium, magnesium, FBC (exclude provoked causes); ECG (exclude cardiac syncope/arrhythmia).
Antiseizure medications (NICE NG217)
The overarching principle: treat by seizure type; usually start after a 2nd seizure (or 1st with structural cause/high risk); monotherapy first.

When to start: usually after a second seizure (or after a first if there's a structural lesion, an unequivocal epileptic EEG, or high judged risk).

First-line drugs (NICE NG217):

Seizure typeFirst-line
Generalised tonic-cloniclamotrigine, levetiracetam, or sodium valproate
Focallamotrigine or levetiracetam
Absenceethosuximide (or sodium valproate) — avoid carbamazepine (worsens absence)
Myocloniclevetiracetam or sodium valproate (avoid carbamazepine; lamotrigine may worsen)
Tonic / atonicsodium valproate
Valproate restrictions (critical): valproate is teratogenic (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental effects) → must NOT be used in women/girls of childbearing potential unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place and no alternative. MHRA (2024): do not start valproate in ANYONE under 55 without two specialists documenting no alternative.
Key drug points:
• Carbamazepine — enzyme inducer; can worsen absence + myoclonic seizures (avoid in generalised); SIADH/hyponatraemia.
• Lamotrigine — slow titration (Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk); safest in pregnancy.
• Levetiracetam — neuropsychiatric side effects (irritability, low mood).
• Phenytoin — narrow therapeutic index, zero-order kinetics, gum hyperplasia (used mainly in status now).
  • Withdrawal: consider after ≥2 years seizure-free, with specialist input; taper slowly.
Status epilepticus — the emergency
Definition: a seizure lasting >5 minutes, OR ≥2 seizures without recovery of consciousness in between (older definition was >30 min; ≥5 min now triggers treatment). A medical emergency — prolonged seizures cause neuronal injury, hypoxia, and death.

The stepwise protocol:

StepAction
1. ABCDE + immediatesecure airway, high-flow oxygen, check glucose (treat hypoglycaemia), IV access, thiamine (Pabrinex) if alcohol/malnourished
2. First-line — benzodiazepineIV lorazepam 4 mg (repeat once after 5–10 min if needed); community/no IV access → buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam
3. Second-lineif seizures continue → IV levetiracetam, phenytoin, or sodium valproate
4. Third-line (refractory)general anaesthesia (ICU) — propofol/thiopental/midazolam infusion + intubation
The rules: benzodiazepine first (lorazepam IV, or buccal midazolam if no access) → repeat once → second-line IV antiseizure drug → ICU/anaesthesia if refractory. Look for + treat the cause throughout (hypoglycaemia, infection, eclampsia, drug withdrawal).
DVLA & driving rules
The patient (not the doctor) must inform the DVLA — but the doctor must advise them to, and to stop driving; if they continue driving against advice and lack capacity to understand, confidentiality may be broken to inform the DVLA.

Group 1 (car / motorcycle):

SituationRule
First unprovoked seizure6 months off driving (no structural/EEG abnormality; if there is → 12 months)
Established epilepsy / ≥2 seizuresmust be seizure-free for 12 months to drive
Seizures only ever in sleepmay drive if an established ≥1 year pattern of sleep-only seizures
Medication withdrawalstop driving during withdrawal and for 6 months after; if a seizure occurs → relicensing after 6 months on reinstated medication

Group 2 (HGV / bus — much stricter):

  • First seizure: 5 years seizure-free (off medication) before driving.
  • Epilepsy: 10 years seizure-free and off antiseizure medication.
The high-yield numbers: Group 1 — first seizure = 6 months; epilepsy = 12 months seizure-free; Group 2 — much stricter (5/10 years).
Special considerations
  • Pregnancy: valproate contraindicated; lamotrigine/levetiracetam preferred; high-dose folic acid (5 mg) pre-conception; specialist management.
  • SUDEP (Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy) — a rare but important risk (worse with uncontrolled seizures, non-adherence) → discuss + optimise control.
  • Safety advice: showers not baths, caution with heights/swimming/machinery.
  • Women: some antiseizure drugs (enzyme inducers — carbamazepine) reduce contraceptive efficacy.
Exam pearls
Definition
≥2 unprovoked seizures >24h apart (or 1 + high recurrence risk); classify first: focal vs generalised (determines the drug).
Seizure types
Generalised: tonic-clonic, absence (children, 3 Hz spike-wave, no post-ictal), myoclonic (JME), tonic, atonic. Focal: localises to lobe (temporal = aura/automatisms; Todd's paresis = post-ictal weakness).
Exclude mimics
Provoked (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, alcohol withdrawal, infection) and mimics (syncope, NEAD) first; normal EEG doesn't exclude epilepsy.
First-line (NICE NG217)
Generalised tonic-clonic → lamotrigine/levetiracetam/valproate; focal → lamotrigine/levetiracetam; absence → ethosuximide (carbamazepine worsens absence + myoclonic).
Valproate
Teratogenic → not in women of childbearing potential; don't start in under-55s without 2 specialists (MHRA).
Status epilepticus (>5 min)
ABCDE + glucose → IV lorazepam (repeat once) → IV levetiracetam/phenytoin/valproate → ICU/anaesthesia.
DVLA
Group 1: first seizure = 6 months off; epilepsy = 12 months seizure-free; withdrawal = 6 months off. Group 2 = 5/10 years. Patient informs DVLA.
Pregnancy
Lamotrigine/levetiracetam + 5 mg folic acid; SUDEP risk with poor control.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Diabetic Neuro:
What & why
Diabetic neuropathy = nerve damage caused by chronic hyperglycaemia — the commonest complication of diabetes and the leading cause of peripheral neuropathy worldwide.
The core concept: diabetic neuropathy is not one thing — it takes several forms (symmetrical sensory, autonomic, mononeuropathy, amyotrophy), but the classic and commonest is a distal symmetrical sensory "glove-and-stocking" polyneuropathy driven by length-dependent nerve damage (longest nerves — the feet — first). Clinical priorities: pain control, foot protection (to prevent ulcers/amputation), detecting autonomic involvement — and above all glycaemic control to prevent progression.
  • One of the microvascular complications of diabetes (alongside retinopathy + nephropathy); risk rises with duration + poor glycaemic control.
The decisive fork — which type of diabetic neuropathy?

Diabetic neuropathy has several distinct patterns — recognising which is present guides management:

TypePatternKey features
Distal symmetrical sensory polyneuropathythe commonest — length-dependent"glove-and-stocking" sensory loss (feet first), numbness, burning/tingling pain, loss of proprioception/vibration
Autonomic neuropathyaffects the autonomic nervous systempostural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, silent MI, gustatory sweating
Mononeuropathy / mononeuritis multiplexsingle (or multiple discrete) nervese.g. CN III palsy (pupil-sparing), carpal tunnel, foot drop
Diabetic amyotrophy (proximal motor)lumbosacral plexuspainful, asymmetrical proximal (thigh) weakness + wasting
The rule: distal symmetrical sensory ("glove-and-stocking") is the classic/commonest; but know the others — autonomic (postural drop, gastroparesis, silent MI), mononeuropathy (CN III pupil-sparing), and amyotrophy (proximal painful wasting).
Pathophysiology
  • Chronic hyperglycaemia damages nerves through several mechanisms: microvascular damage to the vasa nervorum (ischaemia), the polyol/sorbitol pathway (osmotic + oxidative stress), advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), and oxidative stress → axonal + demyelinating damage.
  • Sensory > motor in the classic form (contrast with CMT, which is motor-predominant).
The length-dependent principle: the longest nerves are affected first → symptoms start in the feet ("stocking"), then the hands ("glove") as it progresses — this is why it's distal + symmetrical.
Distal symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy — the classic form
  • "Glove-and-stocking" sensory loss — symmetrical, distal, feet before hands.
  • Positive symptoms: burning, tingling, "electric-shock", shooting pain, often worse at night (neuropathic pain).
  • Negative symptoms: numbness, loss of sensation (including loss of protective sensation → the key ulcer risk).
  • Loss of vibration + proprioception (large-fibre — dorsal column), reduced ankle reflexes.
The dangerous consequence: loss of protective sensation → unnoticed trauma → foot ulcers → infection → amputation — the diabetic foot is the major clinical concern. Charcot foot: neuropathy → repeated unnoticed trauma → progressive joint destruction/deformity of the foot.
Autonomic neuropathy — often under-recognised
SystemManifestation
Cardiovascularpostural (orthostatic) hypotension, resting tachycardia, silent myocardial ischaemia (painless MI — a key danger)
GIgastroparesis (early satiety, bloating, vomiting, erratic glycaemic control), diarrhoea/constipation
Genitourinaryerectile dysfunction (often the earliest sign), neurogenic bladder (retention, incontinence)
Othergustatory sweating, hypoglycaemia unawareness (loss of adrenergic warning)
Silent MI: autonomic neuropathy blunts pain perception → diabetics can have "silent" (painless) myocardial infarctions → low threshold to investigate. Hypoglycaemia unawareness: loss of the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia → dangerous.
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is largely clinical — history + examination.
  • Annual diabetic foot check: 10g monofilament (protective sensation), 128 Hz tuning fork (vibration), ankle reflexes, pinprick, foot inspection (deformity, ulcers), pedal pulses (also check for peripheral arterial disease).
  • Lying + standing BP (postural drop — autonomic).
  • Nerve conduction studies — if diagnostic doubt or atypical.
  • Exclude other causes of neuropathy: don't assume all neuropathy in a diabetic is diabetic — check B12/folate, TFTs, U&E, alcohol history, drugs (a treatable cause may coexist).
  • Assess for the other microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy — they cluster).
Management — glycaemic control + pain + foot protection
The overarching principle: optimise glycaemic control (prevents progression) + neuropathic pain management + meticulous foot care + manage autonomic features.
  • Glycaemic control (the foundation): tight glucose control slows/prevents progression (especially in type 1) — the single most important disease-modifying step; also manage BP, lipids, smoking.

Neuropathic pain management (NICE):

  • First-line = one of: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin (any of the four).
  • Duloxetine is often preferred in diabetic neuropathy specifically (licensed for it; helpful if comorbid low mood).
  • If the first is ineffective/not tolerated → switch to one of the other three (and can switch again).
  • Tramadol only for acute rescue; capsaicin cream for localised pain if oral treatments unsuitable.
  • Foot care (critical — prevents amputation): diabetic foot protection — regular podiatry, patient education (daily foot checks, appropriate footwear), prompt treatment of ulcers, MDT diabetic foot service.
  • Autonomic: postural hypotension → conservative measures ± fludrocortisone/midodrine; gastroparesis → dietary measures, prokinetics (metoclopramide/domperidone); erectile dysfunction → PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil).
  • Multidisciplinary: diabetology, podiatry, pain team.
Key point: neuropathic pain responds to the agents above (amitriptyline/duloxetine/gabapentin/pregabalin), NOT to standard analgesics/NSAIDs.
Exam pearls
What it is
Commonest complication of diabetes; a microvascular complication (with retinopathy + nephropathy).
Types
Distal symmetrical sensory (commonest — "glove-and-stocking"), autonomic, mononeuropathy (CN III pupil-sparing, carpal tunnel), amyotrophy (proximal painful wasting).
Length-dependent
Feet first (stocking) then hands (glove); sensory > motor (contrast CMT = motor-predominant).
Key danger
Loss of protective sensation → foot ulcers → amputation (+ Charcot foot).
Autonomic
Postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, silent MI, hypoglycaemia unawareness.
Assessment
Annual foot check — 10g monofilament + 128 Hz tuning fork + reflexes + pulses; lying/standing BP; exclude other causes (B12, thyroid, alcohol).
Management
Glycaemic control (prevents progression) + neuropathic pain (amitriptyline/duloxetine/gabapentin/pregabalin — duloxetine favoured in diabetes) + foot care + autonomic management.
Pain agents
Neuropathic pain does NOT respond to standard analgesics/NSAIDs.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Creutzfeldt-Ja:
What & why
CJD = a rapidly progressive, fatal neurodegenerative disease caused by prions — misfolded proteins that induce further misfolding in the brain.
The core concept: CJD is the archetypal prion disease — an infectious/misfolding protein (not a virus or bacterium) triggers a chain reaction of protein misfolding → spongiform (vacuolated) brain degeneration → a rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus, invariably fatal within ~1 year. The hallmark that flags it is rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus — far faster than Alzheimer's or the other dementias.
  • Rare; the prototype of the transmissible spongiform encephalopathies; no cure — management is palliative.
The prion mechanism
  • Prions = abnormal, misfolded forms of a normal cellular protein (PrP): the misfolded prion protein induces normal PrP to misfold too → a self-propagating chain reaction.
  • The misfolded protein forms tightly-packed β-pleated sheets resistant to proteases → they accumulate, can't be broken down, and cause spongiform (vacuolated) neurodegeneration.
Key features of prions: not a conventional pathogen — no nucleic acid (DNA/RNA); a protein-only infectious agent. Resistant to standard sterilisation (protease-, heat-, radiation-resistant) → an infection-control concern (e.g. contaminated neurosurgical instruments). Transmissible in some forms.
The decisive fork — which type of CJD?

CJD has several forms, distinguished by how the prion arose:

Type% / mechanismKey features
Sporadic CJD~85% (the commonest); spontaneous misfoldingelderly (~60s); rapid dementia + myoclonus
Variant CJD (vCJD)acquired — eating BSE-infected beef ("mad cow disease")younger patients; psychiatric/behavioural onset + sensory symptoms; slower; pulvinar sign on MRI
Familial (inherited) CJD~10–15% — autosomal dominant PRNP mutationfamily history; younger onset
Iatrogenic CJDacquired — medical transmission (contaminated instruments, dura mater grafts, human-derived growth hormone)history of relevant procedure
The high-yield distinctions: sporadic = commonest, elderly, rapid dementia + myoclonus; variant (vCJD) = younger, from BSE beef, psychiatric onset, pulvinar sign.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Rapidly progressive dementiathe hallmark — cognitive decline over weeks–months (far faster than other dementias)
Myoclonussudden involuntary jerks — the classic accompanying sign
Other neurologycerebellar signs (ataxia), visual disturbance, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs, akinetic mutism (late)
vCJDearly psychiatric/behavioural changes + painful sensory symptoms
The rule: rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus = CJD until proven otherwise — the speed (weeks–months) is the key clue distinguishing it from Alzheimer's/other dementias. Death usually within a year.
Investigations
  • CSF (lumbar puncture): normal on routine analysis — but can send 14-3-3 protein + RT-QuIC (raised/positive support the diagnosis).
  • EEG: biphasic, high-amplitude sharp waves (periodic sharp-wave complexes) — classic in sporadic CJD.
  • MRI: hyperintense signals in the basal ganglia and thalamus (on DWI/FLAIR); in vCJD, the "pulvinar sign" (bilateral posterior thalamic hyperintensity).
  • Definitive diagnosis = tissue biopsy: brain biopsy / post-mortem showing spongiform change + prion protein (rarely done ante-mortem due to risk + transmissibility).
  • Genetic testing (PRNP) for familial forms.
The differential — rapidly progressive dementia

CJD is the classic cause, but exclude treatable mimics of rapid cognitive decline:

CauseNote
CJD (prion)rapid dementia + myoclonus; EEG/MRI/CSF as above
Autoimmune / limbic encephalitistreatable — anti-NMDA, paraneoplastic; check autoantibodies
InfectionHIV, neurosyphilis, PML, viral encephalitis
Metabolic / toxicB12 deficiency, thyroid, Wernicke's
MalignancyCNS lymphoma, paraneoplastic
The point: rapidly progressive dementia warrants a workup for treatable causes (autoimmune encephalitis especially) before concluding CJD.
Management — palliative
The overarching principle: no cure → supportive/palliative care + infection control + notification.
  • No cure / no disease-modifying treatment — invariably fatal (usually within a year).
  • Palliative + supportive care: symptom control (myoclonus → clonazepam/levetiracetam, agitation, pain), MDT, family support, end-of-life care planning.
  • Infection control: prions are resistant to standard decontamination → special instrument-handling/quarantine precautions (especially for neurosurgery/LP) to prevent iatrogenic transmission.
  • Notification: CJD is notifiable to the National CJD Research & Surveillance Unit.
  • Genetic counselling for familial CJD.
Exam pearls
What it is
Rapidly progressive, fatal prion disease → rapid dementia + myoclonus, death usually within ~1 year.
Prion mechanism
Misfolded PrP induces normal protein to misfold → protease-resistant β-pleated sheets → spongiform neurodegeneration; protein-only agent (no DNA/RNA), resistant to sterilisation.
Types
Sporadic (~85%, commonest, elderly); variant vCJD (BSE beef, younger, psychiatric onset, pulvinar sign); familial (PRNP mutation); iatrogenic (contaminated instruments/grafts/hGH).
The hallmark
Rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus = CJD until proven otherwise (speed distinguishes from other dementias).
Investigations
CSF normal (± 14-3-3/RT-QuIC); EEG = biphasic high-amplitude sharp waves; MRI = basal ganglia/thalamus hyperintensity (pulvinar sign in vCJD); definitive = tissue biopsy.
Exclude treatable mimics
Rapid dementia workup — especially autoimmune encephalitis.
Management
No cure → palliative; symptom control (myoclonus → clonazepam); prion infection-control precautions; notifiable disease.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Charcot-Marie-:
What & why
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) = an inherited (hereditary) peripheral neuropathy affecting motor and sensory peripheral nerves — also called hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN).
The core concept: CMT is a length-dependent, predominantly motor peripheral neuropathy — so it hits the longest nerves first (the feet/legs), producing the classic distal wasting + foot deformity + high-stepping gait picture. It's the commonest inherited neuropathy, is slowly progressive, and has no cure — management is supportive.
  • Usually presents in childhood/adolescence; mostly autosomal dominant; a lower motor neuron (LMN) pattern (it's a peripheral nerve disease).
The decisive fork — inherited or acquired neuropathy?

CMT must be distinguished from acquired peripheral neuropathies (far commoner and often treatable):

Points to CMT (inherited)Points to acquired neuropathy
Family history (autosomal dominant)no family history
Very slow onset (years), from childhoodsubacute/acute onset
Marked foot deformity (pes cavus, hammer toes) — implies long-standingless deformity
Symmetrical, distal, predominantly motorpattern varies (e.g. diabetic = sensory)
Normal until you look for the patternidentifiable cause (diabetes, B12, alcohol, drugs)
The rule: pes cavus + a positive family history + slow distal weakness = CMT; the foot deformity implies a long-standing (hence inherited) neuropathy. Always exclude acquired causes first (diabetes, B12 deficiency, alcohol, drugs, thyroid).
Pathophysiology
  • Caused by mutations affecting peripheral nerve myelin or axons → demyelinating (CMT1 — commonest, e.g. PMP22 duplication) or axonal (CMT2) subtypes.
  • Predominantly motor — motor > sensory involvement.
The length-dependent principle: the longest nerves are affected first → symptoms start in the feet/legs, then progress to the hands ("stocking then glove") → this explains the distal-first pattern.
Clinical features — the classic picture

A peripheral neuropathy — predominantly motor weakness, with characteristic signs:

FeatureDetail
Pes cavushigh foot arches — the classic deformity
Hammer toes—
Foot dropweak dorsiflexion → high-stepping gait as compensation
"Inverted champagne bottle legs"distal muscle wasting + weakness — thin lower legs with preserved thighs
Hyporeflexia + hypotoniaLMN signs — reduced/absent reflexes, reduced tone
Distal sensory lossmilder (stocking distribution)
The signature signs: pes cavus + "inverted champagne bottle" legs + high-stepping (foot drop) gait + areflexia = the classic CMT tetrad.
The LMN pattern (cross-ref motor pathways): because CMT is a peripheral nerve (LMN) disease, it produces LMN signs — wasting, hyporeflexia, hypotonia (not the ↑tone/hyperreflexia of a UMN lesion). Also: distal hand wasting/weakness (later), foot ulcers (sensory loss), palpably thickened nerves (demyelinating types).
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical (characteristic picture + family history), supported by:
  • Nerve conduction studies (NCS) — slowed conduction (demyelinating CMT1) or reduced amplitudes (axonal CMT2); confirms a peripheral neuropathy and its type.
  • Genetic testing — confirms diagnosis + subtype (e.g. PMP22 duplication in CMT1A).
  • Nerve biopsy (rarely needed) — "onion bulb" formation in demyelinating types.
  • Exclude acquired causes: glucose/HbA1c (diabetes), B12/folate, TFTs, U&E, LFT.
Management — supportive, no cure
The overarching principle: no cure → multidisciplinary supportive care to maintain function and mobility.
  • Physiotherapy — maintain strength, range of movement, mobility.
  • Occupational therapy — aids and adaptations.
  • Orthotics — ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) for foot drop, special footwear for pes cavus.
  • Podiatry — foot care (deformity, ulcer prevention from sensory loss).
  • Analgesia — including neuropathic pain agents (gabapentinoids, amitriptyline) if neuropathic pain.
  • Orthopaedic surgery — for severe foot deformity/contractures.
  • Genetic counselling — given autosomal dominant inheritance (50% risk to offspring).
Safety point: avoid neurotoxic drugs — e.g. vincristine can dramatically worsen CMT.
Exam pearls
What it is
CMT (HMSN) = inherited, predominantly motor, length-dependent peripheral neuropathy; mostly autosomal dominant; commonest inherited neuropathy.
Classic picture
Pes cavus + hammer toes + foot drop (high-stepping gait) + "inverted champagne bottle" legs (distal wasting) + hyporeflexia/hypotonia.
LMN pattern
Peripheral nerve disease → wasting, ↓reflexes, ↓tone (NOT UMN signs).
Length-dependent
Feet/legs first (stocking), then hands (glove).
Inherited vs acquired
Family history + long-standing foot deformity = inherited (CMT); always exclude diabetes, B12, alcohol, thyroid.
Investigations
Nerve conduction studies (demyelinating CMT1 = slow conduction; axonal CMT2 = ↓amplitude) + genetic testing (PMP22).
Management
No cure → supportive — physiotherapy, orthotics (AFOs for foot drop), podiatry, analgesia, genetic counselling; avoid vincristine (worsens it).
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cerebral Venou:
What & why
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) = a thrombus in the cerebral venous sinuses (or cerebral veins) obstructing venous drainage of the brain.
The core concept: unlike arterial stroke (which cuts off supply), CVST obstructs venous drainage → venous congestion → raised pressure → cerebral oedema, raised ICP, and venous (often haemorrhagic) infarction. This "backing-up" mechanism explains everything: the headache/raised ICP, the seizures, and — critically — why anticoagulation is given even when there's a haemorrhage (the bleed is caused by the venous congestion, so treating the clot relieves it).
  • Rare but important — a cause of stroke in young adults, women (hormonal), and pregnancy/puerperium; frequently missed/delayed because the presentation is variable.
The decisive fork — which sinus/vein is thrombosed?

The clinical syndrome depends on which venous structure is occluded:

SiteFrequency / features
Superior sagittal sinus~50% (the commonest); headache, raised ICP, seizures + hemiplegia, ↓consciousness
Cavernous sinusperiorbital erythema + oedema, ophthalmoplegia, eye pain (see below)
Transverse/sigmoid sinusheadache, ear/mastoid involvement (can follow otitis/mastoiditis)
Deep venous system (straight sinus)severe — thalamic/deep involvement, ↓consciousness
The rule: ~50% are isolated sagittal sinus thromboses (the commonest); cavernous sinus thrombosis has a distinctive eye-centred picture.
Clinical features

The presentation is variable — the common threads:

FeatureDetail
Headachethe commonest symptom — may be sudden onset (can mimic subarachnoid haemorrhage) or gradual/progressive; often a raised-ICP headache (worse lying down, worse on Valsalva)
Nausea + vomitingraised ICP
Reduced consciousness—
Seizuresmore common than in arterial stroke (a useful clue)
Focal deficitse.g. hemiplegia (sagittal sinus)
Papilloedema / visual symptomsraised ICP
Clues that point to CVST over arterial stroke: headache + seizures + focal signs that don't fit a single arterial territory + a young patient with thrombotic risk factors. Can mimic subarachnoid haemorrhage, IIH, meningoencephalitis, arterial stroke.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis — the distinctive eye syndrome

A specific, exam-favourite subtype — because of what runs through the cavernous sinus:

FeatureMechanism
Periorbital erythema + oedemavenous congestion of orbital drainage
Ophthalmoplegia — CN VI (6th) affected before CN III/IVCN VI runs freely through the middle of the sinus (most vulnerable); III/IV run in the wall
Eye pain + facial hyperaesthesia (upper face)trigeminal (CN V₁/V₂) involvement
Proptosis, chemosisvenous congestion
The CN VI-first point: in cavernous sinus pathology the 6th nerve is affected before the 3rd/4th (it sits centrally, exposed) → early lateral rectus palsy (failure of abduction). Cavernous sinus thrombosis is often septic (spreading from facial/sinus/dental infection — the "danger triangle" of the face) → needs antibiotics too.
Risk factors — think "prothrombotic"

CVST is fundamentally a thrombotic disorder — look for a hypercoagulable state (Virchow's triad):

CategoryExamples
Hormonalcombined oral contraceptive pill, pregnancy + puerperium (postpartum — ~20% of cases), HRT
ThrombophiliaFactor V Leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency
Malignancyprothrombotic states
Infectionlocal (sinusitis, otitis/mastoiditis, dental, facial → cavernous/transverse sinus), meningitis
Dehydration, systemicdehydration, inflammatory disease (Behçet's, IBD, SLE), nephrotic syndrome
Otherhead injury, recent LP/neurosurgery; VITT (vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia — a rare cause)
The high-yield associations: a young woman on the COCP or postpartum → classic CVST context.
Investigations
  • 1st-line / investigation of choice: MRI venography (MRV) — visualises the thrombosed sinus and any venous infarct/oedema; CT venography is an equally good alternative.
  • Non-contrast CT head can be normal in around 30% of cases — a key pitfall: a normal CT does NOT exclude CVST → if suspected, proceed to venography.
  • The "empty delta sign": on contrast CT/venography, a filling defect in the (superior sagittal) sinus — contrast outlines the sinus wall but not the clot → a triangular "empty" centre.
  • D-dimer: may support (often raised) but a normal D-dimer does NOT exclude CVST → don't rely on it.
  • Investigate the cause: thrombophilia screen, pregnancy test, look for infection/malignancy.
Management — the counterintuitive anticoagulation point
The overarching principle: anticoagulate — even if there's a haemorrhage — plus treat the cause, seizures, and raised ICP.
  • Acute: anticoagulation with LMWH — low-molecular-weight heparin is first-line acute treatment.
  • Long-term: warfarin (or a DOAC) — typically for 3–12 months (3–6 months if a transient/reversible factor e.g. pregnancy/COCP; 6–12 months if idiopathic; lifelong if recurrent/persistent thrombophilia/malignancy).
  • Treat the underlying cause: antibiotics if septic (esp. cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial/sinus infection); stop the COCP; treat malignancy/thrombophilia.
  • Supportive: antiepileptics for seizures; manage raised ICP; endovascular thrombectomy or decompressive surgery reserved for severe/deteriorating cases.
  • Pregnancy/future: avoid oestrogen-containing contraception afterwards; prophylactic LMWH in future pregnancies if prior CVST.
CRITICAL, counterintuitive: anticoagulate EVEN IN THE PRESENCE OF INTRACRANIAL HAEMORRHAGE — the venous (haemorrhagic) infarct is caused by the venous congestion, and anticoagulation (by clearing the clot) relieves the congestion and does not worsen the bleed. This is the opposite of arterial haemorrhagic stroke (where you would never anticoagulate).
Exam pearls
What it is
Thrombosis of the cerebral venous sinuses → obstructs venous drainage → congestion → raised ICP + cerebral oedema + (often haemorrhagic) venous infarction.
Commonest site
~50% = superior sagittal sinus → headache, seizures, hemiplegia.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Periorbital oedema/erythema, ophthalmoplegia (CN VI before III/IV), eye pain + upper-face hyperaesthesia (CN V); often septic (facial infection).
Features
Headache (commonest, may be sudden), N+V, seizures (more than arterial stroke), focal deficits, ↓consciousness, papilloedema.
Risk factors
COCP, pregnancy/puerperium (classic), thrombophilia, malignancy, local infection (sinusitis/otitis), dehydration, VITT.
Investigations
MRI/CT venography (1st-line); non-contrast CT is normal in most (doesn't exclude it); empty delta sign; D-dimer doesn't exclude.
Management
LMWH acutely → warfarin long-term (3–12 months) — anticoagulate EVEN WITH intracranial haemorrhage (opposite of arterial stroke); treat cause (antibiotics if septic, stop COCP), antiepileptics, manage raised ICP.
Afterwards
Avoid oestrogen contraception; prophylactic LMWH in future pregnancy.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cerebral Palsy:
What & why
Cerebral palsy (CP) = a disorder of movement and posture due to a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain's motor pathways (occurring before, during, or shortly after birth).
The core concept: the two defining features are that the lesion is non-progressive (a fixed, one-off brain injury — it doesn't get worse), but the clinical picture evolves as the child develops (the motor signs become more apparent over time). CP is a clinical, umbrella diagnosis, classified by the type of motor disorder, which localises the injury (spastic → UMN/cortex; dyskinetic → basal ganglia; ataxic → cerebellum).
  • The commonest cause of physical disability in children; non-progressive is the key word (distinguishes it from neurodegenerative conditions).
The decisive fork — which type of motor disorder?

CP is classified by the predominant motor abnormality, which points to where the brain was injured:

Type%Motor abnormalityLesion site
Spastic~70% (commonest)increased tone (spasticity) — UMN patternupper motor neurons (motor cortex/pyramidal tracts)
Dyskineticathetoid movements (slow writhing) + oro-motor problemsbasal ganglia + substantia nigra
Ataxiccerebellar signs (incoordination, ataxia)cerebellum
Mixedcombinationmultiple
The localisation logic (cross-ref motor pathways / basal ganglia / cerebellum):
• Spastic = UMN damage → ↑tone, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars.
• Dyskinetic = basal ganglia damage → athetoid/involuntary movements.
• Ataxic = cerebellar damage → the DANISH cerebellar signs.
The rule: the type of motor disorder tells you which part of the motor system was injured — a direct application of the "three motor flavours" (weakness/tone vs movement vs coordination).
Spastic CP subtypes

Spastic CP (the commonest) is subdivided by which limbs are affected:

SubtypeDistribution
Hemiplegiaone side (arm + leg)
Diplegiaboth legs (arms mild/spared) — classically associated with prematurity
Quadriplegiaall four limbs (most severe; often with seizures, learning disability)
The spastic pattern: increased tone from damage to UMNs — so all spastic subtypes show the UMN signs (↑tone, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing plantars).
Causes — mostly antenatal
TimingCauses
Antenatal (commonest)cerebral malformation, congenital infection (CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis), placental insufficiency, genetic
Perinatalhypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (birth asphyxia), prematurity, low birth weight
Postnatalmeningitis/encephalitis, head injury (incl. non-accidental), kernicterus (severe neonatal jaundice), intraventricular haemorrhage
High-yield links: CMV, rubella, and toxoplasmosis are TORCH infections that all cause CP (cross-ref congenital infections). Prematurity → periventricular leukomalacia / intraventricular haemorrhage → spastic diplegia classically.
Clinical features & presentation

CP typically presents in infancy/early childhood with:

  • Delayed motor milestones (not sitting/walking on time).
  • Abnormal tone (hypertonia/spasticity, or early hypotonia).
  • Abnormal posture/movements, asymmetry of movement (early hand preference <1 year is abnormal — suggests hemiplegia).
  • Persistent primitive reflexes, brisk reflexes (UMN signs).
  • Feeding difficulties (oro-motor).
Associated comorbidities (CP is rarely isolated): learning disability, epilepsy, visual/hearing impairment, speech/language difficulties, behavioural problems, GORD/feeding problems, constipation, hip subluxation, scoliosis → CP needs multidisciplinary care.
Non-progressive but evolving: the underlying lesion doesn't progress, but the manifestations change as the nervous system matures → worsening function over time should prompt reconsideration (a progressive picture is NOT CP).
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — history (risk factors, milestones) + examination (tone, posture, reflexes, movement pattern).
  • MRI brain — to identify the underlying lesion (e.g. periventricular leukomalacia, malformation) and support the diagnosis (not to make it).
  • Exclude progressive/mimicking conditions (metabolic, neurodegenerative) — because CP is by definition non-progressive.
  • Assess for the comorbidities (vision, hearing, cognition, epilepsy, feeding, orthopaedic).
  • GMFCS (Gross Motor Function Classification System) grades functional severity.
Management — MDT + symptom control
The overarching principle: no cure (the lesion is fixed) → multidisciplinary supportive care aimed at maximising function and managing spasticity + comorbidities.
  • Multidisciplinary team: physiotherapy (the cornerstone — maintain range of movement, function), occupational therapy, speech & language therapy (communication + feeding), dietitian, orthotics, social/educational support, paediatric neurology.

Managing spasticity:

  • Oral diazepam.
  • Oral and intrathecal baclofen.
  • Botulinum toxin type A (targeted intramuscular — for focal spasticity).
  • Orthopaedic surgery (for contractures, hip/spine).
  • Selective dorsal rhizotomy (neurosurgical — for severe spastic diplegia).
  • Anticonvulsants for epilepsy; analgesia as required.
  • Manage comorbidities: GORD/feeding (may need gastrostomy), constipation, drooling, hip surveillance, visual/hearing support, learning support.
  • The goal: not cure, but optimise function, comfort, and participation — lifelong support.
Exam pearls
What it is
Non-progressive lesion of the developing brain → disorder of movement & posture; the lesion is fixed but the clinical picture evolves with development.
Classification (localises the lesion)
Spastic (~70%, UMN damage — ↑tone), dyskinetic (basal ganglia — athetoid movements), ataxic (cerebellum — cerebellar signs), mixed.
Spastic subtypes
Hemiplegia, diplegia (prematurity), quadriplegia (most severe).
Causes
Mostly antenatal — cerebral malformation, congenital infection (CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis); also perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, prematurity, postnatal (meningitis, kernicterus, trauma).
Presentation
Delayed motor milestones, abnormal tone/posture, early hand preference (<1yr), persistent primitive reflexes.
Comorbidities
Epilepsy, learning disability, visual/hearing/speech impairment, feeding problems (rarely isolated).
Non-progressive
A worsening course is NOT CP (reconsider the diagnosis).
Management (no cure — MDT)
Physiotherapy (cornerstone) + OT/SALT; spasticity → diazepam, baclofen (oral/intrathecal), botulinum toxin A, orthopaedic surgery, selective dorsal rhizotomy; anticonvulsants; manage comorbidities.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Brain Abscess:
What & why
A brain abscess = a focal collection of pus within the brain parenchyma, usually bacterial, surrounded by a capsule and oedema — a neurosurgical + infective emergency.
The core concept: a brain abscess presents as a combination of infection (fever) + a space-occupying lesion (raised ICP, focal deficit) + seizures — but the "classic triad" is often incomplete, so a high index of suspicion is needed, especially with a predisposing source. The diagnostic hallmark is a ring-enhancing lesion on imaging, and management combines prolonged antibiotics + neurosurgical drainage.
  • Can be fatal if untreated (raised ICP → herniation); higher risk in the immunocompromised.
The decisive fork — how did the infection reach the brain?
📷 Image placeholder — Routes of spread mapped to abscess site — otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe/cerebellum, sinusitis → frontal lobe, haematogenous (endocarditis, lung, cyanotic right-to-left shunt) → multiple grey–white junction lesions

The route of spread points to the likely organism and any co-existing focus to treat:

RouteSourceTypical organisms / location
Direct / contiguous spreadotitis media / mastoiditis → temporal lobe / cerebellum; sinusitis → frontal lobe; dental infectionstreptococci, anaerobes (Bacteroides), oral flora
Haematogenous spreaddistant infection — endocarditis, lung abscess/bronchiectasis, skin, dental; cyanotic congenital heart disease (right-to-left shunt bypasses lung filter)often multiple abscesses, at grey-white junction; streptococci, Staph aureus
Penetrating trauma / neurosurgeryopen skull fracture, surgeryStaph aureus
ImmunocompromisedHIV, transplantToxoplasma (HIV), fungi (Aspergillus, Candida), Nocardia, TB
  • The high-yield source links: otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe/cerebellar abscess; sinusitis → frontal lobe; cyanotic congenital heart disease → haematogenous (the right-to-left shunt lets bacteria bypass the pulmonary filter).
In HIV: a ring-enhancing lesion is Toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise — the key immunocompromised differential.
Clinical features — the triad (often incomplete)

The classic triad is present in <50% — so don't rely on all three:

FeatureFrom
Feverthe infection (may be absent — an important pitfall)
Headacheraised ICP / the mass (often the commonest symptom — dull, progressive, unremitting)
Focal neurological deficitdepends on abscess location (hemiparesis, aphasia, ataxia, visual field defect)
  • Also: seizures, nausea/vomiting, ↓consciousness/confusion, personality change, signs of raised ICP (papilloedema, worsening headache) — evolving over days to weeks.
The pitfall: fever is often absent and the presentation can be subacute → a brain abscess can masquerade as a tumour → the predisposing source (recent otitis/sinusitis/endocarditis) is a key clue.
Investigations — imaging is key
📷 Image placeholder — Contrast MRI — a ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis and surrounding oedema, with the DWI panel showing central restricted diffusion (the key discriminator from a necrotic tumour)
  • Neuroimaging — the diagnostic hallmark: contrast MRI (preferred) or CT → RING-ENHANCING LESION with surrounding oedema and central necrosis.
  • MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is key: a brain abscess shows restricted diffusion centrally → distinguishes it from a necrotic tumour (which doesn't restrict) — the crucial radiological discriminator.
  • Blood cultures (before antibiotics — positive in ~25%), FBC/CRP (inflammatory markers, though can be normal), consider HIV test.
  • Identify the source: examine ears/sinuses/teeth; echocardiogram (endocarditis), CXR (lung source).
  • Definitive microbiology: from surgical aspiration of the abscess (send for culture — guides targeted therapy).
CRITICAL — do NOT do a lumbar puncture: LP is contraindicated in a space-occupying lesion with raised ICP → risk of coning (herniation) (cross-ref Raised Intracranial Pressure).
The ring-enhancing lesion differential

A ring-enhancing lesion isn't only abscess — the classic differential (mnemonic "MAGIC DR"):

CauseClue
Metastases / Malignancyoften multiple; no DWI restriction
AbscessDWI restriction; source of infection
Glioblastomairregular, older patient
Infarct (subacute)vascular territory
Contusiontrauma history
Demyelination (MS — incomplete ring)younger, other lesions
Radiation necrosis / Resolving haematomaprior treatment/bleed
Toxoplasmosis (in HIV)immunocompromised
The DWI point: abscess restricts on DWI; tumour does not — the key distinguisher.
Management — antibiotics + neurosurgery
📷 Image placeholder — Combined pathway — empirical IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + metronidazole (± vancomycin) for several weeks, stereotactic aspiration of larger abscesses, treat the source; NO lumbar puncture (coning risk)
The overarching principle: empirical IV antibiotics + neurosurgical aspiration/drainage + treat the source + manage raised ICP — a combined medical-surgical emergency.

Empirical IV antibiotics (start promptly, after blood cultures):

  • 3rd-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) + metronidazole (covers streptococci, anaerobes/Bacteroides, and Gram-negatives) — the standard empirical regimen.
  • ADD vancomycin if MRSA/Staph aureus is suspected (post-trauma, post-neurosurgery, endocarditis).
  • Then tailor to culture results from aspiration; prolonged course: IV for ~4–8 weeks (abscesses are hard to penetrate).

Neurosurgical drainage:

  • Stereotactic (CT-guided) aspiration or surgical excision — both diagnostic (get pus for culture) and therapeutic.
  • Generally abscesses >2 cm are aspirated/drained; small/multiple ones may be treated with antibiotics + monitoring.
  • Manage raised ICP: neurosurgical involvement; dexamethasone only if significant oedema/mass effect (used cautiously — can reduce antibiotic penetration).
  • Seizures: antiepileptics (often prophylactically).
  • Treat the source: e.g. ENT surgery for mastoiditis/sinusitis, treat endocarditis.
  • Monitor with serial imaging (weekly CT/MRI) to track resolution.
Exam pearls
What it is
Focal pus collection in the brain — an infective + neurosurgical emergency.
Triad (often incomplete)
Fever + headache + focal deficit — present in <50%; fever often ABSENT — don't be reassured.
Sources
Otitis/mastoiditis → temporal/cerebellar; sinusitis → frontal; haematogenous (endocarditis, lung, cyanotic congenital heart disease); trauma/surgery → Staph aureus; HIV → Toxoplasmosis.
Imaging
RING-ENHANCING LESION; MRI with DWI shows restricted diffusion → distinguishes abscess from necrotic tumour.
No LP
Contraindicated — raised ICP → coning (herniation) risk.
Ring-enhancing differential (MAGIC DR)
Metastases/glioblastoma, abscess, toxoplasmosis, demyelination, infarct.
Management
Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + metronidazole (± vancomycin for Staph) IV 4–8 weeks + neurosurgical aspiration (>2 cm) + treat source + antiepileptics; dexamethasone only for significant oedema.
In HIV
Ring-enhancing lesion = Toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Bell's Palsy:
What & why
Bell's palsy = an acute, idiopathic, unilateral lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve (CN VII) palsy — a diagnosis of exclusion.
The core concept: the single most important clinical task is distinguishing this LMN facial palsy (forehead involved) from an upper motor neuron (UMN) facial palsy (forehead spared → stroke). Because CN VII also carries fibres for taste, tears, saliva, and the stapedius, an LMN lesion produces a characteristic cluster beyond just facial droop. It's a stroke mimic, so getting the UMN/LMN distinction right is what prevents a missed stroke.
  • Commonest cause of facial nerve palsy; ~3× more common in pregnancy and in diabetes; thought to involve viral reactivation (HSV) causing nerve inflammation/oedema in the facial canal.
The decisive fork — UMN vs LMN facial weakness (forehead sparing)
📷 Image placeholder — Face diagram — LMN (Bell's) palsy weakens the WHOLE half of the face including the forehead, whereas an UMN (stroke) lesion spares the forehead (bilateral cortical innervation of frontalis)

This is the exam and clinical point — it determines whether you're looking at Bell's palsy or a stroke:

LMN facial palsy (Bell's palsy)UMN facial palsy (stroke/tumour)
ForeheadINVOLVED (can't wrinkle forehead / raise eyebrow / close eye)SPARED (can still wrinkle forehead)
Weaknesswhole half of the face (forehead + lower face)lower face only (spares forehead)
Lesionfacial nerve nucleus or nerve (pons → periphery)above the nucleus (cortex / internal capsule)
Other signsisolated CN VII (± its branches)often limb weakness, other deficits
The mechanism (cross-ref motor pathways): the forehead (frontalis) has bilateral cortical innervation (input from both hemispheres). So:
• a UMN lesion (one side) → the forehead is still driven by the other hemisphere → forehead spared.
• an LMN lesion (the final common pathway) → no input reaches the forehead → whole side including forehead is paralysed.
The rule: forehead SPARED → UMN → think stroke; forehead INVOLVED → LMN → Bell's palsy (or other LMN cause). If unsure, treat as stroke and escalate.
Clinical features — the LMN CN VII cluster
📷 Image placeholder — CN VII lesion map linking each branch to its sign — stapedius (hyperacusis), chorda tympani (loss of taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue), motor (facial droop + Bell's phenomenon on attempted eye closure)
  • Rapid onset (<72 hours) of unilateral facial weakness — the whole half of the face: drooping mouth, inability to smile on that side, inability to close the eye or wrinkle the forehead, drooling.

Because CN VII carries more than motor fibres, associated features can include:

  • Bell's phenomenon: the eye rolls up and out on attempted closure (visible because the lid won't close).
  • Hyperacusis (sounds seem loud — loss of stapedius muscle dampening).
  • Loss of taste on the anterior ⅔ of the tongue (chorda tympani).
  • Reduced/altered tear + saliva production, post-auricular pain.

Onset is acute, typically progressing over ~24–72 hours; usually reaches maximal weakness within days.

Is it really Bell's, or a secondary cause? — exclude these

Bell's palsy is idiopathic and a diagnosis of exclusion — features that suggest an alternative cause (and warrant further investigation):

Red flag / alternativeCause to consider
Vesicular rash (ear/palate) + severe painRamsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion)
Forehead sparing / limb weakness / other deficitsstroke / UMN lesion
Gradual onset or progressivetumour (e.g. parotid, acoustic neuroma)
Bilateral facial palsyLyme disease, sarcoidosis, Guillain-Barré, leukaemia
Recurrentconsider underlying pathology
Associated ear/parotid signsotitis media, cholesteatoma, parotid tumour (CN VII runs through the parotid)
Systemic / other cranial nervesbrainstem lesion, MS
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: herpes zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion → LMN facial palsy + painful vesicular rash in the ear/auditory canal/palate + often vertigo/hearing loss → treat with aciclovir + prednisolone (worse prognosis than Bell's).
Investigations — largely clinical
  • Diagnosis is clinical — an acute isolated LMN facial palsy with no other neurology and no alternative cause; routine bloods/imaging are NOT needed in typical cases.
  • Investigate only if atypical: red flags above → consider MRI (mass lesion, if not recovering by ~3 months), Lyme serology (exposure/geography), blood glucose (diabetes), examine the ear + parotid.
  • Grade severity: House-Brackmann grading (I–VI) is used to document facial nerve function.
Management (NICE CKS) — steroids + eye care
📷 Image placeholder — Management — oral prednisolone started within 72h (age ≥16) plus eye protection (daytime lubricant drops, night-time ointment + taping); add an antiviral to the steroid only in severe cases / Ramsay Hunt
The overarching principle: prednisolone within 72 hours + meticulous eye protection; most recover well.
  • Prednisolone (the key drug): give oral prednisolone to those ≥16 presenting within 72 hours of onset (e.g. 50 mg daily for 10 days, or a tapering regimen). No evidence for steroids started after 72 hours — the 72-hour window is critical.
  • Antivirals: antiviral alone is NOT recommended; adding an antiviral (e.g. aciclovir/valaciclovir) to prednisolone may be considered in severe cases (evidence modest/mixed).
  • Eye care (CRITICAL): because the eye won't close, there's a risk of exposure keratopathy / corneal damage → lubricating eye drops (daytime) + ointment + taping the eye shut at night; urgent ophthalmology if corneal symptoms (pain, redness, visual change).
  • Supportive: reassurance (good prognosis but recovery may take weeks–months); soft diet/straw if eating affected; facial physiotherapy/retraining for persistent weakness or synkinesis.
  • Follow-up: review if not improving by ~3 weeks, or incomplete recovery by ~3 months → refer (MRI to exclude a structural cause).
Prognosis
  • Most patients recover fully (majority within weeks; ~70–85% complete recovery), especially with early steroids.
  • Worse prognosis: complete (vs partial) palsy, older age, Ramsay Hunt (worse than Bell's), no recovery by 3 weeks.
  • Complications: incomplete recovery, synkinesis (aberrant reinnervation → involuntary co-movements, e.g. eye closes when smiling), crocodile tears (tearing while eating), exposure keratopathy.
Exam pearls
Definition
Acute idiopathic UNILATERAL LMN facial (CN VII) palsy — a diagnosis of exclusion.
Forehead sparing (THE key)
LMN (Bell's) = whole side, forehead INVOLVED; UMN (stroke) = forehead SPARED (bilateral cortical innervation of frontalis). If unsure, treat as stroke.
Features
Rapid onset (<72h) unilateral weakness + can't close eye/wrinkle forehead, Bell's phenomenon, hyperacusis (stapedius), loss of taste anterior ⅔ tongue (chorda tympani).
Red flags (not Bell's)
Vesicular rash → Ramsay Hunt; forehead sparing/limb weakness → stroke; gradual/progressive → tumour; bilateral → Lyme/sarcoid/GBS.
Ramsay Hunt
Zoster of geniculate ganglion (facial palsy + ear vesicles + vertigo) → aciclovir + prednisolone.
Management
Prednisolone within 72 hours (≥16 yrs); antiviral only added to steroids in severe cases (not alone); meticulous EYE CARE (lubricants + tape at night; ophthalmology if corneal symptoms).
Prognosis
Most recover fully (weeks–months); complications = synkinesis, crocodile tears.
Associations
Pregnancy (3×), diabetes.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Arteriovenous:
What & why
A cerebral AVM = an abnormal tangle of blood vessels connecting arteries directly to veins, bypassing the normal capillary bed — a high-flow, high-pressure lesion.
The core concept: the abnormal direct artery-to-vein shunt (no capillary bed to buffer the pressure) means the draining veins are exposed to arterial pressure → they become fragile and prone to rupture. The whole clinical concern is the risk of haemorrhage — which is what management aims to prevent.
  • Usually congenital; often asymptomatic (found incidentally); the commonest symptomatic presentation is haemorrhage, frequently in young adults.
The abnormal shunt — why AVMs are dangerous
Normal: artery → capillary bed (high resistance, drops the pressure) → vein.
AVM: artery → direct connection (the "nidus" — a tangle of vessels) → vein, with no capillary bed.
  • The draining veins receive blood at arterial pressure → become dilated, tortuous, and fragile → rupture → haemorrhage (the main risk).
  • The shunt "steals" blood from surrounding brain (arteriovenous shunting) → local ischaemia → can cause seizures and focal deficits.
The rule: an AVM's danger = rupture → intracranial haemorrhage (typically intracerebral ± subarachnoid).
Risk factors / associations
  • Usually sporadic/congenital, but associated with several inherited neurocutaneous syndromes (phakomatoses):
    • Neurofibromatosis
    • Von Hippel-Lindau disease
    • Sturge-Weber syndrome
    • Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT / Osler-Weber-Rendu) — a classic AVM association
  • Cross-ref the phakomatoses (Neurocutaneous Syndromes / genetics notes).
Clinical features
Most brain AVMs are asymptomatic and picked up incidentally (on imaging done for another reason). Of those that are symptomatic:
PresentationFrequency
Haemorrhage (intracerebral ± subarachnoid)~50% — the commonest and most serious
Seizures~25–40%
Persistent headaches~20%
Focal neurological deficit~15% (mass effect or vascular steal)
  • Haemorrhage: presents like any intracranial bleed — sudden severe headache, focal deficit, ↓consciousness, seizures; a leading cause of haemorrhagic stroke in young adults (cross-ref Stroke / TIA).
  • Pulsatile bruit may occasionally be heard over the skull (high-flow shunt).
Investigations
Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) = gold standard — defines the location, size, feeding arteries, and draining veins (essential for planning treatment).
  • CT/MRI — first-line to detect the AVM and any haemorrhage; CT angiography (CTA) / MR angiography (MRA) for non-invasive vascular imaging.
  • Transcranial Doppler — for monitoring / follow-up.
  • In acute haemorrhage: urgent non-contrast CT head first (detect the bleed), then angiography to find the source.
The Spetzler-Martin grading system
Grades the AVM to guide management + predict surgical risk, based on three features:
ComponentGraded as
Sizesmall / medium / large
Eloquence of adjacent brainwhether it sits in a functionally critical area — non-eloquent / eloquent
Venous drainagesuperficial / deep
  • Higher grade = higher surgical risk (larger, in eloquent cortex, with deep venous drainage = harder/riskier to treat).
  • Management classes map to the grade: Class A = surgery; Class B = multimodality treatment; Class C = observation.
Management — prevent haemorrhage
The overarching principle: the goal is to prevent haemorrhage/rupture; treatment choice is guided by the Spetzler-Martin grade (risk vs benefit).
  • Surgical resection (microsurgery) — definitive removal; best for low-grade, accessible, non-eloquent AVMs (Class A).
  • Endovascular embolisation — catheter-delivered occlusion of feeding vessels; often used to reduce the AVM before surgery/radiosurgery.
  • Stereotactic radiosurgery (e.g. Gamma Knife) — for small, deep, or eloquent AVMs unsuitable for surgery (works gradually over months–years).
  • Multimodality (combinations of the above) — Class B.
  • Observation / conservative — for high-grade, high-risk AVMs where treatment risk outweighs benefit, or asymptomatic incidental lesions — Class C.
Acute haemorrhage: manage as for intracranial haemorrhage — reverse any anticoagulation/antiplatelet, control seizures, neurosurgical evacuation in selected cases (cross-ref haemorrhagic stroke); definitive AVM treatment once stabilised. Symptomatic: antiepileptics for seizures; analgesia for headache.
Exam pearls
What it is
Abnormal tangle (nidus) connecting arteries directly to veins, NO capillary bed → high-pressure shunt → fragile draining veins → rupture.
Main risk
Haemorrhage (intracerebral ± subarachnoid) — a leading cause of haemorrhagic stroke in young adults.
Presentations
~50% haemorrhage, ~25–40% seizures, ~20% headaches, ~15% focal deficit; many asymptomatic/incidental.
Associations
Phakomatoses — neurofibromatosis, von Hippel-Lindau, Sturge-Weber, HHT.
Gold-standard Ix
DSA (digital subtraction angiography); CT/MRI + angiography for detection/bleed.
Spetzler-Martin grading
Size + eloquence + venous drainage → predicts surgical risk (Class A → surgery, B → multimodality, C → observation).
Management goal
Prevent haemorrhage: surgery, embolisation, stereotactic radiosurgery, or observation (by grade); antiepileptics for seizures.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Aphasia & Cort:
What & why
Aphasia (dysphasia) = an acquired disorder of language (production and/or comprehension) due to damage to the language areas of the dominant hemisphere (usually left). Cortical syndromes = the characteristic deficits produced by damage to each lobe — patterns that localise the lesion.
The core concept: higher cortical function is anatomically localised, so the pattern of deficit tells you where the lesion is. The whole clinical skill is mapping the deficit to the cortical area — which makes aphasia one of the most powerful localising signs in neurology (and a stroke red flag).
  • Aphasia ≠ dysarthria: aphasia is a language disorder (the words/meaning are wrong); dysarthria is a motor speech disorder (articulation slurred but language intact) — high-yield distinction.
The dominant hemisphere & the language pathway
  • Language sits in the dominant hemisphere — left in ~95% of right-handers and most left-handers.
The language circuit: spoken word heard at the ear → Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) → comprehension → signal passes via the arcuate fasciculus → Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) → generates the motor plan → fluent speech.
  • Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) = comprehension — supplied by the inferior division of the left MCA.
  • Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) = speech production — supplied by the superior division of the left MCA.
  • Arcuate fasciculus = the tract connecting Wernicke's → Broca's (allows repetition).
The vascular link (high-yield): the language areas are MCA territory → aphasia is a classic sign of an MCA stroke (cross-ref Stroke / TIA).
The decisive fork — fluency, comprehension, repetition
Every aphasia is classified by three questions: Is speech fluent? Is comprehension intact? Is repetition intact?
AphasiaFluent?Comprehension?Repetition?Lesion
Broca's (expressive)NO (effortful, "BRoken")intactimpairedinferior frontal gyrus
Wernicke's (receptive)YES ("Waffly", neologisms)impairedimpairedsuperior temporal gyrus
ConductionYES (fluent)intactPOOR (the hallmark)arcuate fasciculus
GlobalNOimpairedimpairedlarge (Broca's + Wernicke's — big MCA stroke)
Transcortical motorNOintactintactaround Broca's (spares it)
Transcortical sensoryyesimpairedintactaround Wernicke's (spares it)
Anomicyesintactintactnaming difficulty (angular gyrus)
The high-yield trio
  • Broca's = BRoken speech — non-fluent, effortful, but understands (frustrated because they know what they want to say) — frontal.
  • Wernicke's = Waffly speech — fluent but nonsensical (word salad, neologisms), doesn't understand (unaware of the error) — temporal.
  • Conduction = fluent + comprehends but CAN'T REPEAT — arcuate fasciculus.
The repetition rule: repetition distinguishes conduction (impaired) from the transcortical aphasias (intact) — if comprehension + fluency seem fine but repetition is out → conduction aphasia.
Broca's vs Wernicke's — the bedside contrast
Broca's (expressive / non-fluent)Wernicke's (receptive / fluent)
Speechhalting, effortful, telegraphic, few wordsfluent, normal rhythm, but meaningless (neologisms, paraphasias)
Comprehensionpreservedimpaired
Insightaware + frustratedoften unaware of the deficit
Associatedoften right hemiparesis (adjacent motor cortex)often no hemiparesis; ± visual field defect
Locationfrontal (Broca's)temporal (Wernicke's)
The frustration clue: Broca's patients know what they want to say and are frustrated (comprehension intact); Wernicke's patients talk fluently but nonsensically and are often unaware — a useful bedside discriminator.
Aphasia vs dysarthria vs dysphonia
ProblemFeature
Aphasialanguage (cortical)wrong words/meaning; comprehension and/or production affected
Dysarthriamotor articulation (speech muscles — CN or cerebellar/UMN)slurred but language intact (right words, badly pronounced)
Dysphoniavoice production (larynx / vocal cords)hoarse / quiet voice
The rule: aphasia = language; dysarthria = articulation; dysphonia = voice — don't conflate them.
The cortical lobe syndromes — localising by lobe
LobeKey deficits
Frontalpersonality/behaviour change (disinhibition/apathy), expressive (Broca's) aphasia (dominant), primitive reflexes, contralateral motor weakness, perseveration, anosmia, urinary incontinence
Temporalreceptive (Wernicke's) aphasia (dominant), memory impairment, superior quadrantanopia (Meyer's loop), auditory/complex hallucinations, temporal lobe epilepsy
Parietalcortical sensory loss, apraxia, agnosia, neglect (non-dominant), inferior quadrantanopia, Gerstmann's syndrome (dominant)
Occipitalvisual field defects, cortical blindness, visual agnosia (cross-ref Visual Field Defects)
Dominant vs non-dominant parietal:
• Dominant (left) parietal → Gerstmann's syndrome: acalculia (can't calculate), agraphia (can't write), finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.
• Non-dominant (right) parietal → neglect (of the left side/space), dressing/constructional apraxia, anosognosia.
The quadrantanopia rule — PITS: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior → parietal lesion = inferior quadrantanopia; temporal lesion (Meyer's loop) = superior quadrantanopia (cross-ref Visual Field Defects).
The key cortical deficits (the "A" signs)
SignMeaning
Aphasia / dysphasialanguage disorder
Apraxiainability to perform learned skilled movements despite intact motor/sensory function
Agnosiainability to recognise/interpret (objects, faces = prosopagnosia) despite intact senses
Acalculiainability to calculate (Gerstmann's)
Agraphiainability to write
Neglectfailure to attend to one side of space (non-dominant parietal)
Assessment — the bedside language exam
  • Test the components systematically: fluency (listen to spontaneous speech), comprehension (follow commands), repetition ("no ifs, ands, or buts"), naming (name objects), reading + writing.
