  • This localises the aphasia: fluency → Broca's vs Wernicke's; comprehension → receptive involvement; repetition → conduction vs transcortical; naming → anomic.
  • Then examine for associated signs (hemiparesis, visual fields, neglect) to localise the lobe.
  • Context: sudden-onset aphasia = stroke until proven otherwise → stroke pathway (cross-ref Stroke / TIA); consider tumour, abscess, MS, migraine, post-ictal (Todd's) for other tempos.
  • Imaging: CT/MRI to localise the lesion.
Exam pearls
Aphasia ≠ dysarthria ≠ dysphonia
Aphasia = language (dominant/left hemisphere); dysarthria = articulation; dysphonia = voice.
Classify by 3 questions
Is speech fluent? Is comprehension intact? Is repetition intact? — these three answers localise every aphasia.
Broca's = BRoken
Non-fluent, effortful, but comprehends (frustrated) → frontal (inferior frontal gyrus).
Wernicke's = Waffly
Fluent but nonsensical (neologisms), poor comprehension, unaware → temporal (superior temporal gyrus).
Conduction
Fluent + comprehends but CAN'T REPEAT → arcuate fasciculus. Global = all impaired (large MCA stroke).
Repetition rule
Repetition intact → transcortical; repetition impaired → conduction.
Vascular link
Language areas = MCA territory → aphasia is a classic MCA stroke sign.
Lobe syndromes
Frontal (personality, Broca's, motor); temporal (Wernicke's, memory, superior quadrantanopia); parietal (sensory, neglect, apraxia, Gerstmann's if dominant, inferior quadrantanopia); occipital (visual).
Gerstmann's (dominant parietal)
Acalculia + agraphia + finger agnosia + left-right disorientation.
Quadrantanopia PITS
Parietal = Inferior, Temporal = Superior.
Sudden aphasia
Stroke until proven otherwise.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Neuromuscular:
Overview — neuromuscular junction disorders
Disorders of transmission across the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), causing fatigable weakness. The two to know — myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — are classically contrasted by which side of the junction fails and how the weakness behaves with use.
The organising principle: MG = postsynaptic (antibodies block ACh receptors) → weakness worsens with use (fatigability); LEMS = presynaptic (antibodies block voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → less ACh release) → weakness improves briefly with use. Both are antibody-mediated and both have an important association (thymoma / small-cell lung cancer).
MG vs LEMS (high-yield comparison)
Myasthenia gravis Lambert-Eaton (LEMS)
Defectpostsynaptic — anti-AChR (± anti-MuSK) antibodiespresynaptic — anti-voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel (VGCC), ↓ACh release
Weakness with useworsens (fatigability) — worse through the dayimproves transiently (post-exercise facilitation)
Patternocular first (ptosis, diplopia), bulbar, proximal limbproximal legs first, gait; ocular/bulbar less prominent
Reflexes / autonomicreflexes normal; no autonomic featureshyporeflexia (may return after exercise); autonomic (dry mouth)
Associationthymoma / thymic hyperplasiasmall-cell lung cancer (paraneoplastic)
Key treatmentpyridostigmine; immunosuppression; thymectomytreat underlying cancer; 3,4-diaminopyridine
The one-liner: MG = fatigues with use, postsynaptic (AChR), thymoma; LEMS = improves with use, presynaptic (VGCC), small-cell lung cancer + hyporeflexia + autonomic.
What & why
Myasthenia gravis (MG) = an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) — antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) → impaired neuromuscular transmission → fatigable muscle weakness.
The core concept: the defining feature is fatigability — weakness that worsens with use and improves with rest. Each nerve impulse releases less effective ACh signalling (receptors are blocked/destroyed), so with repeated activity the muscle progressively fails, then recovers after rest. The clinical priorities are recognising the fatigable, ocular/bulbar-predominant pattern, checking for a thymoma, and being alert to myasthenic crisis (respiratory failure).
  • Postsynaptic disorder (contrast Lambert-Eaton = presynaptic — see LEMS tab); associated with thymic abnormalities and other autoimmune disease; bimodal (young women, older men).
The decisive fork: MG vs LEMS vs the mimics
The rule (high-yield): MG = postsynaptic, anti-AChR, thymoma, weakness WORSENS with use, prominent eye involvement; LEMS = presynaptic, anti-VGCC, small cell lung cancer, weakness IMPROVES with use, reduced reflexes + autonomic features. (Full side-by-side table on the Overview tab.)

Other mimics to exclude:

  • MND — no fatigability, has UMN signs + fasciculations, and spares the eyes.
  • Botulism — descending paralysis, presynaptic.
  • Thyroid eye disease — ophthalmoplegia/lid signs without fatigable limb weakness.
  • Muscular dystrophy — inherited, non-fatigable, ↑CK.
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — Annotated neuromuscular junction — myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic anti-AChR antibody blockade/destruction) vs Lambert-Eaton (presynaptic anti-P/Q voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies)
  • Autoantibodies against the postsynaptic AChR (present in ~85% of generalised MG): they block + cross-link + destroy AChRs (complement-mediated) → fewer functional receptors → each impulse produces a smaller endplate potential → transmission fails, especially with repeated use → fatigable weakness.
  • Anti-MuSK antibodies (muscle-specific kinase) — in some AChR-negative patients (more bulbar/respiratory, respond less to pyridostigmine).
The thymus link (high-yield): the thymus is abnormal in most MG — thymic hyperplasia (~70%) or thymoma (~10–15%) → the thymus drives the autoimmunity → all MG patients need a CT chest to look for a thymoma.
Clinical features — the fatigable pattern
📷 Image placeholder — Fatigable bilateral ptosis worsening on sustained upgaze with complex diplopia — the ocular-first presentation of myasthenia gravis

The hallmark: fatigable weakness — worse with repeated use / towards the end of the day, better with rest.

RegionFeatures
Ocular (often first)ptosis (worse on sustained upgaze), diplopia (extraocular muscle weakness) — eye involvement is characteristic
Bulbardysarthria, dysphagia, "fatigable" chewing, facial weakness (myasthenic "snarl")
Limbproximal weakness (worsens with repetition)
Respiratoryrespiratory muscle weakness → myasthenic crisis (§6)
Eye involvement (high-yield): MG characteristically affects the eyes (ptosis + diplopia), often as the presenting feature — a key contrast with MND (which spares the eyes). Fatigability signs: ptosis worsens on sustained upgaze; weakness worsens on repeated testing and recovers with rest. ~15% remain purely ocular (ocular MG); the rest generalise.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Repetitive nerve stimulation — a decremental response in myasthenia gravis vs a low-baseline incremental (post-exercise facilitation) response in LEMS
  • Antibodies: anti-AChR — positive in ~85% of generalised MG (the key test); anti-MuSK — if AChR-negative.
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation / single-fibre EMG: decremental response on repetitive stimulation (single-fibre EMG most sensitive).
  • CT/MRI chest (high-yield): look for a thymoma / thymic hyperplasia — essential in all MG.
  • Bedside: ice-pack test (ice on a ptotic lid improves it — cooling improves NMJ transmission), fatigability testing; the edrophonium/Tensilon test is largely historical.
  • Screen for associated autoimmune disease (esp. thyroid — check TFTs).
Myasthenic crisis (the emergency)
Myasthenic crisis = severe weakness involving the respiratory muscles → respiratory failure — life-threatening.
  • Triggers: infection, surgery, stress, pregnancy, or certain drugs — importantly some drugs worsen MG (e.g. aminoglycosides, macrolides, beta-blockers, quinine).
  • Management: monitor respiratory function (FVC) → ITU + ventilatory support if failing; IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange (PLEX) as rapid rescue; treat the trigger.
  • Distinguish from cholinergic crisis: excessive anticholinesterase → weakness + muscarinic excess (SLUDGE); in practice IVIG/PLEX + ventilation is the priority.
Management of MG
The overarching principle: symptomatic pyridostigmine + immunosuppression + thymectomy where indicated; IVIG/plasma exchange for crisis.
  • Symptomatic — 1st-line: pyridostigmine (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor → ↑ACh at the NMJ → improves transmission) — the mainstay for symptom control.
  • Immunosuppression: corticosteroids (prednisolone) for more than mild disease, usually + a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine, or mycophenolate).
  • Thymectomy: indicated if a thymoma is present (any MG); also beneficial in AChR-positive generalised MG up to ~65 (improves outcomes, reduces medication) — even without thymoma.
  • Rescue / crisis / refractory: IVIG or plasma exchange (PLEX) — for myasthenic crisis, severe exacerbation, or pre-operative stabilisation; rituximab (esp. MuSK MG) and newer complement inhibitors (eculizumab) / FcRn blockers (efgartigimod) for refractory disease.
  • Avoid drugs that worsen MG (aminoglycosides, macrolides, beta-blockers, quinine).
Exam pearls
What it is
Autoimmune, POSTsynaptic NMJ disorder; anti-AChR antibodies → fatigable weakness (worse with use, better with rest).
Characteristic pattern
Ocular (ptosis + diplopia, often first) + bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria) + proximal limb + respiratory weakness.
Thymus
Thymic hyperplasia (~70%) or thymoma (~10–15%) → CT chest in all MG.
Investigations
Anti-AChR (±anti-MuSK), repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement) / single-fibre EMG, CT chest (thymoma), ice-pack test.
MG vs LEMS
MG = postsynaptic, anti-AChR, thymoma, WORSENS with use, eye involvement; LEMS = presynaptic, anti-VGCC, SCLC, IMPROVES with use, ↓reflexes + autonomic.
MG vs MND
MG = fatigable + eye involvement, no UMN signs; MND = mixed UMN/LMN, spares eyes.
Myasthenic crisis
Respiratory muscle failure → monitor FVC, ITU, IVIG/plasma exchange; beware aminoglycosides, macrolides, beta-blockers.
Management
Pyridostigmine (symptomatic) + prednisolone/azathioprine + thymectomy (thymoma, or AChR+ generalised MG <65); IVIG/PLEX for crisis.
What & why
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) = an autoimmune disorder of the PREsynaptic neuromuscular junction — antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) → reduced acetylcholine (ACh) release → muscle weakness.
The core concept: LEMS is the presynaptic mirror-image of myasthenia gravis. Where MG blocks the postsynaptic receptor, LEMS blocks the presynaptic calcium channel that triggers ACh release — this single difference explains its two signatures: weakness that IMPROVES with use (repeated firing lets calcium accumulate → more ACh released) and its strong link to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) as a paraneoplastic syndrome. The clinical priority: recognise the pattern, and hunt for an underlying SCLC.
  • Much rarer than MG; often paraneoplastic (SCLC), sometimes primary autoimmune.
The decisive fork: paraneoplastic (SCLC) or primary autoimmune?

The first question in LEMS is whether there's an underlying cancer — because ~50% are paraneoplastic:

Paraneoplastic LEMSPrimary autoimmune LEMS
Causesmall cell lung cancer (SCLC)autoimmune, no cancer
Frequency~50–60%the rest
Clueolder, smoker, weight loss, coughyounger, other autoimmune disease
PriorityFIND + treat the SCLCimmunosuppression
The rule (high-yield): LEMS is in most cases a paraneoplastic syndrome occurring with SCLC, but can also be a primary autoimmune condition → every LEMS patient needs a hunt for SCLC (CT chest ± PET, and ongoing surveillance, as LEMS can precede the cancer by months–years).
The decisive fork: LEMS vs MG (the mirror image)
The single best discriminator (high-yield): LEMS IMPROVES with repeated use (post-exercise facilitation); MG WORSENS with use (fatigability) — opposite behaviours, both explained by the pre- vs postsynaptic mechanism. The other LEMS-specific clues: reduced/absent reflexes + autonomic dysfunction (both typically absent in MG). (Full side-by-side table on the Overview tab.)
Pathophysiology
  • Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC): VGCCs are needed for ACh release — when the impulse arrives, Ca²⁺ influx through the VGCC triggers ACh vesicle release into the synapse.
  • Antibody-mediated destruction of the Ca²⁺ channels → less Ca²⁺ influx → less ACh released → reduced muscle contraction.
The facilitation mechanism (why it improves with use): with repeated/sustained stimulation, calcium accumulates in the presynaptic terminal → progressively more ACh released → weakness (and reflexes) temporarily improve after brief exercise — the physiological signature of a presynaptic disorder.
  • The paraneoplastic mechanism: SCLC cells express VGCCs → the anti-tumour immune response cross-reacts with the NMJ calcium channels (molecular mimicry) → explains the SCLC link.
Clinical features
  • Proximal muscle weakness — difficulty climbing stairs, standing from a seat, raising arms overhead (a proximal, legs > arms pattern); improves transiently with exercise (facilitation), then fatigues with sustained effort.
  • Autonomic dysfunction: dry mouth (commonest), blurred vision, impotence/erectile dysfunction, constipation, postural hypotension.
  • Reduced/absent tendon reflexes — which may return/increase after brief exercise (post-exercise facilitation of reflexes).
  • Eye/bulbar involvement is usually mild (contrast MG — where it's prominent).
The triad (high-yield): proximal weakness + autonomic dysfunction + hyporeflexia = LEMS.
Investigations
  • Anti-VGCC antibodies (anti-P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel) — the specific test.
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation / EMG (high-yield): low baseline amplitude that INCREMENTS (increases) with high-frequency repetitive stimulation or after exercise — the electrophysiological hallmark of facilitation (opposite to MG's decremental response).
  • Hunt for SCLC (essential): CT chest ± PET-CT; if negative, ongoing surveillance (LEMS can precede the cancer).
  • Screen for associated autoimmune disease.
Management
The overarching principle: treat the underlying SCLC + enhance ACh release + immunosuppression.
  • Treat the underlying cancer (high-yield): if SCLC is found, treating it often improves the LEMS — the priority in paraneoplastic cases.
  • Symptomatic — enhance ACh release: 3,4-diaminopyridine (amifampridine) — blocks presynaptic potassium channels → prolongs depolarisation → more Ca²⁺ influx → more ACh release (the first-line symptomatic drug).
  • Pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) — may be added (less effective than in MG).
  • Immunosuppression: corticosteroids + steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine); IVIG or plasma exchange for severe cases.
  • Surveillance: continued screening for SCLC if not initially found.
Exam pearls
What it is
Autoimmune PRESYNAPTIC NMJ disorder; anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibodies → ↓ACh release.
SCLC link
~50% paraneoplastic → small cell lung cancer → always hunt for SCLC (CT chest ± PET; can precede the cancer).
Triad
Proximal weakness (legs > arms) + autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth, impotence) + reduced/absent reflexes.
The signature
Weakness + reflexes IMPROVE with exercise (facilitation) — the opposite of MG's fatigability.
LEMS vs MG
LEMS = presynaptic, anti-VGCC, SCLC, improves with use, ↓reflexes + autonomic, mild eye involvement; MG = postsynaptic, anti-AChR, thymoma, worsens with use, prominent eye involvement.
Investigations
Anti-VGCC antibodies; EMG = INCREMENTAL response to high-frequency stimulation (vs MG's decrement); CT chest for SCLC.
Management
Treat the SCLC; 3,4-diaminopyridine (↑ACh release); pyridostigmine; immunosuppression/IVIG/PLEX.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Brain Tumours:
Overview — brain & CNS tumours
Intracranial tumours are primary (arising from CNS tissue — glioma, meningioma, pituitary, schwannoma) or secondary/metastatic. In adults, metastases are the commonest intracranial tumour overall; of the primaries, gliomas and meningiomas dominate.
The organising principle: tumours present through three mechanisms — raised ICP (morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema), focal deficit (by location), and seizures (new-onset seizure in an adult → image the brain). The cell of origin + location define the specific tumour.
The common tumours (high-yield)
Tumour Origin Key points
Glioma (incl. glioblastoma)glial cells (astrocytes)commonest malignant primary; GBM = grade 4, poor prognosis
Meningiomameninges (arachnoid)commonest benign primary; extra-axial, dural-based; often slow/incidental
Pituitary adenomaanterior pituitarybitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm); hormone excess (prolactin) or hypopituitarism
Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma)Schwann cells of CN VIIIcerebellopontine angle; unilateral SNHL + tinnitus + balance; bilateral → NF2
Metastasesextracranial primarycommonest overall; from lung, breast, melanoma, renal, GI; often multiple
Management principles: MRI with contrast; MDT (neurosurgery/oncology); surgery (resection/biopsy), radiotherapy, chemotherapy; dexamethasone for peritumoural oedema; treat seizures. Detail per tumour in each tab.
What & why
Gliomas = tumours arising from the glial (neuroepithelial support) cells of the brain/spinal cord — astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells.
The core concept: gliomas are the commonest primary malignant brain tumour, behaving along a spectrum from low-grade (slow, well-differentiated) to high-grade (aggressive, poorly-differentiated) — with glioblastoma the most aggressive. They present like any space-occupying lesion (seizures, focal deficit, raised ICP), and the modern classification integrates molecular markers alongside histology.
  • Glial cells surround and support neurones; gliomas are graded WHO 1–4 by aggressiveness.
The decisive fork — which glial cell type, and what grade?

Gliomas are classified by cell of origin and grade (1–4) — the three types most → least malignant:

TypeOriginNotes
Astrocytomaastrocytesthe commonest; most aggressive form = glioblastoma (grade 4)
Oligodendrogliomaoligodendrocytesoften frontal; calcification; better prognosis if 1p/19q co-deleted
Ependymomaependymal cells (line ventricles)can cause hydrocephalus; commoner in children
WHO grading: Grade 1 = slow-growing, well-differentiated (most benign) → Grade 4 = fast-growing, aggressive, poorly-differentiated (most malignant). The astrocytoma spectrum: low-grade astrocytoma → anaplastic astrocytoma → glioblastoma (grade 4).
Glioblastoma — the most aggressive
  • Glioblastoma (GBM) = grade 4 astrocytoma — the commonest malignant primary brain tumour in adults; peak age 50–60; very poor prognosis (median survival ~12–15 months).
  • The classic imaging sign: a frontal mass that crosses the corpus callosum — the "butterfly glioma" appearance; typically ring enhancement + central necrosis + surrounding oedema.
  • Histology: necrosis + microvascular proliferation.
The 2021 WHO molecular reclassification
A major change: gliomas are now classified by molecular markers integrated with histology (WHO 2021 CNS5), not histology alone.
MarkerSignificance
IDH mutationIDH-mutant = better prognosis (usually lower-grade/secondary); IDH-wildtype = worse. Glioblastoma is now defined as IDH-wildtype grade 4 astrocytoma
1p/19q co-deletiondefines oligodendroglioma (+ IDH mutation); predicts better response to chemo (PCV) + radiotherapy
MGMT promoter methylationpredicts better response to temozolomide + better prognosis (methylated → temozolomide works better)
The point: modern glioma diagnosis is histology + molecular markers — IDH status, 1p/19q co-deletion, and MGMT methylation guide classification, treatment, and prognosis.
Clinical features — a space-occupying lesion
FeatureDetail
Seizuresthe commonest first symptom leading to diagnosis (new-onset seizure in an adult → image the brain)
Raised ICPheadache worse on waking / coughing / bending forward, papilloedema, nausea/vomiting, altered mental state, CN III/VI palsies (false localising)
Focal deficitsdepends on location — cranial nerve palsies, visual field defects, aphasia, hemiparesis
Progressivesubacute, progressive course (vs stroke's sudden onset)
High-yield: the raised-ICP headache is worse on waking, coughing, bending forward + papilloedema + vomiting (cross-ref headache red flags). New-onset seizure in an adult → think brain tumour until proven otherwise → image.
Investigations
  • 1st-line: CT head with IV contrast — detects the mass.
  • MRI (with contrast) — further characterises + assesses the lesion (soft-tissue detail, planning).
  • Angiography — assesses the tumour's blood supply.
  • Biopsy = definitive diagnosis — stereotactic (burr hole) or at craniotomy → histology + molecular markers (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT).
  • Avoid LP if raised ICP (coning risk).
Management
The overarching principle: grade-directed — watch-and-wait/surgery for low grade; maximal safe resection + radiotherapy + temozolomide (Stupp protocol) for high grade.

Low-grade glioma:

  • Watch and wait with radiological surveillance (serial imaging) if asymptomatic/stable.
  • Surgery (resection/debulking) if needed, with radiotherapy afterwards if residual tissue remains.

High-grade glioma / glioblastoma:

  • Maximal safe surgical resection (debulking) = mainstay.
  • Glioblastoma → the Stupp protocol: maximal safe resection → concurrent radiotherapy + temozolomide → adjuvant temozolomide (in previously fit patients). MGMT-methylated tumours respond better to temozolomide.
  • Oligodendroglioma (1p/19q co-deleted): radiotherapy + PCV chemotherapy (procarbazine, lomustine, vincristine).
  • Supportive: dexamethasone for tumour-associated oedema/raised ICP; antiepileptics for seizures; neuro-oncology MDT; palliative care where appropriate.
Exam pearls
What it is
Tumour of glial cells (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependymal cells) — commonest primary malignant brain tumour.
Types (most → least malignant)
Astrocytoma (→ glioblastoma = grade 4), oligodendroglioma, ependymoma; WHO grade 1 (slow/benign) → 4 (aggressive/malignant).
Glioblastoma
Grade 4 astrocytoma; frontal mass crossing the corpus callosum ("butterfly glioma"); ring enhancement + necrosis; median survival ~12–15 months.
2021 WHO molecular markers
IDH mutation (mutant = better), 1p/19q co-deletion (oligodendroglioma), MGMT methylation (→ better temozolomide response).
Clinical
Space-occupying lesion — seizures (commonest first symptom), raised ICP (headache worse on waking/coughing/bending, papilloedema, vomiting), focal deficits.
New-onset adult seizure
Image for a tumour.
Investigations
CT with contrast (1st-line) → MRI → biopsy (definitive + molecular markers); avoid LP if raised ICP.
Management
Low grade → watch-and-wait/surgery ± radiotherapy; high grade/GBM → maximal safe resection + radiotherapy + temozolomide (Stupp); dexamethasone for oedema, antiepileptics for seizures.
What & why
Meningioma = a non-glial tumour arising from the arachnoid (meningothelial) "cap" cells of the meninges — an extra-axial tumour (arising outside the brain parenchyma, from its coverings).
The core concept: meningiomas are the commonest primary brain tumour overall. The key contrast with glioma: they are usually benign, slow-growing, and extra-axial — causing symptoms by compressing adjacent brain (mass effect), not invading it. Hence often incidental, frequently curable by surgery, and much better prognosis than gliomas.
  • Commoner in women and with increasing age.
The decisive fork — extra-axial (meningioma) vs intra-axial (glioma)
Meningioma (extra-axial)Glioma (intra-axial)
Originarachnoid cap cells (meninges — outside brain)glial cells (within brain parenchyma)
Relationship to braincompresses brain from outside (mass effect)infiltrates brain from within
Behaviourusually benign, slow-growingoften malignant/infiltrative
Imagingwell-circumscribed, extra-axial, uniform enhancement, "dural tail"ill-defined, intra-axial, often irregular/necrotic
Prognosisgood (often curable)worse (esp. glioblastoma)
The rule: meningioma = extra-axial, benign, compresses; glioma = intra-axial, malignant, infiltrates — the extra-axial location + dural attachment identifies a meningioma on imaging.
Location
  • ~90% are intracranial; common sites: ~25% falx cerebri (parasagittal), ~20% convexity (over the hemispheres), ~20% sphenoid wing.
  • Also: olfactory groove, tuberculum sellae, posterior fossa, spinal.
The point: the location determines the symptoms — sphenoid wing → visual/eye signs; parasagittal → leg weakness/seizures; olfactory groove → anosmia.
WHO grading
GradeType%Behaviour
Grade 1meningioma (benign)~90%benign, slow-growing
Grade 2atypical meningioma~5%abnormal cells, likely to recur post-op
Grade 3anaplastic (malignant)~5%malignant, fast-growing, recurs post-op
The point: the vast majority (~90%) are benign grade 1 — hence the generally good prognosis; higher grades recur and behave aggressively.
Risk factors
  • Idiopathic (most).
  • Increasing age; female sex (hormone-sensitive — express progesterone receptors).
  • Previous cranial irradiation (a well-recognised risk).
  • Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) — a classic association (also causes bilateral acoustic neuromas).
Clinical features — mass effect
  • Often an incidental finding (asymptomatic, benign — found on imaging for another reason).

When symptomatic, presents as a space-occupying lesion via mass effect:

FeatureDetail
Seizurescommon (cortical compression)
Raised ICPheadache worse on waking/coughing/bending, papilloedema, vomiting
Focal deficitscranial nerve palsies, visual field defects, language dysfunction — depend on location
High-yield: because meningiomas compress rather than infiltrate, the deficit is focal and localises to the site (parasagittal → contralateral leg weakness; sphenoid wing → proptosis/visual loss; olfactory groove → anosmia). Slow growth → insidious symptoms; they can become large before presenting.
Investigations
  • 1st-line: CT head with IV contrast — well-circumscribed ("globose") extra-axial mass with uniform contrast enhancement, ± dural thickening; the "dural tail" sign is characteristic; ± surrounding oedema, calcification, and hyperostosis (thickening of adjacent bone).
  • MRI (with contrast) — to characterise + assess the lesion.
  • Angiography — assesses blood supply (relevant for pre-operative embolisation — meningiomas are vascular).
  • Biopsy — to confirm diagnosis (stereotactic burr hole or craniotomy).
Management
The overarching principle: observe if small/asymptomatic; surgical resection is the mainstay for symptomatic/growing tumours; radiotherapy for residual/high-grade/inoperable.
  • Observation (watch-and-wait): small, asymptomatic, incidental meningiomas → serial imaging surveillance (many never need treatment).
  • Endovascular embolisation — pre-operative, to reduce vascular supply and bleeding at surgery.
  • Surgical removal (mainstay for symptomatic tumours): gross total resection (curative for grade 1 if completely removed), subtotal resection, or biopsy only — depending on location/resectability.
  • Radiotherapy: for residual/recurrent tumour, high-grade (2/3), or surgically inaccessible lesions; stereotactic radiosurgery for small/deep lesions.
  • Supportive: dexamethasone for peritumoural oedema; antiepileptics for seizures.
Exam pearls
What it is
Benign, slow-growing EXTRA-AXIAL tumour of arachnoid cap cells — commonest primary brain tumour; compresses (doesn't infiltrate).
vs Glioma
Meningioma (extra-axial, benign, compresses) vs glioma (intra-axial, malignant, infiltrates).
Locations
Falx (parasagittal) ~25%, convexity ~20%, sphenoid wing ~20%; location determines symptoms.
WHO grade
~90% grade 1 (benign), ~5% atypical (recur), ~5% anaplastic (malignant).
Risk factors
Age, female sex (progesterone receptors), prior cranial irradiation, NF2 (+ bilateral acoustic neuromas).
Presentation
Often incidental; when symptomatic → space-occupying (seizures, raised ICP, focal deficits by location); insidious onset (slow-growing).
Imaging
CT/MRI with contrast → well-circumscribed extra-axial mass, uniform enhancement, "dural tail" sign, ± calcification/hyperostosis.
Management
Observe if small/asymptomatic; surgical resection = mainstay (gross total = curative for grade 1); radiotherapy for residual/high-grade/inoperable; embolisation pre-op.
What & why
A pituitary adenoma = a benign tumour of the anterior pituitary gland, arising within the sella turcica.
The core concept: pituitary adenomas cause problems in three ways — (1) mass effect (compressing local structures, classically the optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia), (2) hormone hypersecretion (a functioning adenoma → an endocrine syndrome), and (3) hormone hyposecretion (compressing normal gland → hypopituitarism). The whole picture flows from which of these three is happening — and crucially, prolactinoma is treated medically first, not surgically.
  • Commonest cause of pituitary dysfunction; sit at the crossroads of neurology (mass effect), endocrinology (hormones), and ophthalmology (visual fields).
The decisive fork — mass effect vs hypersecretion vs hyposecretion
MechanismHow it presents
Mass effectbitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm), headache, cranial nerve palsies, hypopituitarism, (rarely) CSF rhinorrhoea, pituitary apoplexy
Hormone HYPERsecretionan endocrine excess syndrome — prolactinoma, acromegaly, Cushing's disease, (rarely) TSH-oma
Hormone HYPOsecretionhypopituitarism — from compression of the normal gland
The rule: a functioning microadenoma presents with a hormone syndrome; a non-functioning macroadenoma presents with mass effect + hypopituitarism.
Classification

By size:

TermSize
Microadenoma< 1 cm
Macroadenoma> 1 cm
Giant adenomaprolactinoma > 4 cm

By function (hormone):

TypeSecretesSyndrome
Prolactinoma (commonest)prolactinhyperprolactinaemia
SomatotrophGHacromegaly (adults) / gigantism (children)
CorticotrophACTHCushing's disease
Non-functioningnonemass effect + hypopituitarism
Thyrotroph (rare)TSHsecondary hyperthyroidism
The size-function link: microadenomas usually present via hormone hypersecretion (small but functioning); macroadenomas present via mass effect + hypopituitarism.
Mass effect features
FeatureMechanism
Bitemporal hemianopia (superior fields first)compression of the optic chiasm (which sits above the pituitary) — the classic sign
Non-specific headachesstretching of the dura/sella
Cranial nerve palsieslateral extension into the cavernous sinus (CN III, IV, VI, Va/b) → diplopia
Hypopituitarismcompression of the normal anterior pituitary
CSF rhinorrhoea (rare)downward erosion through the sellar floor
Pituitary apoplexy (rare, emergency)haemorrhage/infarction of the tumour
Bitemporal hemianopia (cross-ref visual pathways): the optic chiasm sits directly above the pituitary → an enlarging adenoma compresses the crossing nasal fibres → loss of both temporal (outer) visual fields (classically upper quadrants first, as it compresses from below) — the single most examined pituitary sign.
The functioning adenomas (cross-ref Endocrinology)
  • Prolactinoma (commonest functioning): women — galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea, infertility, ↓libido (present early → usually microadenomas); men — ↓libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia (present late → often macroadenomas).
  • The "stalk effect" caveat: any large pituitary mass can mildly ↑ prolactin by compressing the stalk (dopamine can't reach the lactotrophs) — but very high prolactin = a true prolactinoma.
  • Acromegaly (GH): enlarged hands/feet/jaw, coarse features, sweating, organomegaly.
  • Cushing's disease (ACTH): central obesity, striae, hypertension, hyperglycaemia.
Investigations
  • Gold standard: MRI (pituitary/sella with contrast) — defines size, extent, chiasm/cavernous sinus involvement.
  • Test ALL pituitary hormones: prolactin, IGF-1 (GH), cortisol/ACTH (± dexamethasone suppression), TFTs, LH/FSH/oestrogen/testosterone — to identify hypersecretion and hyposecretion.
  • Formal visual field testing (perimetry) — to detect/monitor bitemporal hemianopia.
  • The main differential: craniopharyngioma — a sellar/suprasellar tumour from Rathke's pouch remnants (commoner in children, often calcified, classically lower quadrant field loss first from superior compression).
Pituitary apoplexy — the emergency
Sudden haemorrhage into or infarction of a pituitary tumour → a neurosurgical/endocrine emergency.
Features: sudden severe headache, visual loss/ophthalmoplegia, ↓consciousness, and acute hypopituitarism — critically adrenal (cortisol) crisis.
Management: urgent hydrocortisone (steroid cover for adrenal insufficiency — life-saving), fluid/electrolyte support, urgent MRI, neurosurgical + endocrine input.
Management
The overarching principle: PROLACTINOMA → dopamine agonist first-line (medical); ALL OTHER symptomatic adenomas → transsphenoidal surgery first-line; replace deficient hormones.
  • Prolactinoma (the exception): 1st-line = dopamine agonist (cabergoline > bromocriptine) — shrinks the tumour and normalises prolactin → medical treatment is first-line, surgery rarely needed.
  • All other functioning + symptomatic non-functioning adenomas: 1st-line = transsphenoidal surgery (the sella is accessed via the nose/sphenoid sinus). Complications: CSF leak, meningitis, bleeding, endocrine disturbance (hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus).
  • Acromegaly: surgery first-line; if not cured → somatostatin analogues (octreotide/lanreotide), GH-receptor antagonist (pegvisomant), or dopamine agonist.
  • Cushing's disease: transsphenoidal surgery first-line; medical adrenal-blocking therapy/radiotherapy if not cured.
  • Radiotherapy for residual/recurrent/inoperable tumour.
  • Hormone replacement for hyposecretion: hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, sex steroids, ± desmopressin for DI.
  • Non-functioning microadenoma, asymptomatic: observe with serial imaging (incidentalomas).
Exam pearls
What it is
Benign anterior pituitary tumour → presents 3 ways: mass effect, hormone hypersecretion, hormone hyposecretion.
Classification
Micro (<1 cm) vs macro (>1 cm); micro → hormone syndromes, macro → mass effect + hypopituitarism.
Mass effect
BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA (optic chiasm — upper quadrants first), headache, cavernous sinus CN palsies, hypopituitarism.
Functioning types
Prolactinoma (commonest), GH → acromegaly, ACTH → Cushing's disease.
Investigations
MRI (gold standard) + full pituitary hormone profile + visual field testing; differential = craniopharyngioma.
Pituitary apoplexy
Sudden haemorrhage into tumour → thunderclap headache + visual loss + adrenal crisis → urgent hydrocortisone.
Management
PROLACTINOMA → dopamine agonist (cabergoline) FIRST-LINE; all other symptomatic adenomas → transsphenoidal surgery; replace deficient hormones; observe asymptomatic incidentalomas.
Acromegaly / Cushing's
Surgery first-line + medical adjuncts (somatostatin analogues/pegvisomant; adrenal blockers).
What & why
Metastatic (secondary) brain tumours = cancer that has spread to the brain from a primary tumour elsewhere — the commonest brain tumour overall (secondary >> primary).
The core concept: in an adult with known cancer and new neurology — or with multiple brain lesions — think metastases first, not a primary brain tumour. Priorities: identify the primary, define the number/extent of lesions, and match treatment (local vs whole-brain vs systemic) to disease burden and prognosis.
  • Occur in ~20–40% of cancer patients; the commonest intracranial tumour in adults; usually a marker of advanced (stage IV) disease.
The decisive fork — metastases vs primary brain tumour
Metastases (secondary)Primary brain tumour
Numberoften MULTIPLE lesionsusually single
Locationgrey-white matter junction (small vessels trap emboli)varies
Historyknown primary cancer / systemic diseaseoften none
Imagingmultiple ring-enhancing lesions + marked oedemasingle, may cross midline (GBM)
Contextcommonest brain tumour overallrarer
The rule: multiple brain lesions in an adult = metastases until proven otherwise; a known cancer + new neurology = brain mets until excluded. Metastases are far commoner than primary brain tumours.
The common primaries
PrimaryNote
Lungthe commonest source (small cell + non-small cell)
Breastsecond commonest; common in women
Melanomahigh propensity for brain (often multiple + haemorrhagic)
Renal (kidney)renal cell carcinoma — can be haemorrhagic
Colorectal (GI)bowel cancer
(Thyroid, testicular)less common
The high-yield five: Lung, Breast, Melanoma, Renal, Colorectal — lung the commonest, melanoma the most likely to be multiple/haemorrhagic. Haemorrhagic mets: melanoma, renal cell, thyroid, choriocarcinoma classically bleed.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Raised ICPheadache (worse on waking/coughing/bending), papilloedema, nausea/vomiting, ↓consciousness
Seizuresnew-onset seizure in an adult
Focal deficitshemiparesis, aphasia, visual field defects, ataxia — often multifocal with mets
Cognitive/personality changeespecially with multiple lesions
Systemicfeatures of the primary cancer (weight loss, the known malignancy)
The multifocal clue: because mets are often multiple, deficits may be multifocal (several unrelated signs) — a clue to metastatic rather than single primary disease. New neurology in a known cancer patient = brain mets until proven otherwise.
Investigations
  • MRI with contrast (most sensitive): typically multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white junction with disproportionate surrounding vasogenic oedema. The ring-enhancing differential applies (MAGIC DR); DWI helps distinguish met from abscess.
  • Find the primary (if not known): CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, examine skin (melanoma) + breasts, consider PET-CT, tumour markers. The brain lesion may be the FIRST presentation of an occult cancer.
  • Biopsy — if no known primary or diagnostic doubt → confirms metastatic and identifies tissue of origin.
  • Avoid LP if raised ICP (coning).
Management
The overarching principle: treatment is matched to the number of metastases, the primary, and the prognosis — combining local control (surgery/radiosurgery), whole-brain radiotherapy where appropriate, systemic therapy, and symptom control.
  • Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) — symptomatic first step: reduces peritumoural (vasogenic) oedema → rapidly improves symptoms; antiepileptics for seizures.
  • Surgical resection — for a single/accessible metastasis (large, symptomatic, mass effect, or primary controlled/unknown).
  • Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS, e.g. Gamma Knife) — for a limited number (typically 1–4) of metastases → ablates the lesion while sparing healthy brain (modern preferred approach for limited disease).
  • Whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT): for multiple metastases or adjuvant after surgery/SRS. The modern shift: WBRT improves intracranial control but impairs neurocognition/quality of life → practice has moved toward SRS alone for limited metastases, reserving WBRT for extensive disease.
  • Systemic therapy: chemotherapy, targeted therapy / immunotherapy (increasingly effective, esp. melanoma and some lung cancers — some cross the BBB).
  • Best supportive / palliative care: for poor-prognosis patients, supportive care ± dexamethasone may be most appropriate.
  • MDT (neuro-oncology + primary team) decision — guided by performance status, extracranial control, number of lesions, primary type.
Prognosis
  • Generally poor (marker of advanced disease), but highly variable — improving with SRS + effective systemic/targeted therapies; better with single met, controlled primary, good performance status, targetable tumour.
Exam pearls
Commonest overall
Metastases = commonest brain tumour overall (secondary >> primary); multiple lesions in an adult = mets until proven otherwise; known cancer + new neurology = brain mets.
Common primaries
Lung (commonest), Breast, Melanoma, Renal, Colorectal.
Haemorrhagic mets
Melanoma, renal, thyroid, choriocarcinoma.
Location & imaging
Grey-white matter junction; multiple ring-enhancing lesions + marked oedema (MRI most sensitive).
Presentation
Space-occupying (raised ICP, seizures, often multifocal deficits); may be the first presentation of an occult cancer.
Management
Dexamethasone (oedema) + antiepileptics; surgery (single/accessible) or SRS (limited 1–4 mets); WBRT for multiple mets (impairs cognition → shift toward SRS alone); systemic/targeted/immunotherapy; palliative care for poor prognosis.
Cautions
Avoid LP if raised ICP; biopsy if no known primary.
What & why
An acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) = a benign tumour of the Schwann cells surrounding the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), arising at the cerebellopontine angle (CPA).
The core concept: it grows in a specific space — the cerebellopontine angle — where CN VIII, VII, and V run close together. So it starts with unilateral CN VIII symptoms (sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance) and, as it enlarges, compresses neighbouring nerves (VII, V) then the brainstem/cerebellum. The key trigger: unilateral (asymmetric) sensorineural hearing loss → image to exclude an acoustic neuroma.
  • Benign and slow-growing; typically presents at 40–60 years; "vestibular schwannoma" is more accurate (usually arises from the vestibular division of CN VIII).
The decisive fork — unilateral vs bilateral
Unilateral acoustic neuromaBilateral acoustic neuromas
Causesporadic (the usual case)Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Significanceisolated tumoura genetic diagnosis — NF2
Age40–60younger
The rule: BILATERAL acoustic neuromas = Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) until proven otherwise — a pathognomonic association. Suspect NF2 in a young patient or with a family history.
The anatomy — the cerebellopontine angle

The tumour arises at the CPA, where several cranial nerves are packed together → this explains the symptom sequence as it grows:

NerveEffect when involved
CN VIII (vestibulocochlear)first affected — sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance/vertigo
CN VII (facial)facial nerve palsy (if large enough to compress it)
CN V (trigeminal)loss of the corneal reflex, facial numbness
Brainstem / cerebellumataxia, raised ICP, hydrocephalus (large tumours)
The "CN VIII → VII → V" sequence: starts with VIII (hearing/balance), then compresses VII (facial) and V (corneal reflex/facial sensation) as it enlarges. Loss of the corneal reflex (CN V afferent) is an important early sign of CPA compression.
Clinical features

Typical patient: 40–60 years, with gradual-onset UNILATERAL:

FeatureNote
Sensorineural hearing lossoften the first symptom — unilateral, gradual
Tinnitusunilateral
Dizziness / imbalancevestibular involvement
Sensation of fullness in the ear—
Facial nerve palsyif large → CN VII compression → loss of corneal reflex (CN V)
The key trigger: unilateral/asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss ± tinnitus → always exclude an acoustic neuroma with MRI (don't dismiss one-sided hearing loss as age-related). Vertigo caveat: imbalance is common but true rotational vertigo is often mild/absent (slow growth allows central compensation) — distinguishing it from Ménière's/BPPV.
Investigations
  • MRI of the cerebellopontine angle (internal auditory meatus) = investigation of choice — with contrast; detects even small tumours.
  • Audiometry — confirms a sensorineural pattern of hearing loss, typically unilateral/asymmetric, high-frequency.
  • (Historically brainstem-evoked response audiometry was used as screening; MRI is now the gold standard.)
The differential — unilateral SNHL / a CPA mass
  • Unilateral SNHL differential: acoustic neuroma, Ménière's disease, sudden SNHL, other CPA tumours (meningioma, epidermoid), vascular.
  • The rule: asymmetric SNHL is acoustic neuroma until excluded (cross-ref ENT hearing loss — Weber/Rinne localise SNHL vs conductive).
Management
The overarching principle: observe if small/slow; treat (surgery or radiotherapy) if growing/symptomatic — balancing tumour control against hearing and facial nerve preservation.
  • Observation ("watch and wait"): small, asymptomatic, or slow-growing tumours (especially older patients) → serial MRI surveillance (many grow very slowly or not at all).
  • Surgery: microsurgical resection — for larger/growing tumours or brainstem compression; balances removal against hearing and facial nerve preservation.
  • Radiotherapy: stereotactic radiosurgery (e.g. Gamma Knife) — for small–medium tumours, or those unsuitable for/declining surgery → controls growth with lower upfront morbidity.
  • NF2: needs specialist genetic + MDT management (bilateral tumours → complex hearing-preservation decisions).
The management principle: the decision balances tumour size/growth vs the risks to hearing and the facial nerve — hence observation is often appropriate for small tumours.
Exam pearls
What it is
Benign Schwann cell tumour of CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) at the cerebellopontine angle; "vestibular schwannoma".
Typical patient
40–60 yrs, gradual UNILATERAL sensorineural hearing loss (often first symptom) + tinnitus + imbalance + ear fullness.
As it grows
Compresses CN VII (facial palsy) and CN V (loss of corneal reflex) → "affects CN V, VII, VIII".
Bilateral = NF2
BILATERAL acoustic neuromas = Neurofibromatosis type 2 — pathognomonic.
Key trigger
Unilateral/asymmetric SNHL → MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma (don't dismiss as age-related).
Vertigo
True vertigo often mild/absent (slow growth → central compensation).
Investigations
MRI of the cerebellopontine angle/IAM (gold standard) + audiometry (sensorineural pattern).
Management
Observation (small/slow), surgery (large/growing), or stereotactic radiosurgery — balancing tumour control vs hearing + facial nerve preservation.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Spinal Cord Di:
Overview — the spinal cord disorders
Disorders affecting the spinal cord (and, for cauda equina, the lumbosacral nerve roots below it). The clinical skill is reading the pattern of motor, sensory and sphincter signs to localise the lesion — which tract, which level — then finding the cause.
The organising principle: a cord lesion gives UMN signs below the level (hyperreflexia, ↑tone, upgoing plantars) + a sensory level + sphincter involvement. The tracts affected define the syndrome: corticospinal (motor, same side below), dorsal columns (fine touch/proprioception/vibration, same side), spinothalamic (pain/temperature, opposite side).
Classic cord syndromes (high-yield)
Syndrome Tracts / pattern Classic cause
Brown-Séquard (hemisection)ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss; contralateral pain/temp losspenetrating injury
Anterior cordmotor + pain/temp lost; dorsal columns sparedanterior spinal artery infarct
Central cordupper > lower limb weakness ("cape" sensory loss)hyperextension in cervical spondylosis; syrinx
Dorsal columnproprioception/vibration loss, sensory ataxiaB12 deficiency (SACD), tabes dorsalis
Cauda equinaLMN signs, saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel — a nerve-root, not cord, lesionlarge disc prolapse
Cord vs cauda equina (high-yield): the cord ends at ~L1/L2 (conus medullaris). Lesions above → UMN signs (spastic, hyperreflexia); lesions below (cauda equina) → LMN signs (flaccid, areflexia) + saddle anaesthesia. Cauda equina + acute cord compression = surgical emergencies.
What & why
Spinal cord compression = compression of the spinal cord by a mass, causing progressive neurological deficit — a neurosurgical/oncological emergency.
The core concept: the cord is squeezed within the rigid spinal canal and the priority is time — the deficit is an UPPER motor neurone (UMN) pattern BELOW the lesion + a sensory level. The skill is recognising this early (before permanent paralysis), getting an urgent whole-spine MRI, and treating fast. The commonest serious cause is metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC).
  • Recovery depends on function lost before treatment → a "don't wait" diagnosis.
The decisive fork: cord compression vs cauda equina
Cord compressionCauda equina
Levelabove L1/L2 (cord ends ~L1)below L1/L2 (nerve roots)
MotorUMN — spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantarsLMN — flaccid, hyporeflexia
Sensorya sensory levelsaddle anaesthesia
Bladder/bowellate (spastic bladder)early (retention, incontinence)
The rule: cord compression = UMN + sensory level (above L1); cauda equina = LMN + saddle anaesthesia + early bladder/bowel (below L1). Other differentials: transverse myelitis, MS, spinal abscess, disc prolapse, spinal stenosis, subacute combined degeneration.
Causes
  • Malignant (metastatic) — MSCC (commonest serious cause): occurs in ~3–5% of cancer patients annually and is the initial manifestation of malignancy in ~20% (can be the first sign of cancer). Commonest primaries: breast, lung, prostate, renal, thyroid, myeloma (vertebral mets → collapse/extension into the canal).
  • Non-malignant: disc prolapse/herniation, vertebral fracture (trauma/osteoporosis), spinal stenosis, epidural abscess/haematoma, degenerative cervical myelopathy (§7).
Clinical features
Back pain (earliest + commonest): often precedes neurology by weeks; red-flag pain is worse on lying down, at night, and on coughing/straining/Valsalva; thoracic or band-like pain is suggestive. New/progressive back pain in a cancer patient = MSCC until proven otherwise.
  • Motor: progressive limb weakness below the level; UMN pattern (spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) — may be flaccid acutely (spinal shock).
  • Sensory: a sensory level (sensation lost below a specific dermatome — localises the lesion).
  • Bladder/bowel: later — hesitancy/retention then incontinence (a late, ominous sign).
  • Localising: cervical → arms + legs (tetra); thoracic → legs (para) + trunk sensory level.
Investigations (urgent MRI)
  • Whole-spine MRI = investigation of choice, reported within 24 hours to enable rapid treatment.
  • NICE timing: whole-spine MRI within 24 hours for spinal pain suggestive of mets with neurology suggestive of MSCC (within 1 week if pain suggestive of mets without neurology).
  • Whole spine (not just the symptomatic level) — multiple levels of compression are common; CT with contrast if MRI contraindicated.
  • Identify the primary (if new cancer): CT chest/abdo/pelvis, myeloma screen, PSA, biopsy. Neuro exam for level + baseline function (prognostic).
Management (NICE)
The principle: immediate high-dose dexamethasone + urgent whole-spine MRI + definitive treatment (surgery ± radiotherapy) within 24 hours — time-critical to preserve function.
  • Immediate corticosteroids: unless contraindicated, a loading dose of ≥16 mg dexamethasone ASAP, then 16 mg daily while planning treatment (with PPI cover + glucose monitoring) — reduces cord oedema. Hold steroids if lymphoma is suspected (can mask the diagnosis).
  • Supportive: thromboprophylaxis, MSCC coordinator for MRI, spinal immobilisation if instability suspected, analgesia; nurse flat with spinal precautions until stability confirmed.
  • Definitive (within 24h of confirmation): surgery is first-line in suitable patients — decompressive surgery ± stabilisation, followed by radiotherapy (the treatment of choice for fit patients with good prognosis); radiotherapy within 24h for those not suitable for surgery; best supportive care where prognosis is poor.
The prognosis rule: patients with no motor function for over 48 hours are unlikely to recover useful function → the pre-treatment neurological status is the key prognostic factor → treat early, before paralysis is established.
Degenerative cervical myelopathy
  • Degenerative cervical myelopathy = chronic cord compression in the cervical spine from degenerative change (spondylosis, disc, ligament hypertrophy) — the commonest cause of cord dysfunction in older adults.
  • Features: pain, classically loss of motor function in both upper limbs; gait disturbance, clumsy hands, sensory loss, bladder symptoms; UMN signs in the legs.
  • Hoffman's sign: flick one finger → positive = reflex flexion/twitching of the other fingers (a UMN sign of cervical myelopathy).
  • Investigation: MRI cervical spine = gold standard. Management: urgent assessment for decompressive surgery (to halt progression — deficits often don't fully reverse).
Exam pearls
What it is
Emergency; deficit = UMN pattern below the lesion + a SENSORY LEVEL (lesion above L1); vs cauda equina = LMN + saddle anaesthesia + early bladder/bowel (below L1).
Commonest serious cause
Metastatic (MSCC) — breast, lung, prostate, renal, thyroid, myeloma; can be the first sign of cancer (~20%).
Back pain
Earliest sign — worse lying down, at night, on coughing/straining; new back pain in a cancer patient = MSCC until excluded.
Investigation
Urgent WHOLE-spine MRI within 24 hours (multiple levels common; CT with contrast if MRI contraindicated).
Management
Dexamethasone ≥16 mg immediately (PPI cover; hold if lymphoma suspected) → definitive treatment within 24h — surgery (first-line if fit) then radiotherapy, or radiotherapy alone.
Prognosis
Pre-treatment function is key — no motor function >48h → unlikely to recover → treat EARLY.
Degenerative cervical myelopathy
Chronic cervical cord compression → bilateral UMN signs, clumsy hands, gait disturbance, Hoffman's sign; MRI cervical spine → urgent decompressive surgery.
What & why
Spinal cord injury (SCI) = traumatic (or acute) damage to the spinal cord → loss of motor, sensory, and autonomic function below the level of injury.
The core concept: the picture is defined by the LEVEL (tetraplegia vs paraplegia; whether breathing/autonomic control is affected) and whether it's COMPLETE or INCOMPLETE (prognosis + the recognisable cord syndromes). Layered on top are the acute complications unique to SCI — spinal shock, neurogenic shock, and (later) autonomic dysreflexia. Priorities: immobilisation + ABCDE, defining level/completeness, preventing secondary injury.
  • Usually trauma (RTA, falls, sport, assault); devastating, often permanent; management is time-critical to limit secondary damage.
The decisive fork: complete vs incomplete injury
CompleteIncomplete
Function belowtotal loss of motor + sensory (incl. sacral)some preserved function below the level
Sacral sparingabsentpresent (perianal sensation / anal squeeze)
Prognosispoorbetter (depends on the syndrome)
The rule: sacral sparing (preserved perianal sensation / voluntary anal contraction) = an incomplete injury = better prognosis → always examine the perineum / PR. The ASIA classification grades injury (A = complete → E = normal) by motor + sensory testing.
Determining the level

The neurological level = the lowest level with normal motor + sensory function; it determines what's lost:

LevelConsequence
High cervical (above C3–5)diaphragm (C3,4,5) affected → respiratory failure / ventilator-dependent
Cervicaltetraplegia (all four limbs)
Thoracic/lumbarparaplegia (legs) + trunk
Above T6risk of autonomic dysreflexia + neurogenic shock (§6, §5)
High-yield: "C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive" — injuries above this → the patient can't breathe → immediate ventilatory support.
The incomplete cord syndromes

Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection): a lateral hemisection → the classic dissociated picture:

  • ipsilateral weakness below the lesion (corticospinal — UMN)
  • ipsilateral loss of proprioception + vibration (dorsal columns)
  • contralateral loss of pain + temperature (spinothalamic)
The mechanism: the dorsal columns + corticospinal tract are ipsilateral (they cross higher up / in the medulla) → same-side deficits; the spinothalamic tract crosses at the level of entry → its damage affects the opposite side below — hence ipsilateral motor/proprioception + contralateral pain/temp.
SyndromeCausePattern
Central cordhyperextension (elderly, spondylosis)arms > legs ("man in a barrel"), sacral sparing — commonest incomplete syndrome
Anterior cordanterior spinal artery infarct / flexionmotor + pain/temp lost, dorsal columns spared; poor prognosis
Posterior cordrareloss of proprioception/vibration
Central cord (high-yield): arms > legs ("man in a barrel"), typically an elderly patient with a hyperextension injury on a spondylotic spine.
Spinal shock vs neurogenic shock
Spinal shockNeurogenic shock
Whattransient loss of ALL cord function below the lesion (a reflex phenomenon)a distributive shock (a circulatory problem)
Signsflaccid paralysis, areflexia, ↓tone (temporary)hypotension + BRADYCARDIA + warm peripheries
Mechanismtemporary "stunning"; reflexes return over days–weeksloss of sympathetic outflow (injury above T6) → unopposed vagal tone
Clueflaccidity later becomes spastic (UMN)hypotension WITH bradycardia (vs hypovolaemia = tachycardia)
The key discriminator: neurogenic shock = hypotension + BRADYCARDIA (loss of sympathetic tone; injury above T6) — the bradycardia distinguishes it from hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia) — critical in trauma (don't miss a bleed, but recognise neurogenic shock).
Autonomic dysreflexia
A clinical syndrome in patients with a spinal injury at or above T6.
  • Mechanism: a noxious stimulus below the level triggers a massive reflex sympathetic surge → severe vasoconstriction + hypertension below the lesion; compensatory vagal bradycardia + vasodilation above can't override it below (sympathetic outflow disconnected from higher control) → dangerous hypertension.
  • Triggers: faecal impaction, urinary retention (the commonest — blocked catheter/full bladder or bowel); pressure sores, ingrown nails.
  • Features: extreme hypertension, flushing + sweating ABOVE the level, pounding headache, haemorrhagic stroke in extreme cases.
The rule: SCI above T6 + sudden severe hypertension + headache + sweating above the lesion = autonomic dysreflexia → remove the stimulus (unblock catheter, relieve retention/impaction — the priority) + treat the BP (sit up, antihypertensives if needed).
Assessment & acute management
  • Immobilise + ABCDE: full spinal immobilisation (collar, blocks, board) until excluded/stabilised; Airway with C-spine control, Breathing (high cervical → ventilate), Circulation (distinguish neurogenic from haemorrhagic shock).
  • Neurological assessment: level + completeness (ASIA — motor/sensory, sacral sparing / PR).
  • Imaging: CT (bony injury) + MRI (cord, ligaments, soft tissue).
  • Definitive: surgical decompression/stabilisation for unstable injuries/cord compression; neuroprotection (avoid hypotension/hypoxia → prevent secondary injury); high-dose steroids are now controversial / not routinely recommended.
  • Rehabilitation: MDT spinal unit — prevent pressure sores, VTE, contractures, UTIs, respiratory + bladder/bowel problems, autonomic dysreflexia; physio, OT, psychological support.
Exam pearls
Define it
LEVEL (tetraplegia if cervical, paraplegia if thoracolumbar; C3,4,5 = diaphragm → ventilation) + COMPLETE vs INCOMPLETE (sacral sparing = incomplete = better prognosis).
Brown-Séquard
Ipsilateral weakness + ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss + contralateral pain/temp loss (spinothalamic crosses at the level; dorsal columns/corticospinal ipsilateral).
Central vs anterior cord
Central = arms > legs, elderly hyperextension; anterior = motor + pain/temp lost, dorsal columns spared.
Spinal shock
Temporary flaccid areflexia below the lesion (resolves → spastic UMN).
Neurogenic shock
Hypotension + BRADYCARDIA + warm peripheries (loss of sympathetic tone, injury above T6) — bradycardia distinguishes it from hypovolaemic shock.
Autonomic dysreflexia
Injury ≥T6: noxious stimulus below (bladder/bowel) → extreme hypertension + headache + sweating/flushing above the lesion → remove the trigger + treat BP.
Acute
Immobilise + ABCDE, CT + MRI, decompression/stabilisation, prevent secondary injury; MDT rehab.
What & why
Cauda equina syndrome (CES) = compression of the cauda equina — the bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord — a surgical emergency.
The core concept: the cord ends at ~L1 (the conus medullaris); below that the canal holds only the nerve roots (the "horse's tail"). So CES is a LOWER motor neurone (LMN), root-level problem — distinguishing it from cord compression (UMN). These roots carry bladder, bowel, sexual, saddle sensory, and leg function → compression threatens permanent incontinence + paralysis → recognise the red flags → emergency MRI → decompress.
  • A "must-not-miss, must-not-delay" diagnosis — consider in any new or worsening lower back pain.
The decisive fork: cauda equina vs cord compression
Cauda equinaCord compression
Levelbelow L1/L2 (roots)above L1 (the cord)
MotorLMN — flaccid, ↓tone + reflexesUMN — spastic, ↑tone/reflexes, upgoing plantars
Sensorysaddle anaesthesiaa sensory level
Bladder/bowelearly + prominentlater
The rule: CES = LMN (below L1) + saddle anaesthesia + early bladder/bowel dysfunction; cord compression = UMN + sensory level (above L1). (A conus medullaris lesion at L1 gives a mixed UMN/LMN picture — the transition zone.)
Anatomy

The spinal cord tapers to an end (the conus medullaris) at ~L1; the roots below (travelling in the canal after L2/3) are the cauda equina. What they supply explains every red flag:

FunctionTerritory
Sensorylower limbs, perineum, bladder, rectum
Motorlower limbs, anal + urethral sphincters
Parasympatheticbladder + rectum (emptying, defecation)
Because these roots carry saddle sensation, sphincter motor control, and bladder/bowel parasympathetics, compression → saddle anaesthesia + incontinence/retention + leg weakness — the red flags map directly onto the anatomy.
Causes
CauseNote
Herniated (prolapsed) discthe commonest — typically L4/5 or L5/S1
Tumoursespecially metastases
Spondylolisthesisanterior displacement of a vertebra
Abscessepidural abscess
Trauma—
Commonest cause: a large central lumbar disc herniation (L4/5 or L5/S1) compressing the roots.
Red flags: the clinical features
Red flagDetail
Saddle anaesthesialoss of perineal sensation; ask: "does it feel normal when you wipe after opening your bowels?"
Loss of bladder/rectal sensationnot knowing when they're full
Urinary retention or incontinencepainless retention with overflow is a late, ominous sign
Faecal incontinence—
Bilateral sciatica—
Bilateral / severe leg weakness—
Reduced anal tone (PR exam)—
Screening approach: ask about bladder/bowel/saddle symptoms + sexual dysfunction, and do a PR (anal tone) + assess perineal sensation in any suspicious back pain. Urinary retention is the most consistent finding (assess palpable bladder + post-void residual). CES-I (incomplete — altered sensation, the window to intervene) vs CES-R (retention — established, worse prognosis).
Investigations
  • Immediate hospital admission.
  • Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine — the investigation of choice; confirms compression + level + cause. Do NOT delay.
  • Bladder scan (post-void residual — objective evidence of retention); identify the cause (e.g. mets → find the primary).
Management
The principle: emergency surgical decompression ASAP — the sooner, the better the outcome.
  • Emergency lumbar decompression / discectomy ASAP to relieve pressure on the roots.
  • Timing: outcomes (especially bladder/bowel + sexual function) depend on how early decompression happens; once complete (retention) develops, recovery is much less likely → operate before that point.
  • Treat the cause: dexamethasone + radiotherapy/surgery if malignant (MSCC-type); antibiotics + drainage for abscess.
  • Supportive/rehab: bladder/bowel management, physiotherapy, pressure-area care, psychological support.
Exam pearls
What it is
Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots (below L1/conus) — a SURGICAL EMERGENCY; consider in any new/worsening lower back pain.
CES vs cord compression
CES (LMN, below L1) = flaccid + reduced reflexes + saddle anaesthesia + early bladder/bowel; cord = UMN + sensory level (above L1).
Anatomy
Cord ends ~L1 (conus); roots below = cauda equina → supply legs, perineum, sphincters, bladder/rectum (+ parasympathetics).
Commonest cause
Central disc herniation (L4/5, L5/S1); also mets, spondylolisthesis, abscess, trauma.
RED FLAGS
Saddle anaesthesia (ask about wiping sensation), urinary retention/incontinence, faecal incontinence, bilateral sciatica, bilateral leg weakness, reduced anal tone (PR).
Investigation
Immediate admission + emergency MRI lumbosacral spine + bladder scan.
Management
Emergency surgical decompression ASAP — outcome depends on early surgery (operate before painless retention becomes established).
What & why
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SACD) = degeneration of specific spinal cord tracts due to vitamin B12 deficiency — affecting the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts.
The core concept: "combined" = multiple tracts degenerate together → a mixed picture (dorsal column sensory loss + corticospinal UMN + spinocerebellar ataxia). The signature exam finding is the paradox of UMN signs (upgoing plantars, spasticity) WITH an LMN sign (absent ankle jerks). Priorities: recognise the pattern, check B12, and replace B12 urgently (reversible if early, permanent if not) — plus the two traps: nitrous oxide and giving folate before B12.
  • A treatable myelopathy — B12 is needed for myelin integrity (deficiency demyelinates these tracts).
The decisive fork: which tracts are affected?
TractFunctionDeficit
Dorsal columnsproprioception + vibration + fine touchdistal symmetrical tingling/burning/sensory loss (legs > arms), impaired proprioception + vibration
Lateral corticospinalUMN motorweakness, hyperreflexia, spasticity (legs first); brisk knee reflexes, upgoing plantars
Spinocerebellarproprioceptive input to cerebellumsensory ataxia → gait problems, positive Romberg's
The rule: SACD = dorsal columns (sensory/proprioception) + corticospinal (UMN weakness/spasticity) + spinocerebellar (sensory ataxia).
The signature mixed UMN/LMN picture
SignType
Extensor (upgoing) plantarsUMN (corticospinal)
Brisk knee reflexesUMN
ABSENT ankle jerksLMN (peripheral neuropathy component)
Impaired proprioception + vibrationdorsal columns
The paradox (high-yield): absent ankle jerks (LMN) + upgoing plantars/brisk knee jerks (UMN) together — because B12 deficiency causes a peripheral neuropathy (→ absent ankle jerks) alongside the corticospinal disease (→ upgoing plantars). Romberg's positive: loss of proprioception → falls when eyes close (sensory ataxia).
Causes (the classic traps)
  • Anything causing vitamin B12 deficiency: pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor — commonest), gastrectomy/ileal disease/Crohn's, vegan diet, malabsorption.
Trap 1 — nitrous oxide (recreational "laughing gas"): N₂O inactivates B12 (oxidises the cobalt) → can precipitate SACD even with normal B12 stores; increasingly common in young people.
Trap 2 — giving folate before B12: folate makes new RBCs which use up already-low B12 stores → precipitates/worsens SACD. The rule: always replace B12 BEFORE (or with) folate.
Clinical features

Symmetrical, distal, legs > arms:

  • Sensory: distal tingling/burning/paraesthesia + numbness, loss of proprioception + vibration → sensory ataxia, positive Romberg's.
  • Motor: progressive leg weakness + spasticity (UMN), later gait difficulty.
  • Mixed reflexes: absent ankle jerks + brisk knee jerks + upgoing plantars.
Other B12 features: megaloblastic anaemia (the neurology can occur without anaemia), glossitis, and cognitive/psychiatric change ("megaloblastic madness"). Progression is subacute (weeks–months); untreated → permanent.

ConditionDiscriminator

Copper deficiencycan cause an almost identical myelopathy (a mimic)
Investigations
  • Serum vitamin B12 (low) — the key test; folate, FBC + blood film (megaloblastic/macrocytic anaemia, hypersegmented neutrophils).
  • Methylmalonic acid + homocysteine (raised — more sensitive markers if B12 borderline).
  • Pernicious anaemia work-up: intrinsic factor + anti-parietal cell antibodies.
  • MRI spine: may show increased signal in the dorsal/lateral columns (classically posterior columns — "inverted V / rabbit ears" sign). Ask about nitrous oxide use and diet (vegan).
Management
The principle: urgent B12 replacement (before folate) — the earlier, the better the recovery; treat the cause.
  • Vitamin B12 replacement: IM hydroxocobalamin — urgent, often alternate-day loading then maintenance (neuro cases get more intensive loading).
  • CRITICAL: give B12 BEFORE folate — folate first in B12 deficiency can precipitate/worsen SACD → correct B12 first (or together, B12 prioritised).
  • Treat the cause: pernicious anaemia (lifelong B12), stop nitrous oxide, dietary advice (vegans), treat malabsorption.
  • Prognosis: early treatment → recovery/improvement possible; delayed → permanent deficit → treat urgently. Physio/OT for residual deficits.
Exam pearls
What it is
B12 deficiency → "combined" degeneration of dorsal columns + lateral corticospinal + spinocerebellar tracts.
Tract signs
Dorsal columns → proprioception/vibration loss, sensory ataxia, Romberg's, distal paraesthesia (legs > arms); corticospinal → UMN (spasticity, upgoing plantars, brisk knee jerks); spinocerebellar → ataxia.
Signature
Mixed UMN + LMN: absent ankle jerks (LMN) + upgoing plantars/brisk knee jerks (UMN).
Causes/traps
Pernicious anaemia (commonest), vegan diet, malabsorption; traps → nitrous oxide (inactivates B12) and giving FOLATE before B12.
Investigations
Low B12, macrocytic/megaloblastic anaemia + hypersegmented neutrophils, ↑MMA/homocysteine, IF/parietal cell antibodies; MRI (dorsal column signal).
Management
Urgent IM B12 (hydroxocobalamin) — BEFORE folate; treat cause (stop nitrous oxide, lifelong B12 in pernicious anaemia); early → reversible, delayed → permanent.
What & why
Syringomyelia = a fluid-filled cavity (a "syrinx") within the spinal cord — a collection of CSF-like fluid inside the cord substance.
The core concept: the syrinx forms centrally and expands outward → it hits the crossing spinothalamic fibres (pain + temperature) FIRST, sparing the peripheral dorsal columns until later. Hallmark: a "dissociated" sensory loss — pain + temperature lost but light touch/proprioception/vibration preserved — classically in a "cape" distribution (neck, shoulders, arms).
  • Mnemonic: "Syringomyelia = Superman — a cape, and can't feel pain" (cape distribution + loss of pain). Often associated with a Chiari malformation; slowly progressive.
The decisive fork: dissociated sensory loss
Syringomyelia (central cord)
Lostpain + temperature (spinothalamic)
Preserved (early)light touch, proprioception, vibration (dorsal columns)
Distribution"cape" (neck/shoulders/arms — the syrinx is usually cervical)
Whycentral syrinx hits the decussating spinothalamic fibres first
The rule: dissociated sensory loss (pain/temp lost, touch/proprioception preserved) in a cape distribution = syringomyelia — a central cord lesion affecting the crossing spinothalamic fibres. (Contrast SACD/tabes = dorsal columns lost.)
The mechanism
  • The spinothalamic tract (STT) carries pain + temperature, and its fibres DECUSSATE in the anterior (white) commissure — in the centre of the cord, just anterior to the central canal.
  • A central syrinx expands outward → compresses/destroys these crossing STT fibres FIRST → loss of pain + temperature at those levels.
  • The dorsal columns (light touch, proprioception, vibration) run peripherally (posteriorly) → spared early → hence the dissociation.
  • Cape distribution: the syrinx is typically cervical/upper thoracic → affects segments supplying the neck, shoulders, arms.
The classic clue: the patient burns or injures their hands without realising (can't feel pain/temperature) → painless burns/injuries + Charcot joints.
Aetiology
CauseNote
Chiari malformationthe cerebellar tonsils bulge through the foramen magnum — the commonest association; disrupts CSF flow → syrinx
Traumapost-traumatic syrinx
Tumoursspinal cord tumours
Idiopathic—
The Chiari link: Chiari I malformation (low cerebellar tonsils) is the classic association → always image the brain (craniocervical junction) in syringomyelia.
Clinical features

Cape-like dissociated sensory loss (the hallmark): loss of pain + temperature over the neck/shoulders/arms; preserved light touch/proprioception/vibration → painless burns/injuries.

As the syrinx expands it compresses adjacent structures:

FeatureMechanism
Spastic weakness (esp. legs)corticospinal tract → UMN signs, upgoing plantars
Horner's syndromesympathetic fibres (T1) — ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis
Bladder/bowel dysfunctionautonomic tracts
Scoliosisasymmetric paraspinal muscle involvement
Hand wasting / LMN signsanterior horn cell involvement (claw hand, wasting)
Horner's (high-yield): a cervical syrinx can involve the sympathetic outflow (T1) → Horner's syndrome. Syringobulbia: extension into the brainstem (medulla) → cranial nerve signs, tongue wasting, nystagmus.
Investigations
  • Full spine MRI with contrast — visualises the syrinx; contrast to exclude a tumour or tethered cord.
  • Brain MRI — to exclude a Chiari malformation at the craniocervical junction.
  • MRI both confirms the syrinx and identifies the cause (Chiari, tumour, tethered cord) — which determines management.
Management
The principle: treat the underlying cause of the syrinx; shunt a persistent/symptomatic syrinx.
  • Directed at the cause: e.g. surgical decompression of a Chiari malformation (foramen magnum decompression restores CSF flow and can collapse the syrinx), resect a tumour, release a tethered cord.
  • Persistent/symptomatic syrinx: place a shunt into the syrinx (syringo-subarachnoid/pleural/peritoneal) to drain it.
  • Supportive: neuropathic pain management, physiotherapy, skin/joint protection (prevent burns, injuries, Charcot joints), serial MRI to monitor progression.
Exam pearls
What it is
Fluid-filled cavity ("syrinx") within the cord; mnemonic "Superman — cape + can't feel pain".
Hallmark
DISSOCIATED sensory loss in a CAPE distribution (neck/shoulders/arms): loss of pain + temperature, preserved light touch/proprioception/vibration.
Mechanism
Central syrinx destroys the spinothalamic fibres decussating in the anterior commissure (pain/temp) first; dorsal columns spared early.
Classic clue
Painless burns/injuries to the hands (can't feel pain/temperature).
Associations
Chiari malformation (commonest — image the brain), trauma, tumours, tethered cord.
As it expands
Spastic weakness + upgoing plantars (corticospinal), Horner's (T1 sympathetic), bladder/bowel dysfunction, scoliosis, hand wasting.
Ix & Mx
Full spine MRI with contrast (+ brain MRI for Chiari); treat the cause (e.g. Chiari decompression) + shunt a persistent/symptomatic syrinx; protect insensate skin/joints.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Headaches:
Overview — approach to headache
Headache is split into primary (no underlying structural cause — migraine, tension-type, cluster) and secondary (a cause — SAH, GCA, raised ICP, meningitis, medication-overuse). Trigeminal neuralgia is a facial neuralgia grouped here.
The organising principle: the pattern (character, duration, timing, associated features) usually gives the diagnosis. First job in any headache = screen for red flags pointing to a secondary cause.
The primary headaches (high-yield comparison)
Migraine Tension-type Cluster
Characterunilateral, throbbing/pulsatilebilateral, "tight band", pressingunilateral, severe around the eye
Duration4–72 hours30 min–days15 min–3 hours, in clusters
