Red flags — think secondary headache
  • Thunderclap (sudden, "worst ever") → subarachnoid haemorrhage (cross-ref Intracranial Haemorrhages)
  • New headache + scalp tenderness/jaw claudication in >50s → giant cell arteritis (ESR, steroids)
  • Worse on waking / lying / Valsalva + papilloedema → raised ICP (tumour, IIH)
  • Fever + neck stiffness + photophobia → meningitis
  • Focal neurology, reduced GCS, new headache in cancer/immunosuppression, or in pregnancy (→ CVST/pre-eclampsia)
  • Medication-overuse headache — regular analgesic/triptan use ≥10–15 days/month → withdraw the overused drug
What & why
📷 Image placeholder — migraine visual aura — fortification spectra / scintillating scotoma with an expanding zig-zag margin
Migraine = a primary headache disorder — recurrent, moderate–severe, often unilateral, pulsating headaches with associated features (nausea, photophobia, phonophobia), lasting 4–72 hours.
The core concept: diagnosed by its characteristic pattern (throbbing, unilateral, disabling, + nausea/photophobia/phonophobia, ± aura); first duty is to exclude red-flag secondary causes. Management splits into acute (abort the attack) and prophylaxis (reduce frequency) — with the key safety points that triptans are contraindicated in cardiovascular disease and combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in migraine WITH aura (stroke risk).
  • One of the commonest disabling conditions; commoner in women; strong genetic component; onset often in adolescence/young adulthood.
The decisive fork — exclude red-flag secondary causes first

Before diagnosing migraine (a primary headache), exclude dangerous secondary causes (do a non-contrast CT):

Red flagPoints to
Fever, photophobia, or neck stiffnessmeningitis, encephalitis, brain abscess
New neurological symptomshaemorrhage or tumour
Visual disturbanceGCA, glaucoma, tumour (fundoscopy for papilloedema)
Sudden (thunderclap) occipital headachesubarachnoid haemorrhage
Worse on coughing/straining/Valsalva; worse lying/bendingraised ICP
Vomitingraised ICP, CO poisoning
Impaired consciousness / trauma / cancer / pregnancyhaemorrhage, mets, pre-eclampsia
The rule: migraine is a diagnosis made after excluding red flags — a thunderclap headache is SAH until proven otherwise; new neurology / raised-ICP features → image.
The migraine phases & aura
PhaseFeatures
Prodrome(hours–days before) mood/appetite change, yawning, fatigue
Aura (in ~⅓)fully reversible neurological symptoms developing over 5–20 min, lasting <60 min
Headacheunilateral, pulsating/throbbing, moderate–severe, worse with activity, + nausea, photophobia, phonophobia; 4–72 hours
Postdrome(after) fatigue, poor concentration ("migraine hangover")
Aura: fully reversible and typically visual — zigzag/fortification lines, scintillating scotoma, flashing lights; can be sensory or dysphasic; precedes/accompanies the headache, resolves within an hour. ~⅓ have aura — the distinction matters for contraception safety.
Diagnostic pattern & the POUND mnemonic
  • Migraine without aura: ≥5 attacks lasting 4–72 h with ≥2 of (unilateral, pulsating, moderate–severe, aggravated by activity) and ≥1 of (nausea/vomiting, photophobia + phonophobia).
  • POUND (the more, the more likely migraine): Pulsatile, O = 4–72 h(Ours), Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling.
  • Triggers ("CHOCOLATE"): chocolate, hunger/dehydration, oestrogen (menstrual), caffeine, oral contraceptive, lie-ins, alcohol, travel, exercise, stress, sleep disturbance.
Investigations: diagnosis is clinical — characteristic pattern + no red flags; a headache diary helps. No investigations in typical migraine with a normal exam; image only if red flags. Examine fundi, visual fields, neurology; check BP.
Management — acute (abort the attack)
The principle: treat early; triptan + NSAID/paracetamol first-line; add an antiemetic; watch for medication-overuse headache.
  • First-line (NICE): a triptan PLUS an NSAID, OR a triptan plus paracetamol — taken early. Triptans (e.g. sumatriptan) = 5-HT₁ agonists → cranial vasoconstriction.
  • Antiemetic (add for nausea, even without vomiting): metoclopramide or prochlorperazine (also aid absorption).
  • If oral not tolerated: non-oral triptan (nasal/SC sumatriptan), non-oral NSAID, or antiemetic.
  • AVOID opioids (ineffective + medication-overuse risk).
  • Medication-overuse headache: keep triptans/opioids <10 days/month, simple analgesics <15 days/month.
Triptan safety (CRITICAL): contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, and previous stroke/TIA (they vasoconstrict).
Management — prophylaxis (reduce frequency)

Offer prophylaxis if migraines are frequent/disabling (e.g. ≥4 migraine days/month or significantly affecting quality of life):

  • Propranolol (β-blocker) — good if hypertension/anxiety; avoid in asthma.
  • Topiramate — but TERATOGENIC + reduces contraceptive efficacy → NOT in women of childbearing potential without a pregnancy prevention programme.
  • Amitriptyline — good if comorbid low mood/insomnia/tension-type headache.
  • Others: riboflavin (vitamin B2) 400 mg/day; acupuncture if the above fail.
  • Refractory/chronic (specialist): CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) or gepants (rimegepant) after ≥3 preventives fail; botulinum toxin for chronic migraine.
  • Menstrual migraine: triptans + NSAIDs (mefenamic acid); perimenstrual prophylaxis (e.g. frovatriptan). Review prophylaxis after ~6 months.
Migraine, contraception & stroke — the critical safety point
Migraine WITH aura + combined hormonal contraception (COCP) = CONTRAINDICATED — both independently raise ischaemic stroke risk, and together the risk is multiplied (UKMEC 4 — absolute contraindication). Migraine without aura: COCP is UKMEC 2/3 (relative). The rule: migraine + aura → NO combined pill (use progestogen-only or non-hormonal).
Special situations
  • Hemiplegic migraine: aura includes motor weakness → mimics stroke (exclude stroke first).
  • Pregnancy: paracetamol first-line acute; avoid topiramate/most triptans; specialist input.
  • Migraine + focal aura: always exclude TIA/stroke — aura should be fully reversible and stereotyped.
Exam pearls
What it is
Recurrent unilateral pulsating headache, 4–72h, + nausea/photophobia/phonophobia, ± aura; worse with activity.
Exclude red flags first
Thunderclap → SAH; raised-ICP features; new neurology; fever/neck stiffness → meningitis.

Fully reversible, develops over 5–20 min, lasts <60 min — classically visual (zigzags, scintillating scotoma).

Propranolol / topiramate / amitriptyline; topiramate teratogenic; CGRP mAbs/gepants if refractory.

What & why

Cluster headache = a severe, strictly unilateral headache around the eye/temple, occurring in "clusters" (bouts) with prominent ipsilateral cranial autonomic features — one of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs).
The core concept: a very characteristic pattern — excruciating unilateral peri-orbital pain + ipsilateral autonomic signs (red/watering eye, miosis, ptosis, nasal congestion) + restlessness + a striking clustering time-pattern. One of the most severe pains known ("suicide headache"). Two almost-unique management priorities: high-flow 100% oxygen (acute) and verapamil (prophylaxis).
  • Commoner in men and smokers; onset typically 20s–40s; the clustering pattern is the diagnostic signature.
The decisive fork — cluster vs migraine vs trigeminal neuralgia

Duration15 min–3 h4–72 hseconds (shock-like)
Siteunilateral, around eye/templeoften unilateraltrigeminal (V2/V3)
Autonomic featuresPROMINENT ipsilateral (red/watering eye, miosis, ptosis, congestion)mild/nonenone
Behaviourrestless/agitated (paces)still (dark room)avoids triggers

The rules: cluster = short (15 min–3 h) + severe + prominent autonomic + RESTLESS + clusters; migraine = longer (4–72 h) + nausea/photophobia + lies STILL. The restless-vs-still contrast is a classic bedside discriminator.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Painsevere pain behind the eye, lasting 15 min–3 hours; strictly unilateral; excruciating, boring/burning
Ipsilateral autonomicred, swollen, watering eye, miosis, ptosis, nasal discharge/congestion, facial sweating
Restlessnessrestless/agitated (paces, can't keep still — unlike migraine)
Timingoften nocturnal / same time each day; occur in clusters — e.g. 3–4 a day then nothing for a year
The autonomic signature: the ipsilateral partial Horner's-like picture (miosis + ptosis) + red/watering eye + nasal congestion — the eye and nose "run" on the same side as the pain. The clustering pattern (bouts separated by long remissions) is the defining time-course.
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — characteristic peri-orbital pain + ipsilateral autonomic features + clustering + restlessness.
  • Exclude secondary causes: consider neuroimaging (MRI brain, incl. pituitary/cavernous sinus), especially at first presentation or if atypical.
  • Distinguish from other TACs: paroxysmal hemicrania (shorter, more frequent, completely responsive to indomethacin) and SUNCT.
  • Advise on smoking + alcohol (alcohol classically triggers attacks during a bout).
Management — acute (abort the attack)
The principle: high-flow 100% oxygen + a subcutaneous/intranasal triptan — the two acute treatments almost unique to cluster headache.
  • High-flow 100% oxygen: 15 L/min via a non-rebreathe mask → aborts many attacks (a hallmark treatment).
  • Triptans: subcutaneous or intranasal sumatriptan (NOT oral — attacks are too short for oral absorption) → fast-acting.
  • The rule: acute cluster = 100% oxygen + SC/intranasal triptan — oral triptans and simple analgesics are ineffective (too slow).
  • Triptan cautions: contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease / uncontrolled hypertension.
Management — prophylaxis (during a bout)
  • First-line: verapamil (calcium channel blocker) — monitor ECG (heart block / PR prolongation risk).
  • Other options: occipital nerve block, prednisolone (short steroid course to break a bout while verapamil takes effect).
  • Lifestyle: avoid alcohol during a cluster bout; smoking cessation.
  • (Specialist options for refractory/chronic: lithium, galcanezumab, neurostimulation.)

Severe UNILATERAL peri-orbital pain, 15 min–3 hours, in CLUSTERS (bouts then remission); a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia.
Demographics
Commoner in men + smokers; often nocturnal/same time daily.
Autonomic features
Ipsilateral: red/watering eye, miosis, ptosis, nasal congestion/discharge, facial sweating.
Restless
Agitated/paces — contrast with migraine (lies still in the dark). A key discriminator.

Cluster = shorter (15 min–3 h) + autonomic + restless; migraine = 4–72 h + nausea/photophobia + still.

Verapamil (1st-line, ECG monitoring); occipital nerve block, prednisolone to break a bout.

What & why
Tension-type headache (TTH) = the commonest primary headache — a mild-to-moderate, bilateral, band-like "pressure" headache without the disabling features of migraine or the autonomic features of cluster.
The core concept: TTH is defined largely by what it lacks — featureless, non-throbbing, non-disabling, with no aura, no significant nausea, no autonomic signs, not worse with activity. It's essentially a benign headache once red flags, migraine, and medication-overuse headache are excluded. Management = reassurance + simple analgesia, with amitriptyline for frequent/chronic cases.
  • Extremely common; often related to stress, poor posture, fatigue; the mildest and most benign primary headache.

Medication-overuse headache — the key overlap
Frequent analgesia use → a chronic daily headache resembling tension headache: present ≥15 days/month, developed/worsened while taking regular symptomatic medication, with non-specific tension-like features.
  • Immediately withdraw simple analgesics and triptans (headaches may initially worsen before improving).
  • SLOWLY withdraw opioids (abrupt opioid withdrawal is problematic).
The rule: always ask about analgesic frequency in a chronic daily "tension" headache — the treatment is to stop the overused analgesic, not add more.
Management
The principle: reassurance + simple analgesia for acute episodes; amitriptyline for frequent/chronic; avoid analgesic overuse.
  • Acute/episodic: reassurance + aspirin, paracetamol, or an oral NSAID (ibuprofen); avoid opioids; limit acute analgesic use (<15 days/month) to avoid medication-overuse headache.
  • Chronic/frequent: amitriptyline (low-dose tricyclic) — first-line prophylaxis; address triggers/lifestyle (stress management, sleep, hydration, regular meals, posture, treat comorbid depression/anxiety); acupuncture is an option.
  • Reassurance is key — it's benign; explain the mechanism and avoid over-investigation.

What & why
📷 Image placeholder — the trigeminal nerve (CN V) dermatomes — ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) divisions, with V2/V3 most affected in trigeminal neuralgia
Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) = a disorder of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) causing sudden, severe, brief, "electric-shock"-like unilateral facial pain in a trigeminal distribution.
The core concept: paroxysms of stabbing/electric-shock pain, lasting seconds, triggered by innocuous stimuli (touch, chewing, cold, wind), in one or more trigeminal divisions, with no pain between attacks. Two priorities: (1) exclude a secondary cause (MS, tumour, or a compressing vessel — via MRI) and (2) treat with carbamazepine (an anticonvulsant — the pain is neuropathic).
  • Commoner in older adults + women; usually idiopathic/vascular, but a significant minority are secondary (especially MS in younger/bilateral cases).
The decisive fork — classic (idiopathic/vascular) vs secondary TN
Classic / idiopathicSecondary
Causeneurovascular compression (aberrant artery/vein at the pons) or no identifiable causeMS (pontine plaque), tumour (CPA/acoustic neuroma, meningioma), other structural lesion

The rule: classic TN = older, unilateral, normal exam; red flags for secondary = age <40, bilateral, sensory loss, other neurology → think MS or tumour → MRI. ~2–4% of TN is due to MS (a demyelinating plaque on the trigeminal root) → bilateral/young-onset TN should prompt MS investigation.
Pathophysiology
  • Classic TN: compression of the trigeminal root near the pons by an aberrant vascular loop (usually the superior cerebellar artery) → demyelination → ephaptic (abnormal) firing → paroxysmal pain.
  • Secondary TN: the same pathway damaged by a plaque (MS) or compressing/infiltrating lesion (tumour).

The signature: paroxysmal, seconds-long, electric-shock unilateral facial pain, triggered by touch/chewing/cold, pain-free between attacks — the pattern is diagnostic. Patients may avoid eating/washing/talking → weight loss, low mood.

  • Diagnosis is clinical — the characteristic paroxysmal shock-like triggered pain, with a normal neurological examination in classic TN.
  • MRI brain: to exclude secondary causes — neurovascular compression, MS plaques, tumours (CPA/posterior fossa), vascular abnormalities; especially if red flags.
  • Bloods: consider ESR/CRP (exclude GCA).
  • Examine: trigeminal sensation, corneal reflex, other cranial nerves (a sensory deficit suggests a secondary cause).
Management — carbamazepine first-line
The principle: carbamazepine first-line (neuropathic, not standard analgesia); refer to specialist if it fails; microvascular decompression for refractory classic TN.
  • First-line: carbamazepine — an anticonvulsant/sodium-channel blocker (the pain is neuropathic — standard analgesics/NSAIDs/opioids don't work). Side effects: dizziness, drowsiness, diplopia, ataxia, hyponatraemia (SIADH), rash (rarely Stevens-Johnson), enzyme induction (↓contraceptive efficacy). Titrate to effect.
  • If ineffective/not tolerated → refer to a specialist; alternatives: oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, gabapentin, pregabalin, baclofen, phenytoin.
  • Refractory → surgery: Microvascular decompression (MVD) — procedure of choice for classic TN with neurovascular compression (best long-term relief); ablative/percutaneous (radiofrequency, glycerol, balloon) or stereotactic radiosurgery (gamma knife) if unfit/declining MVD.
  • Treat any secondary cause (MS-directed treatment, tumour management). Don't use standard analgesics/opioids.
Exam pearls
What it is
Sudden, severe, "electric-shock" UNILATERAL facial pain, lasting SECONDS, in a trigeminal (usually V2/V3) distribution, triggered by touch/chewing/cold, pain-free between.
Classic (idiopathic/vascular)
Older, unilateral, normal exam — usually neurovascular compression (aberrant vessel at the pons).
Red flags for SECONDARY
Age <40, bilateral, sensory loss, other neurology → suspect MS (plaque) or tumour → MRI.
MS link
~2–4% due to MS (bilateral/young → investigate for MS).
vs cluster vs migraine
Durations distinguish the trio: TN seconds; cluster 15 min–3 h (autonomic, restless); migraine 4–72 h (nausea).
Investigations
Clinical diagnosis + MRI (exclude MS/tumour/vascular compression); ESR (exclude GCA).
Management
Carbamazepine first-line (neuropathic — standard analgesics don't work; watch hyponatraemia); refer if it fails; microvascular decompression for refractory classic TN; ablative/gamma knife if unfit.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Intracranial H:
Overview — the intracranial haemorrhages
Bleeding within the skull, classified by the anatomical space it occupies. The three surgical/traumatic haemorrhages — extradural, subdural and subarachnoid — are distinguished by their vessel of origin, CT appearance, and typical patient/history. (Intracerebral/intraparenchymal haemorrhage is covered under Stroke / TIA.)
The organising principle: the CT shape tells you the space — extradural = lens/lemon (biconvex, doesn't cross sutures); subdural = crescent/banana (concave, crosses sutures); subarachnoid = blood in the sulci/basal cisterns. Match shape → space → vessel → cause.

What & why
📷 Image placeholder — extradural haemorrhage — a hyperdense biconvex (lens-shaped) collection that does not cross suture lines (middle meningeal artery)
An extradural (epidural) haemorrhage = blood in the potential space between the skull and the dura mater — almost always traumatic, and classically arterial.
The core concept: the defining story is the "lucid interval" — knocked out, briefly recovers (talks/walks), then rapidly deteriorates as the arterial bleed expands. Because it's arterial under pressure it enlarges fast → rising ICP → herniation and death → a time-critical neurosurgical emergency, excellent outcome if evacuated promptly but catastrophic if missed. Classic cause: a temporal skull fracture rupturing the middle meningeal artery.
  • Typically young adults (dura is more adherent to the skull in the elderly); trauma to the pterion (temple).
The decisive fork — extradural vs subdural vs subarachnoid
ExtraduralSubduralSubarachnoid
Vesselarterial — middle meningealvenous — bridging veinsBerry aneurysm
CT shapebiconvex / lens (lentiform) — doesn't cross suturescrescent (concave) — crosses suturesblood in sulci/cisterns
Classic patientyoung adult, temporal traumaelderly/alcoholic/anticoagulatedthunderclap headache
Courselucid interval → rapid deteriorationinsidious (chronic) or acutesudden severe headache
The rules: extradural = arterial (middle meningeal), biconvex, lucid interval, young + temporal trauma; subdural = venous, crescent, elderly/anticoagulated. Suture rule: extradural does NOT cross suture lines (dura tightly attached at sutures) but can cross the midline; subdural crosses sutures but not the midline.
Anatomy & mechanism
  • Middle meningeal artery: runs in a groove on the inner skull at the pterion (thin bone at the temple — frontal/parietal/temporal/sphenoid junction).
  • Mechanism: trauma to the temple → temporal/parietal skull fracture → ruptures the middle meningeal artery → arterial blood strips the dura off the skull → expanding biconvex haematoma.
Why the lucid interval: the initial impact causes brief concussion (→ LOC), the patient recovers (lucid interval), then the arterial haematoma expands over minutes–hours → rising ICP → deterioration → the "talk and die" pattern.
Clinical features
PhaseFeatures
Initial impactbrief loss of consciousness (concussion)
Lucid interval (classic)temporary recovery — awake, talking, may seem fine (minutes–hours)
Deteriorationas the haematoma expands: worsening headache, vomiting, falling GCS, drowsiness
Raised ICP / herniation (late)fixed dilated pupil (ipsilateral CN III — uncal herniation), contralateral hemiparesis, Cushing's reflex (↑BP + bradycardia + irregular breathing)
The blown pupil: an ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil from uncal herniation compressing CN III → impending coning → surgical emergency. Cushing's reflex (↑BP + bradycardia + irregular respiration) = impending herniation.
Investigations
  • Urgent non-contrast CT head (gold standard): a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection that does NOT cross suture lines; ± skull fracture, midline shift, effacement of ventricles/cisterns.
  • CT criteria per NICE NG232 — triggers CT within 1 hour (GCS <13, deterioration, focal signs).
  • Bloods: FBC, clotting (correct if abnormal), group & save. Do NOT do an LP (raised ICP → coning).
Management — neurosurgical emergency
The principle: ABCDE + urgent neurosurgical evacuation + manage raised ICP; correct coagulopathy.
  • Immediate (ABCDE): airway + C-spine control, oxygenation, avoid hypoxia/hypotension; GCS ≤8 → intubate.
  • Definitive: craniotomy + evacuation of the haematoma + ligation/control of the bleeding middle meningeal artery; prompt evacuation → excellent prognosis (burr hole may temporise).
  • Manage raised ICP (head-up, avoid hypercapnia, mannitol/hypertonic saline, treat seizures); correct coagulopathy / reverse anticoagulation.
  • Small, asymptomatic extradurals with a good GCS may occasionally be managed conservatively with close monitoring + serial CT (neurosurgical decision).
Prognosis: excellent if evacuated promptly (before herniation — the underlying brain is often uninjured) → the classic "talk and die" is preventable. Poor if missed/late — time is brain.
Exam pearls
What it is
Arterial bleed between skull and dura — classically middle meningeal artery after temporal trauma (pterion).
CT
BICONVEX (lens-shaped) hyperdensity that does NOT cross suture lines (vs subdural = crescent, crosses sutures).
Classic story
LUCID INTERVAL: brief LOC → recovery → rapid deterioration ("talk and die").
Deterioration signs
Falling GCS, ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (CN III/uncal herniation), contralateral hemiparesis, Cushing's reflex.
Demographic
Young adults (dura less adherent than in elderly).
Investigation
Urgent non-contrast CT; no LP (coning); check clotting.
Management
ABCDE + C-spine, avoid hypoxia/hypotension, GCS ≤8 → intubate; urgent craniotomy + evacuation + arterial control; reverse anticoagulation. Prognosis excellent if treated early.
What & why
📷 Image placeholder — subdural haemorrhage — a crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines; acute (hyperdense/bright) vs chronic (hypodense/dark), with midline shift
A subdural haemorrhage (SDH) = blood in the space between the dura and the arachnoid mater — classically a venous bleed from the bridging veins.
The core concept: the "slow, venous, crescent-shaped" bleed — the counterpart to the extradural (fast, arterial, biconvex). Because it's low-pressure venous, it can accumulate slowly — so alongside the acute form there's a crucial chronic form in the elderly presenting weeks later with insidious confusion/decline, often after trivial/forgotten trauma. Classic patients — elderly, alcoholic, anticoagulated — share brain atrophy (stretched bridging veins) and bleeding tendency.
  • A major "can't-miss" cause of confusion/decline in an elderly or alcoholic patient — treatable and easily mistaken for dementia/stroke.
The decisive fork — vs extradural, and acute vs chronic

(a) Subdural vs extradural:

Vesselvenous — bridging veinsarterial — middle meningeal
CT shapeCRESCENT (concave/banana) — crosses sutures, not midlinebiconvex (lens) — doesn't cross sutures

Acute SDHChronic SDH

The rules: subdural = venous (bridging veins) + CRESCENT + crosses sutures + elderly/alcoholic/anticoagulated; acute = hyperdense (bright); chronic = hypodense (dark) — the CT density tells you the age of the bleed.
Anatomy & mechanism
  • Bridging veins: cross the subdural space from cortex to dural sinuses; trauma → these veins tear → slow venous bleed.
  • Why the elderly + alcoholics: brain atrophy → the brain shrinks → bridging veins are stretched taut and more easily torn by minor trauma → SDH after trivial/forgotten head injury.
  • Why anticoagulated: impaired clotting → any bleed is bigger/more likely (warfarin, DOACs, antiplatelets).
Infants: subdural haemorrhage is a red flag for non-accidental injury (shaken baby) — torn bridging veins from shaking; often bilateral + retinal haemorrhages → safeguarding.
Clinical features
  • Acute SDH: significant head trauma → falling GCS, headache, focal neurology (may deteriorate rapidly, like extradural but usually less abrupt).
  • Chronic SDH (the classic elderly presentation): insidious onset over weeks of confusion, cognitive decline, drowsiness, headache, unsteadiness/falls, focal weakness; often fluctuating; trauma history absent/forgotten → mimics dementia, stroke, or delirium.
  • Raised ICP / deterioration (either form): worsening headache, vomiting, falling GCS, fixed dilated pupil (CN III), contralateral hemiparesis, Cushing's reflex.
Investigations
  • Non-contrast CT head (gold standard): a crescent-shaped (concave) collection that crosses suture lines but not the midline; density indicates age (acute = hyperdense/bright, chronic = hypodense/dark, acute-on-chronic = mixed); ± midline shift, effacement.
  • Bloods: FBC, clotting (correct if abnormal), group & save. Do NOT do an LP (coning).
  • In infants: consider safeguarding workup (skeletal survey, ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhages) if NAI suspected.
Management
The principle: ABCDE + reverse coagulopathy; surgical evacuation for significant/symptomatic bleeds (burr holes for chronic, craniotomy for acute); conservative for small/asymptomatic.
  • Immediate (ABCDE): airway + C-spine, avoid hypoxia/hypotension; GCS ≤8 → intubate; reverse anticoagulation (warfarin → PCC + vitamin K; DOAC → reversal agent).
  • Acute SDH (significant/symptomatic): craniotomy + evacuation (the clot is solid).
  • Chronic SDH (symptomatic): burr-hole drainage (the liquefied old blood drains through burr holes) — often dramatic improvement.
  • Conservative: small, asymptomatic subdurals with a good GCS → observation + serial CT.
  • Address the cause: falls assessment, review anticoagulation/alcohol, safeguarding (infants); manage raised ICP; antiepileptics for seizures.
Exam pearls
What it is
Venous bleed (bridging veins) between dura and arachnoid.
CT
CRESCENT-shaped (concave), CROSSES sutures (not midline) (vs extradural = biconvex, doesn't cross sutures).
Density = age
Acute = hyperdense (bright); chronic = hypodense (dark); acute-on-chronic = mixed.
Classic patients
Elderly + alcoholic (brain atrophy → stretched bridging veins) + anticoagulated; infants → non-accidental injury (+ retinal haemorrhages).
Chronic SDH
Insidious confusion/decline over weeks in an elderly patient after trivial/forgotten trauma — a treatable mimic of dementia/stroke.
Investigation
Non-contrast CT; no LP; check clotting.
Management
Acute → craniotomy; chronic → burr-hole drainage; small/asymptomatic → conservative + serial CT; reverse anticoagulation; safeguarding in infants.
What & why
📷 Image placeholder — subarachnoid haemorrhage — hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns and sulci in a “star-shaped” pattern
A subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) = bleeding into the subarachnoid space (between arachnoid and pia, where CSF flows) — most often spontaneous, from a ruptured "berry" aneurysm.
The core concept: the defining presentation is the "thunderclap headache" — sudden, severe, "worst-ever", peaking in seconds–minutes. Priorities: (1) diagnose it fast (CT → LP pathway — easily missed), (2) secure the aneurysm (prevent the catastrophic rebleed, highest in the first 24h), and (3) prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (days 3–14 — nimodipine). A neurosurgical emergency with high mortality.
  • Commoner in women, middle age; associated with hypertension, smoking, and polycystic kidney disease.
The decisive fork — SAH vs other bleeds & the thunderclap differential
SAHExtraduralSubdural

Presentationthunderclap headachelucid interval → deteriorateinsidious (chronic) / elderly

Thunderclap differential: SAH is thunderclap until proven otherwise, but also consider cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, arterial dissection, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, pituitary apoplexy (and benign cough/exertion/coital headache, migraine). The rule: any sudden severe headache peaking within 1–5 minutes = SAH until excluded → urgent CT.
Causes & risk factors
  • Ruptured "berry" (saccular) aneurysm (~85% — the commonest cause) — at branch points of the Circle of Willis; commonest site: anterior communicating artery (also posterior communicating, MCA bifurcation).
  • Non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic haemorrhage (benign, better prognosis), AVM, trauma.
  • Risk factors: hypertension, smoking, excess alcohol, family history; connective tissue/genetic — autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), Ehlers-Danlos, coarctation of the aorta.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Thunderclap headachesudden, severe, "worst headache of my life", occipital, peaks in seconds–minutes — the hallmark
Meningismneck stiffness, photophobia (blood irritates the meninges), develops over hours
Nausea + vomitingcommon

The CN III point: a painful third nerve palsy (dilated pupil, ptosis, down-and-out eye) → posterior communicating artery aneurysm — a classic exam link.
Investigations — the CT → LP pathway
  • 1st-line: urgent non-contrast CT head — hyperdense blood in the subarachnoid space (sulci, basal cisterns — "star-shaped"). CT within 6 hours of onset is ~100% sensitive → a normal CT within 6h effectively rules out SAH; sensitivity falls after 6 hours.
  • Lumbar puncture (if CT negative but suspicion remains): perform ≥12 hours after onset (allows bilirubin to form); look for XANTHOCHROMIA (yellow CSF from bilirubin — spectrophotometry) → distinguishes true SAH from a traumatic tap. (NICE NG228: if CT within 6h is negative and radiologist-reported → do NOT routinely do an LP.)
  • Once confirmed → vascular imaging to find the aneurysm: CT angiography (CTA) and/or digital subtraction angiography (DSA — gold standard); if negative, repeat later (~1–6 weeks).
  • Bloods/ECG: SAH can cause ECG changes (ST/T-wave, arrhythmias) and hyponatraemia.
Management — secure the aneurysm + prevent complications
The principle: stabilise → secure the aneurysm early (coiling/clipping) → nimodipine to prevent vasospasm → manage complications (rebleed, vasospasm/DCI, hydrocephalus).
  • Immediate: ABCDE, neurosurgical-centre referral, bed rest, analgesia, BP control (avoid extremes), reverse anticoagulation.
  • Secure the aneurysm early: endovascular coiling — first-line in most cases (less invasive, better outcomes); surgical clipping if unsuitable for coiling.
  • Nimodipine: a calcium channel blocker — oral 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days — the only drug proven to improve outcomes; prevents cerebral vasospasm / delayed cerebral ischaemia (NOT for treating rebleeding).
ComplicationTiming / detail
Rebleedinghighest risk in the first 24 hours → secure the aneurysm early (high mortality)
Vasospasm → delayed cerebral ischaemiadays 3–14 → nimodipine prevents it; treat with euvolaemia + BP support
Hydrocephalusblood blocks CSF flow/absorption → EVD / shunt
Hyponatraemia (SIADH / cerebral salt wasting)monitor sodium; seizures → antiepileptics
The two timing rules: rebleeding = first 24h (secure the aneurysm early); vasospasm/DCI = days 3–14 (nimodipine). Prognosis graded by WFNS / Hunt & Hess scales; high mortality overall.

Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually ruptured berry aneurysm (commonest site = anterior communicating artery).

Sudden, severe, "worst-ever", occipital, peaks in seconds–minutes + meningism — SAH until proven otherwise.
PCom aneurysm
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm → painful CN III palsy (fixed dilated pupil, ptosis, down-and-out eye).
Risk factors
Hypertension, smoking, ADPKD (polycystic kidneys), family history, Ehlers-Danlos.
Investigations
Urgent non-contrast CT (~100% sensitive within 6h → rules out if negative); if negative + suspicious → LP ≥12h for XANTHOCHROMIA; then CT/DSA angiography.
Management
Secure the aneurysm early — coiling (1st-line) or clipping; nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly × 21 days (prevents vasospasm).
Complications & timing
Rebleed = <24h; vasospasm/DCI = days 3–14 (nimodipine); hydrocephalus; hyponatraemia.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Neurocutaneous:
What & why
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) = an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome (phakomatosis) causing benign nerve-sheath tumours (neurofibromas) throughout the nervous system, plus characteristic skin, eye, and bone features.
The core concept: a tumour-suppressor disorder — loss of neurofibromin → unchecked cell growth along nerves. A multisystem, clinical diagnosis recognised by the CRABBING features, with the priority being lifelong surveillance for complications (disfiguring tumours, malignant transformation, vision loss, hypertension, skeletal problems).
  • One of the neurocutaneous syndromes / phakomatoses (linking skin + nervous system); NF1 is far commoner than NF2.
The decisive fork — NF1 vs NF2
NF1 (von Recklinghausen)NF2
Gene / chromosomechromosome 17 → neurofibrominchromosome 22 → merlin
Tumoursneurofibromas (+ café-au-lait, Lisch nodules)schwannomas — esp. bilateral acoustic neuromas
Hallmarkskin (café-au-lait, freckling, neurofibromas)bilateral acoustic neuromas (hearing loss)
Frequencymuch commonerrarer
The rule: NF1 = chromosome 17, neurofibromin, café-au-lait/skin features; NF2 = chromosome 22, merlin, bilateral acoustic neuromas (memory hook: NF2 → chromosome 22, "2 ears" = bilateral acoustic neuromas).
Genetics
  • Autosomal dominant — but a high spontaneous mutation rate (~50% are new mutations, no family history).
  • NF1 gene on chromosome 17 → codes for neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor → loss → tumour growth.
  • Variable expressivity (severity varies widely, even within a family).

Feature
CCafé-au-lait spots — ≥6, >15 mm in adults; flat, coffee-coloured macules
RRelative with NF1 (first-degree)
AAxillary or inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign)

Diagnostic threshold: ≥2 of the CRABBING criteria = NF1 (a clinical diagnosis). The two most specific: Lisch nodules + optic pathway glioma.
Complications — the reason for surveillance
SystemComplication
Malignancymalignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (transformed neurofibroma), GI stromal tumour (GIST), optic glioma, ↑leukaemia risk

High-yield: NF1 causes secondary hypertension (renal artery stenosis / phaeochromocytoma) → always check BP + investigate hypertension. A neurofibroma that becomes painful, rapidly growing, or hard → suspect malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour → urgent assessment.
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical — ≥2 CRABBING criteria.
  • Examination: full skin exam, eyes (Lisch nodules, visual acuity/fields for optic glioma), BP, spine (scoliosis), developmental/cognitive assessment.
  • Genetic testing — confirms diagnosis (NF1 gene), useful for atypical cases/family planning.
  • MRI — if optic glioma, brain tumour, or plexiform neurofibroma suspected. Investigate hypertension (renal artery imaging, plasma metanephrines).
Management — surveillance + treat complications
The overarching principle: no cure → monitoring, managing symptoms, and treating complications.
  • Regular surveillance: annual review — skin, BP, visual assessment (optic glioma), spine (scoliosis), development/learning, and watching for malignant change.
  • Treat complications: optic glioma → ophthalmology/oncology; malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour → urgent oncology (surgery ± chemo/radiotherapy); hypertension → investigate + treat cause; scoliosis → orthopaedics; learning difficulties/epilepsy → support/treatment; symptomatic/disfiguring neurofibromas → surgical excision.
  • Genetic counselling (autosomal dominant — 50% risk to offspring); MDT (neurology, genetics, ophthalmology, dermatology, orthopaedics, oncology).

What it is
Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome; chromosome 17 → neurofibromin (tumour suppressor); ~50% new mutations.

Café-au-lait (≥6, >15mm), Relative, Axillary/inguinal freckling, Bony dysplasia, Iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), Neurofibromas (≥2), Glioma (optic pathway).
Most specific
Lisch nodules + optic glioma.
NF1 vs NF2
NF1 = chr 17, neurofibromin, skin/café-au-lait; NF2 = chr 22, merlin, BILATERAL acoustic neuromas.
Complications
Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour, GIST, optic glioma → vision loss, epilepsy, learning difficulties, scoliosis, hypertension (renal artery stenosis / phaeochromocytoma).
Always check BP
Secondary hypertension; a changing/painful neurofibroma → suspect malignant transformation.
Management
No cure → surveillance (annual: skin, BP, vision, spine, development) + treat complications + genetic counselling.
What & why
Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) = an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome — multiple benign nervous-system tumours, especially schwannomas, with bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) as its hallmark.
The core concept: NF2 = schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas — above all BILATERAL acoustic neuromas (essentially pathognomonic). Where NF1 is a "skin + café-au-lait" disease, NF2 is a "hearing loss + intracranial/spinal tumour" disease. Priority: recognise the bilateral CN VIII picture, lifelong tumour surveillance, and preserve hearing/function.
  • Much rarer than NF1; caused by loss of merlin (a tumour suppressor important in Schwann cells).
The decisive fork — NF2 vs NF1
NF2NF1
Gene / chromosomechromosome 22 → merlinchromosome 17 → neurofibromin
Hallmark tumoursschwannomas — esp. BILATERAL acoustic neuromas; meningiomas, ependymomasneurofibromas
Skin featuresfew (some skin schwannomas, café-au-lait less prominent)prominent (café-au-lait, freckling, neurofibromas)

The rule: NF2 = chromosome 22, merlin, BILATERAL acoustic neuromas (schwannomas); NF1 = chromosome 17, neurofibromin, café-au-lait/skin. Memory hook: NF2 → "2" ears → bilateral acoustic neuromas → chromosome 22.
Genetics
  • Autosomal dominant (50% risk to offspring); high rate of new mutations (~50%).
  • NF2 gene on chromosome 22 → codes for merlin (schwannomin), a tumour suppressor important in Schwann cells → loss → schwannomas.
  • The merlin → Schwann cell link: because merlin is key in Schwann cells (which myelinate cranial/peripheral nerves), its loss drives schwannomas — explaining why the vestibular nerve (CN VIII) tumours dominate.
Clinical features
  • The hallmark: bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) → bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (often the presenting feature, typically early adulthood), tinnitus, imbalance; as they enlarge → compress CN VII (facial palsy), CN V (loss of corneal reflex), brainstem/cerebellum.
  • Other tumours: meningiomas (often multiple), schwannomas of other cranial/spinal/peripheral nerves, ependymomas + gliomas (spinal cord).
  • Ophthalmic: juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts, retinal hamartomas.
  • Skin: skin schwannomas/plaques; café-au-lait spots may occur but are fewer/less prominent than NF1.
The pattern: a young adult with bilateral hearing loss + multiple CNS tumours → NF2.
Diagnosis / investigations
  • Diagnosis is clinical + radiological — the key criterion is bilateral vestibular schwannomas (or a first-degree relative with NF2 + a unilateral acoustic neuroma or two other NF2-associated tumours).
  • MRI brain + internal auditory meati + whole spine (with contrast): to detect bilateral acoustic neuromas, meningiomas, spinal schwannomas/ependymomas — the mainstay of diagnosis + surveillance.
  • Audiometry: sensorineural hearing loss. Genetic testing: NF2 gene (chromosome 22). Ophthalmology: cataracts, retinal lesions.
Management — surveillance + tumour treatment
The overarching principle: no cure → lifelong surveillance + treat tumours while preserving hearing and neurological function — via a specialist MDT.
  • Tumours can be resected, but with a heavy risk of permanent nerve damage — so decisions balance tumour control vs preserving hearing + the facial nerve.
  • Surveillance: regular MRI (brain + spine) + audiometry to monitor growth.
  • Acoustic neuromas / schwannomas: observation (small/stable), surgery, or stereotactic radiosurgery — timed to balance growth against hearing/facial-nerve preservation.
  • Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) — can shrink vestibular schwannomas / improve hearing in NF2. Hearing rehabilitation: hearing aids, auditory brainstem/cochlear implants (given bilateral deafness risk).
  • Meningiomas/ependymomas → surgery/radiotherapy; genetic counselling (autosomal dominant) + screen at-risk relatives; MDT (neurosurgery, ENT/skull base, neurology, audiology, genetics, ophthalmology).

What it is
Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome; chromosome 22 → merlin (tumour suppressor, important in Schwann cells).

BILATERAL vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) → bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in a young adult (essentially pathognomonic).
Also
Meningiomas (often multiple), schwannomas, ependymomas/gliomas, juvenile cataracts; fewer skin/café-au-lait features than NF1.

NF2 = chr 22, merlin, bilateral acoustic neuromas; NF1 = chr 17, neurofibromin, café-au-lait/neurofibromas.

MRI brain + IAM + whole spine (with contrast) + audiometry + genetic testing.
Management
No cure → surveillance (MRI + audiometry); acoustic neuromas → observation/surgery/radiosurgery (balance tumour control vs hearing + facial nerve); bevacizumab, hearing rehabilitation; genetic counselling.
What & why
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) = an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome (phakomatosis) causing benign tumours (hamartomas) in multiple organs — brain, skin, kidneys, heart, eyes, lungs.
The core concept: a multisystem hamartoma disorder — loss of a tumour suppressor → overactive mTOR pathway → unchecked growth → benign tumours across many organs at once. The signature is the triad of epilepsy + learning disability + skin lesions; modern management centres on seizure control, multi-organ surveillance, and mTOR inhibitors.
  • One of the phakomatoses; presents in childhood (often with infantile spasms/seizures).
The decisive fork — TSC vs other neurocutaneous syndromes
SyndromeDistinguishing hallmark
Tuberous sclerosisash-leaf macules, shagreen patches, angiofibromas + epilepsy + learning disability + renal/cardiac hamartomas
NF1café-au-lait, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules
NF2bilateral acoustic neuromas
Sturge-Weberport-wine stain (facial capillary malformation) + seizures
Von Hippel-Lindauretinal + cerebellar haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma
The rule: epilepsy + learning disability + characteristic skin lesions (ash-leaf, shagreen, angiofibromas) = tuberous sclerosis.
Genetics
  • Autosomal dominant, with ~2/3 arising as new (de novo) mutations and variable expressivity.
  • Two genes (either causes TSC): TSC1 (chromosome 9) → hamartin; TSC2 (chromosome 16) → tuberin.
The mechanism: hamartin + tuberin normally inhibit the mTOR pathway; loss of either → mTOR overactivity → uncontrolled cell growth → hamartomas — which is why mTOR inhibitors (everolimus/sirolimus) are a targeted treatment. Memory hook: TSC1/9 → hamarTin; TSC2/16 → Tuberin (TSC2 on chr 16, more severe).
Clinical features by system

Skin (the cutaneous signs):

LesionDescription
Ash-leaf maculeshypopigmented oval/leaf-shaped patches — fluoresce under Wood's (UV) lamp; often the earliest sign
Shagreen patchesroughened, thickened, "orange-peel" skin, usually lower back
Angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum)red/pink papules over the butterfly/malar area of the face
Subungual/periungual fibromasfibromas around the nails

Neurological:

  • Epilepsy — very common; classically infantile spasms (West syndrome) in infancy, then other seizure types.
  • Learning disability + developmental delay; autism/behavioural problems.
  • Cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs) — which can obstruct CSF → hydrocephalus.

Other organs:

OrganHamartoma
Kidneyangiomyolipomas (can bleed — haematuria/haemorrhage), renal cysts
Heartrhabdomyomas (often detected antenatally/in infancy; usually regress)
Lungslymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) — cystic lung disease (esp. women)
Eyesretinal hamartomas
The triad to remember: epilepsy + learning disability + facial angiofibromas (the classic "Vogt triad") — though incomplete in many.
Assessment / investigations
  • Diagnosis — clinical (major + minor criteria) supported by genetics.
  • Skin exam (incl. Wood's lamp for ash-leaf macules), eyes (retinal hamartomas).
  • MRI brain — cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA; renal imaging — angiomyolipomas, cysts; echocardiogram — rhabdomyomas; EEG — seizures.
  • Genetic testing — TSC1/TSC2; developmental/cognitive assessment.
Management — surveillance + seizures + mTOR inhibitors
The overarching principle: no cure → control seizures, surveillance of multi-organ tumours, and mTOR inhibitors for specific complications — via an MDT.
  • Seizures: vigabatrin is first-line for infantile spasms in TSC (a specific high-yield point); standard AEDs for other seizures; epilepsy surgery in selected cases.
  • mTOR inhibitors (everolimus/sirolimus) — the targeted therapy: shrink SEGAs, renal angiomyolipomas, and LAM — directly target the overactive mTOR pathway.
  • Surveillance: regular MRI brain (SEGA), renal imaging (angiomyolipoma), skin, eyes, BP, developmental review.
  • Organ-specific: SEGA → mTOR inhibitor or surgery (if obstructing CSF); renal angiomyolipoma → mTOR inhibitor/embolisation if large/bleeding; LAM → mTOR inhibitor; learning disability/autism → educational + behavioural support.
  • Genetic counselling (autosomal dominant, 50% risk to offspring); MDT (neurology, nephrology, dermatology, cardiology, genetics, respiratory, ophthalmology).
Exam pearls
What it is
Autosomal dominant multisystem hamartoma disorder; TSC1 (chr 9, hamartin) / TSC2 (chr 16, tuberin) → mTOR overactivity.
Classic triad
Epilepsy + learning disability + skin lesions.
Skin
Ash-leaf macules (hypopigmented, Wood's lamp), shagreen patches (lower back), facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), subungual fibromas.
Neuro
Epilepsy (infantile spasms/West syndrome), learning disability, cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA.
Other organs
Renal angiomyolipomas (can bleed), cardiac rhabdomyomas (regress), pulmonary LAM, retinal hamartomas.
Investigations
Clinical criteria + Wood's lamp, MRI brain, renal imaging, echo, EEG, genetic testing (TSC1/2).
Management
No cure → seizure control (vigabatrin for infantile spasms), mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) for SEGA/angiomyolipoma/LAM, multi-organ surveillance, genetic counselling.
NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Foundations of:
Overview — The Neuron & the Action Potential
📷 Image placeholder — the action-potential trace — resting potential, threshold, depolarisation (Na⁺ influx), repolarisation (K⁺ efflux), hyperpolarisation; and saltatory conduction along a myelinated axon (nodes of Ranvier)
The neuron is the signalling unit of the nervous system, and the action potential is the electrical signal it uses to transmit information rapidly over distance.
The organising principle: a neuron maintains a resting membrane potential (a charge difference across its membrane), and an action potential is a brief, all-or-nothing reversal of that charge — driven by sequential opening of Na⁺ then K⁺ channels — that propagates along the axon. Myelination speeds this up dramatically.
Why it matters: underpins demyelinating disease (MS, Guillain-Barré), local anaesthetics, and the basis of all neural signalling, synaptic transmission, and the nerve conduction studies — cross-ref synaptic transmission (what happens at the end), cardiac action potentials (the comparison), MS, Guillain-Barré, local anaesthetics.
The Neuron Structure — form fits function
Part Role
DendritesReceive incoming signals
Cell body (soma)Integrates inputs
AxonConducts the action potential away
Axon terminalReleases neurotransmitter at the synapse (cross-ref)
Myelin sheathInsulation (Schwann cells in PNS, oligodendrocytes in CNS) — speeds conduction
The myelin point (high-yield): Schwann cells myelinate the PNS; oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS → which is why MS (CNS, oligodendrocytes) and Guillain-Barré (PNS, Schwann cells) are different diseases of the same process.
The Resting Membrane Potential — the starting point
At rest, the inside of the neuron is negative relative to the outside (~−70 mV) — maintained by:
Mechanism Role
Na⁺/K⁺ ATPasePumps 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in → sets up the ion gradients (high Na⁺ outside, high K⁺ inside)
K⁺ leak channelsThe membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest → K⁺ leaks out → leaves the inside negative
The key concept: the resting potential is mainly set by K⁺ (the membrane is most permeable to it at rest) → it sits near the K⁺ equilibrium potential. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains the gradients that make this possible.
The hyperkalaemia link: changing extracellular K⁺ alters the resting potential → the basis of K⁺'s effect on excitable tissue (cross-ref cardiac AP/electrolytes).
The Action Potential — the phases (high-yield)
An action potential is a brief, all-or-nothing reversal of the membrane potential, triggered when a stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (~−55 mV):
Phase What happens Ion
Resting−70 mVK⁺ leak (Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains gradients)
DepolarisationStimulus reaches threshold → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → rapid Na⁺ influx → membrane shoots positive (~+30 mV)Na⁺ IN
RepolarisationNa⁺ channels inactivate + voltage-gated K⁺ channels open → K⁺ efflux → membrane returns negativeK⁺ OUT
HyperpolarisationK⁺ channels close slowly → brief overshoot below restingK⁺ (slow closure)
Return to restNa⁺/K⁺ pump restores gradients—
All-or-nothing (the key principle): once threshold is reached, the action potential fires fully — its size doesn't vary; stimulus strength is coded by frequency of firing, not amplitude.
The threshold concept: subthreshold stimuli don't fire; reaching threshold triggers the positive-feedback Na⁺ influx → the all-or-nothing spike.
The Refractory Periods — one-way signalling (high-yield)
Period What Why
Absolute refractory periodNo new AP possible, however strong the stimulusNa⁺ channels are inactivated (can't reopen yet)
Relative refractory periodA stronger-than-normal stimulus can fireSome Na⁺ channels recovered + hyperpolarisation
The functions: ensures the AP propagates one way only (the area behind is refractory) + limits maximum firing frequency + prevents signals merging.
Conduction Along the Axon — propagation + myelin (high-yield)
  • The AP propagates by local depolarisation triggering the adjacent membrane to threshold → a self-propagating wave down the axon
Myelination + saltatory conduction (the key concept)
  • Myelin insulates the axon; the gaps are the nodes of Ranvier (where the Na⁺ channels are concentrated)
  • The AP "jumps" from node to node (saltatory conduction) → dramatically faster + more energy-efficient than continuous conduction
Factors affecting conduction speed: myelination (faster) + axon diameter (larger = faster).
The demyelination link (the major clinical payoff): losing myelin → conduction slows/fails → MS (CNS) and Guillain-Barré (PNS) → neurological deficits; nerve conduction studies measure this — cross-ref.
Clinical Relevance — the payoff
Concept Action potential explanation
Multiple sclerosisCNS demyelination (oligodendrocytes) → slowed/failed conduction → relapsing neurological deficits
Guillain-Barré syndromePNS demyelination (Schwann cells) → ascending weakness; nerve conduction studies show slowing
Local anaesthetics (lidocaine)Block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → prevent depolarisation → no AP → no pain signal (cross-ref pain)
Hyperkalaemia↑extracellular K⁺ alters resting potential → affects excitable tissue (arrhythmias — cross-ref)
Hypocalcaemia↑neuronal excitability → tetany (Ca²⁺ stabilises the membrane)
Nerve conduction studiesMeasure conduction velocity (↓ in demyelination)
MS heat sensitivity (Uhthoff's)Demyelinated nerves fail at higher temperatures
⭐ Key Points
The unit
Neuron signals via the action potential; Schwann cells myelinate PNS, oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS (→ GBS vs MS).
Resting potential (~−70 mV)
Set mainly by K⁺ leak + maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in).
AP phases
Stimulus → threshold → Na⁺ in (depolarise) → K⁺ out (repolarise) → hyperpolarise → rest; all-or-nothing (strength coded by frequency).
Refractory periods
Absolute (Na⁺ inactivated) ensures one-way propagation + limits firing rate.
Saltatory conduction
AP jumps node-to-node along myelinated axons → fast + efficient; speed ↑ with myelination + axon diameter.
Clinical
Demyelination (MS = CNS, GBS = PNS) → slowed conduction → deficits; local anaesthetics block Na⁺ channels.
Overview — Synaptic Transmission & Neurotransmitters
When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, the signal must cross to the next cell — at most synapses this happens chemically, via neurotransmitter release.
The organising principle: the electrical signal (AP) triggers Ca²⁺-dependent neurotransmitter release → the transmitter crosses the synaptic cleft → binds receptors on the next cell → produces an excitatory or inhibitory effect. The specific neurotransmitter + receptor determines the effect — and most neuro/psychiatric drugs act here.
Why it matters: underpins the neuromuscular junction (myasthenia gravis), Parkinson's, the psychiatric drugs (SSRIs, antipsychotics), benzodiazepines, and the movement disorders — cross-ref the neuron/action potential (the arriving signal), motor pathways/basal ganglia (dopamine), the autonomic NS (ACh/noradrenaline), Parkinson's, myasthenia gravis.
The Steps of Synaptic Transmission — the sequence
Step What happens
1. AP arrivesThe action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal
2. Ca²⁺ influxDepolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → Ca²⁺ enters the terminal
3. Vesicle fusionCa²⁺ triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse + release neurotransmitter into the cleft (exocytosis)
4. Receptor bindingTransmitter diffuses across the cleft → binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
5. Postsynaptic effectExcitatory (depolarise) or inhibitory (hyperpolarise)
6. TerminationTransmitter removed — reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion
The Ca²⁺ point (high-yield): calcium influx is the trigger for neurotransmitter release → which is why Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies vs presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels) impairs ACh release → weakness.
Excitatory vs Inhibitory — the two effects (core concept)
Excitatory Inhibitory
EffectDepolarises the postsynaptic cell (toward threshold) → EPSPHyperpolarises (away from threshold) → IPSP
Main transmitterGlutamate (the main excitatory CNS transmitter)GABA (main inhibitory in brain), glycine (spinal cord)
Summation: a single EPSP usually isn't enough — the postsynaptic cell sums many inputs (spatial + temporal summation) → fires an AP only if the net reaches threshold → this integration is how neurons "compute".
The GABA point (high-yield): GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter → benzodiazepines + alcohol + barbiturates enhance GABA (→ sedation, anxiolysis); anti-epileptics often boost inhibition or reduce excitation.

Receptor Types — ionotropic vs metabotropic
Type Mechanism Speed
Ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels)Transmitter opens an ion channel directlyFast (e.g. nicotinic ACh at the NMJ, GABA-A)
Metabotropic (G-protein-coupled)Transmitter triggers an intracellular cascadeSlower, longer (e.g. muscarinic ACh, most dopamine/serotonin receptors)
The relevance: fast transmission (NMJ, reflexes) uses ionotropic receptors; modulatory/mood effects use metabotropic — and the receptor subtype determines drug specificity.
The Neuromuscular Junction — the high-yield specific synapse
  • The synapse between motor neuron and skeletal muscle — a clinically critical, drug-rich example:
    • AP → Ca²⁺ influx → ACh release → binds nicotinic ACh receptors on the muscle → depolarises → muscle contraction
    • ACh is broken down by acetylcholinesterase (terminates the signal)

Overview — Motor Pathways
📷 Image placeholder — the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract — two-neuron relay with decussation at the medulla; and a UMN-vs-LMN sign comparison
Motor pathways carry the command for movement from the brain to the muscles — and understanding them is the key to localising neurological lesions (the most examined skill in clinical neurology).
The organising principle: voluntary movement travels down the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract via a two-neuron relay — upper motor neuron (UMN) then lower motor neuron (LMN) — and the single most important clinical distinction is UMN vs LMN signs, because where the lesion is determines the pattern. Modulatory systems (basal ganglia, cerebellum) fine-tune this — covered in their own subtabs.
Why it matters: underpins stroke, spinal cord lesions, motor neuron disease, Bell's palsy, and the entire UMN/LMN localisation framework — cross-ref the neuron/AP, synaptic transmission (NMJ), basal ganglia + cerebellum (the modulators — separate subtabs), sensory pathways (the partner), stroke, MND, cord lesions.
The Descending Tracts — pyramidal vs extrapyramidal
Motor output travels via two systems:
System Tracts Function
PyramidalCorticospinal (body) + corticobulbar (face/head)Voluntary movement — the main motor pathway
ExtrapyramidalRubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, tectospinalMuscle tone, posture, involuntary/automatic movement
The pyramidal tracts are the main voluntary motor pathway; the extrapyramidal tracts modulate tone and posture (and the basal ganglia influence movement via these).
The Corticospinal Tract — the two-neuron relay (core)
The pathway for voluntary movement, the two-neuron relay that's central to localisation:
Neuron Path
Upper motor neuron (UMN)Motor cortex → internal capsule → brainstem → decussates (crosses) in the medulla → descends the spinal cord → synapses on the LMN in the anterior horn
Lower motor neuron (LMN)Anterior horn → peripheral nerve → neuromuscular junction → muscle
The decussation point (high-yield): most corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla (the pyramidal decussation) → so one side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body → a left cortical/internal capsule lesion (e.g. stroke) → right-sided weakness.
The relay logic: UMN (brain → cord) → LMN (cord → muscle); a lesion anywhere along this determines whether you get UMN or LMN signs (next section).
UMN vs LMN Signs — the key clinical distinction (high-yield)
The core localisation framework — the pattern of signs tells you whether the lesion is in the UMN (brain/cord) or LMN (anterior horn/peripheral nerve):
Feature UMN lesion LMN lesion
Tone↑ (spasticity)↓ (flaccid)
Reflexes↑ (hyperreflexia) + clonus↓/absent
Plantar responseUpgoing (Babinski +ve)Downgoing/absent
PowerWeaknessWeakness
WastingMinimal (disuse only)Marked (atrophy)
FasciculationsAbsentPresent
The logic: the LMN is the "final common pathway" to the muscle → losing it → flaccid, wasted, areflexic (no signal reaches the muscle); losing the UMN → removes the brain's inhibition of the cord reflexes → spastic, hyperreflexic, upgoing plantar (the cord runs unrestrained).
The memory anchor: UMN = everything UP (tone ↑, reflexes ↑, plantar up); LMN = everything DOWN (tone ↓, reflexes ↓) + wasting + fasciculations.
The localisation payoff: UMN signs → lesion is in the brain or spinal cord (above the anterior horn); LMN signs → anterior horn, root, or peripheral nerve.
Localising by the Pattern — applying it (high-yield)
Lesion site Pattern
Cortex/internal capsule (stroke)Contralateral UMN signs (face + arm + leg, depending on territory)
Spinal cordUMN signs below the level + LMN signs at the level (anterior horn) + a sensory level
Anterior horn (e.g. polio)Pure LMN signs
Peripheral nerveLMN signs in that nerve's distribution
Motor neuron disease (MND)Mixed UMN + LMN signs (degenerates both — the classic clue)
Bell's palsyLMN facial weakness (forehead involved) vs UMN facial (forehead spared — bilateral cortical input)
The MND point (high-yield): MND causes both UMN and LMN signs together (e.g. wasted, fasciculating limb with brisk reflexes) — the combination is the diagnostic clue.
The facial nerve point (high-yield): UMN facial lesion spares the forehead (the forehead gets bilateral cortical input); LMN (Bell's palsy) affects the whole side including the forehead.
Modulating Systems — cross-ref their own subtabs
  • Voluntary movement is fine-tuned by two modulatory systems (each its own subtab):
    • Basal ganglia: initiate/inhibit movement, set muscle tone → lesions = movement disorders (Parkinson's, Huntington's) — cross-ref
    • Cerebellum: coordination, balance, motor learning → lesions = ataxia, incoordination — cross-ref
The distinction: pyramidal lesions → weakness + UMN/LMN signs; basal ganglia → movement disorders (too much/little movement, tone); cerebellar → incoordination (ataxia) — three different "flavours" of motor problem.
Clinical Relevance — the payoff
Concept Motor pathway explanation
StrokeUMN lesion → contralateral spastic weakness (cortex/internal capsule)
Spinal cord lesionUMN below + LMN at the level + sensory level (cross-ref sensory pathways)
Motor neuron diseaseMixed UMN + LMN signs (degenerates both)
Bell's palsy vs UMN facialLMN = forehead affected; UMN = forehead spared
Peripheral neuropathyLMN signs (flaccid, areflexic, wasting)

⭐ Key Points
Two systems
Pyramidal (corticospinal/corticobulbar) = voluntary movement; extrapyramidal = tone/posture.
The relay
Corticospinal tract = two-neuron relay: UMN (cortex → decussates in medulla → cord) → LMN (anterior horn → muscle); decussation → one side of brain controls opposite side of body.
UMN vs LMN (the key distinction)
UMN = ↑tone, ↑reflexes, upgoing plantar, clonus, no wasting; LMN = ↓tone, ↓reflexes, wasting, fasciculations ("UMN up, LMN down + wasting").
Localisation
UMN signs = brain/cord; LMN signs = anterior horn/nerve; MND = mixed UMN + LMN.
Facial nerve
UMN spares the forehead, LMN (Bell's) affects it.
Modulators (own subtabs)
Basal ganglia (movement disorders/tone), cerebellum (ataxia/coordination).
Overview — Sensory Pathways
📷 Image placeholder — the two sensory pathways — DCML (fine touch/proprioception, decussates in the medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain/temperature, decussates at the cord); with Brown-Séquard hemisection and the sensory homunculus
Sensory pathways carry information from the body up to the brain — and like the motor system, understanding them is key to localising lesions (where the sensory loss is, and what type, tells you where the problem is).
The organising principle: there are two main ascending pathways carrying different modalities — the dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) for fine touch/vibration/proprioception, and the spinothalamic tract for pain/temperature/crude touch. The crucial difference is where each crosses the midline, which explains the dissociated sensory patterns (especially Brown-Séquard).
Why it matters: underpins sensory level localisation, Brown-Séquard syndrome, dorsal column signs (B12 deficiency, tabes), and dissociated sensory loss — cross-ref motor pathways (the partner), the neuron/AP, B12 deficiency, spinal cord lesions, pain physiology.
The Two Pathways — the core distinction
Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscus (DCML) Spinothalamic Tract
ModalitiesFine touch, vibration, proprioception (+ two-point discrimination)Pain, temperature, crude touch
Where it crosses (decussates)In the medulla (high up — ascends first, then crosses)In the spinal cord (at/near the level of entry — crosses immediately)
Fibre typeLarge, myelinated (fast)Small (slower)
The single most important point (high-yield): the two pathways cross at different levels — DCML crosses high (in the medulla), spinothalamic crosses low (in the cord, near entry) → this is the key to understanding dissociated sensory loss and Brown-Séquard.
The DCML Pathway — fine touch/proprioception
The three-neuron relay (the pattern for sensory pathways):
  • 1st neuron: peripheral receptor → enters the cord → ascends the dorsal columns on the same side → synapses in the medulla
  • 2nd neuron: crosses (decussates) in the medulla → ascends as the medial lemniscus → thalamus
  • 3rd neuron: thalamus → sensory cortex
The key feature: DCML fibres ascend ipsilaterally first, then cross in the medulla → so a cord lesion affects DCML on the same side as the lesion (below it).
The dorsal column point (high-yield): B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) + tabes dorsalis (syphilis) damage the dorsal columns → loss of vibration + proprioception (→ sensory ataxia, positive Romberg).
The Spinothalamic Tract — pain/temperature
The three-neuron relay:
  • 1st neuron: receptor → enters the cord → synapses immediately (in the dorsal horn)
  • 2nd neuron: crosses (decussates) within the cord (within a segment or two of entry) → ascends the contralateral spinothalamic tract → thalamus
  • 3rd neuron: thalamus → sensory cortex
The key feature: spinothalamic fibres cross almost immediately → so a cord lesion affects pain/temperature on the opposite side (below the lesion).
Brown-Séquard Syndrome — the classic application (high-yield)
Brown-Séquard = hemisection (one half) of the spinal cord → produces a characteristic dissociated, split-sided pattern that's entirely explained by where each pathway crosses:
Deficit Side Why
Motor (UMN) weaknessIpsilateral (same side, below)Corticospinal tract already crossed in the medulla (cross-ref motor)
Fine touch/vibration/proprioception loss (DCML)Ipsilateral (same side, below)DCML hasn't crossed yet (crosses in the medulla, above the lesion)
Pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic)Contralateral (opposite side, below)Spinothalamic already crossed in the cord (below the lesion)
The logic (the whole point): because DCML crosses high and spinothalamic crosses low, a cord hemisection gives ipsilateral motor + fine touch/proprioception loss but contralateral pain/temperature loss → the classic dissociated picture. This is the reason the crossing levels matter.
(You don't need to memorise Brown-Séquard as a list — derive it from the two crossing points.)
Other Sensory Patterns — localising by pattern (high-yield)
Pattern Cause
Sensory level (loss below a dermatome)Spinal cord lesion (transection) — both pathways lost below
Dissociated sensory lossSelective pathway damage (e.g. syringomyelia = central cord → loss of pain/temp, sparing fine touch — "cape" distribution)
Dorsal column loss (vibration/proprioception)B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis → sensory ataxia, +ve Romberg
Glove-and-stockingPeripheral neuropathy (diabetes) — distal, length-dependent
DermatomalNerve root lesion (e.g. shingles, radiculopathy)
The Romberg sign (high-yield): dorsal column (proprioception) loss → unsteady with eyes closed (Romberg +ve) — because they rely on vision to compensate; distinguishes sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia (which is unsteady eyes open or closed).
The Sensory Cortex — the homunculus
  • Sensory information arrives at the primary sensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), organised as a homunculus (body map — disproportionate areas for hands/face)
  • Cortical lesions → contralateral sensory loss + higher-order deficits (e.g. neglect, astereognosis)
Clinical Relevance — the payoff
Concept Sensory pathway explanation

B12 deficiency (SACD)Dorsal column degeneration → ↓vibration/proprioception → sensory ataxia, +ve Romberg (+ cord UMN signs)
SyringomyeliaCentral cord → dissociated loss (pain/temp lost, fine touch spared) — "cape"

Tabes dorsalisDorsal column (neurosyphilis) → sensory ataxia
Peripheral neuropathyGlove-and-stocking (diabetes, B12)
Romberg signDorsal column/proprioceptive loss (worse eyes closed)
⭐ Key Points
Two pathways
DCML (fine touch, vibration, proprioception) vs spinothalamic (pain, temperature, crude touch).
The key difference — where they cross
DCML crosses HIGH (medulla) — ascends ipsilaterally first; spinothalamic crosses LOW (in the cord, near entry).
Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection)
Ipsilateral motor (UMN) + DCML loss (haven't crossed); contralateral pain/temp loss (already crossed) — derive it from the crossing levels.
Dorsal column loss
Vibration/proprioception = B12 deficiency (SACD), tabes → sensory ataxia, +ve Romberg.
Patterns
Sensory level (cord), dissociated (syringomyelia), glove-and-stocking (peripheral neuropathy), dermatomal (root).
Relay & cortex
Three-neuron relay; sensory cortex = postcentral gyrus (homunculus).
Overview — The Autonomic Nervous System
📷 Image placeholder — sympathetic vs parasympathetic outflow — the two-neuron layout, ganglia positions and ACh/noradrenaline transmitters at each synapse
The autonomic nervous system (ANS) controls the body's involuntary functions — heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, glands, pupils, bladder — running automatically in the background.
The organising principle: the ANS has two opposing divisions — sympathetic ("fight or flight") and parasympathetic ("rest and digest") — that work in balance, acting via specific neurotransmitters (ACh, noradrenaline) and receptors (adrenergic, cholinergic). Knowing the receptors is the key that unlocks a huge swathe of pharmacology.
Why it matters: underpins beta-blockers, anticholinergics, inotropes/vasopressors, bronchodilators, Horner's syndrome, and autonomic neuropathy — cross-ref BP regulation (baroreceptor/sympathetic), cardiac AP (autonomic control of heart rate), the limbic system (fight-or-flight), GI motility, the relevant clinical pharmacology.
The Two Divisions — opposing systems
Sympathetic ("fight or flight") Parasympathetic ("rest and digest")
Overall roleMobilises the body for stress/activityConserves energy, restores calm
OriginThoracolumbar (T1–L2 spinal cord)Craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X; sacral S2–4)
Heart↑rate + contractility↓rate
LungsBronchodilationBronchoconstriction
PupilsDilate (mydriasis)Constrict (miosis)
Gut↓motility/secretion↑motility/secretion (digestion)
Other↑glucose, sweating, vasoconstriction↑secretions, bladder emptying
The vagus point (high-yield): the vagus nerve (CN X) carries most parasympathetic output to the heart, lungs, and gut → "vagal tone" slows the heart (cross-ref cardiac AP — why atropine speeds the heart).
The Neurotransmitters & Two-Neuron Layout — the wiring
Both divisions use a two-neuron relay (preganglionic → ganglion → postganglionic → target):
Preganglionic transmitter Postganglionic transmitter
SympatheticACh (nicotinic)Noradrenaline (mostly) — acts on adrenergic receptors
ParasympatheticACh (nicotinic)ACh — acts on muscarinic receptors
The key exceptions (high-yield):
  • Adrenal medulla: sympathetic preganglionic fibres go straight to it → it releases adrenaline into the blood (a modified ganglion — cross-ref adrenal)
  • Sweat glands: sympathetic but use ACh (muscarinic) — the exception to "sympathetic = noradrenaline"
The unifying point: all preganglionic fibres + all parasympathetic + sweat glands = ACh; most sympathetic postganglionic = noradrenaline → this determines which receptors (and drugs) act where.
The Receptors — the pharmacology key (high-yield)
The receptor subtypes are the high-yield content — they're the targets of much of clinical pharmacology:

β2 (adrenergic)Bronchodilation, vasodilation, uterine relaxationβ2-agonists (salbutamol — asthma)
Muscarinic (M, cholinergic)Parasympathetic effects (↓HR, ↑secretions, ↑gut, miosis, bladder)Antimuscarinics (atropine, ipratropium, oxybutynin); muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine)

The drug-mapping payoff (the whole point): knowing the receptors makes the pharmacology derivable:
  • β1 in the heart → β-blockers slow it (angina, HTN, arrhythmia); β2 in lungs → salbutamol dilates airways (asthma)
  • Muscarinic → atropine blocks it (↑HR, dries secretions); ipratropium (bronchodilator); oxybutynin (bladder)
  • α1 → vasoconstriction → α-blockers for BPH/HTN; α-agonists as vasopressors

Overview — Reflexes
A reflex is an automatic, involuntary motor response to a stimulus — fast, stereotyped, and not requiring conscious thought (often not even the brain).
The organising principle: reflexes work through a reflex arc (the basic circuit: sensor → spinal cord → effector), and crucially they're modulated by the brain — which is why reflexes change in UMN vs LMN lesions (the link to the motor pathways note). Testing reflexes is a window into the integrity of that whole circuit.
Why it matters: underpins reflex testing, the UMN/LMN reflex changes, clonus, and reflex-based clinical signs (Babinski, etc.) — cross-ref motor pathways (UMN/LMN), sensory pathways (the afferent limb), the neuron/AP, spinal cord lesions.
The Reflex Arc — the basic circuit
Every reflex has the same components:
Component Role
ReceptorDetects the stimulus (e.g. muscle stretch)
Afferent (sensory) neuronCarries the signal to the spinal cord
Integration centreThe spinal cord (± interneurons) — processes the signal
Efferent (motor) neuronCarries the response from the cord to the muscle (the LMN)
EffectorThe muscle that responds
The key concept: a reflex can occur at the spinal cord level without involving the brain (which is why it's fast + automatic) — but the brain normally modulates (dampens) it from above → this modulation is what's lost in UMN lesions (see below).
The Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex — the classic example (high-yield)
  • The knee-jerk is the model reflex — a monosynaptic stretch reflex:
    • Tendon tap → stretches the muscle → activates the muscle spindle (stretch receptor) → afferent neuron → spinal cord → directly synapses on the LMN (monosynaptic) → muscle contracts (the jerk)
    • Simultaneously, the antagonist muscle is inhibited (reciprocal inhibition, via an interneuron)
The function: the stretch reflex maintains muscle tone + posture (resists unexpected stretch). It's monosynaptic (one synapse, afferent → efferent) → which is why it's so fast.
Reflexes in UMN vs LMN Lesions — the clinical payoff (high-yield)
This is the reason reflexes are tested — they change characteristically depending on where the lesion is (cross-ref motor pathways):
UMN lesion LMN lesion
Reflexes↑ (hyperreflexia) + clonus↓/absent (hyporeflexia)
WhyLoss of the brain's descending inhibition → the spinal reflex arc runs unrestrainedThe reflex arc itself is broken (the efferent LMN is damaged)
The logic (the key insight): the brain normally dampens spinal reflexes from above. A UMN lesion removes that brake → reflexes become brisk (hyperreflexia) + clonus; an LMN lesion breaks the arc itself → reflexes are lost → so reflexes localise the lesion.
Clonus: rhythmic involuntary muscle contractions (e.g. at the ankle) — a sign of UMN lesion (the unrestrained, repetitive stretch reflex).
Other Clinically Important Reflexes
Reflex Significance
Plantar (Babinski)Normal = toes down; upgoing (Babinski +ve) = UMN lesion (cross-ref motor pathways)
Tendon reflexes (biceps, triceps, knee, ankle)Test specific nerve roots (e.g. knee = L3/4, ankle = S1) → localise root lesions
Withdrawal (flexor) reflexPolysynaptic — pull away from a painful stimulus (protective)
Pupillary light reflexTests CN II (afferent) + CN III (efferent) — brainstem integrity
Primitive reflexesNormal in infants (Moro, grasp, rooting); reappearance in adults = frontal/diffuse brain pathology
The root-localising point: each tendon reflex tests specific nerve roots → an absent reflex localises a root/peripheral lesion (e.g. absent ankle jerk = S1).
Clinical Relevance — the payoff
Concept Reflex explanation
Hyperreflexia + clonusUMN lesion (loss of descending inhibition) — stroke, cord lesion, MS
Hyporeflexia/areflexiaLMN lesion (broken arc) — peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy, Guillain-Barré
Babinski signUpgoing plantar = UMN lesion
Absent specific reflexLocalises a nerve root (knee = L3/4, ankle = S1)
Mixed (↑ + ↓ reflexes)MND (UMN + LMN) — cross-ref motor pathways
Pupillary light reflexCN II/III + brainstem (used in coma/brainstem assessment)

Receptor → afferent neuron → spinal cord → efferent (LMN) → effector; can occur at the cord without the brain, but the brain modulates (dampens) it.

LMN lesion
